The **Past Meets the Present** feature boxes help you connect the chapter to today.  
They ask you to look for links between past events and the modern world.  
They also ask why a historical issue still matters now.

This book is a global history.  
We try to respect world cultures.  
We do this by writing people’s names as close as possible to their original language.  
Experts made these spelling choices using current research.

For example, we use the **pinyin** system for Chinese names.  
We do not use the older **Wade-Giles** system.  
We use pinyin because the People’s Republic of China adopted it.  
Pinyin also matches Mandarin sounds more closely.

For languages that use the Latin alphabet, we keep accent marks in names.  
Examples include **Hernán Cortés** and **Napoléon Bonaparte**.  
For names transliterated from languages like Chinese and Arabic, we avoid accents and apostrophes when possible.  
We only use them when they help pronunciation and make the text easier to read.

For events, places, and other historical terms, we usually use the most common English form.  
We give dates using the **Gregorian calendar**, which is the international standard for civil calendars.  
We use **BCE** for dates before the Common Era.  
We use **CE** for dates in the Common Era.

To study world history, you also need strong geography skills.  
You might think maps are simple and factual.  
After all, maps show where things are.  
But for most of history, maps were not objective.

Maps are often debated as historical evidence.  
This is because mapmakers usually showed the world from their own point of view.  
Many civilizations placed themselves at the center of the known world.

Maps have also been used to support conquest and control.  
During the Age of Exploration, the Pope divided inhabited lands that were new to Europeans.  
He then granted these lands to Spain and Portugal.  
Centuries later, in Berlin, Germany, European diplomats drew borders on a map of Africa.  
They used these lines to divide territory among colonial powers.

History might look different if the surviving maps were made by Indigenous peoples.  
Even after people learned more about the size of the world, maps still had errors.  
Many maps showed Europe as larger than it is.  
They often showed parts of the Global South as smaller than they are.  
This includes Latin America, Africa, and parts of Asia and Oceania.

Maps can also be difficult because some places are claimed by more than one government.  
This happened in the past and still happens today.  
Examples include **Crimea** and **Taiwan**.

Crimea is claimed by both Russia and Ukraine.  
Taiwan claims independence.  
China considers Taiwan part of its territory.

This text will point out these contested regions when they appear.  
This will help you explore the complexities of geography.

chapter_key: How Farming Changed the Human Experience
text:
The example of the Indigenous people of Australia shows that not everyone adopted agriculture when they encountered it. This can seem strange today. Our world depends on agriculture. But we are far removed from the difficult changes many ancestors faced.

One major change was the loss of leisure time. Researchers who study modern hunter-gatherers find that they often need about 20 hours per week to get enough food. Similar farming societies spend 30 hours or more each week on farm work. This leaves less time for rest, sharing knowledge, and enjoyable activities. These studies also show that women lost the most leisure time. Women in farming societies often did more hard labor than hunter-gatherer women in similar environments.

Large farming communities also faced new risks. They were more vulnerable to epidemic diseases. This was common in places where large amounts of human and animal waste built up. Farmers also depended more on the weather. Crops needed enough water, but not too much. Unlike hunter-gatherers, farmers could not easily move to better climates.

Farmers also ate a less varied diet. Many relied on one or two staple crops, usually starchy carbohydrates. Farmers did have domesticated animals. But Neolithic communities ate much less meat than hunter-gatherers. Depending on a narrow range of foods could cause vitamin and mineral deficiencies.

Agriculture also brought clear advantages. It supported much larger populations. More people meant more workers to produce food. It also meant more defenders for the settlement. When agriculture worked well, it produced a steady food supply. It could also create a surplus that could be stored.

As humans began leaving hunter-gatherer life around 12,000 years ago, they also moved away from the egalitarianism that life often supported. Agriculture required specialization in a way hunting and gathering did not. A family farming wheat, for example, had to focus on that work and related chores. This left little time for the wide range of tasks common in hunter-gatherer life.

As farming became more advanced, some farmers produced large surpluses. Tools like plows helped. Domesticated animals could pull those plows. Successful farmers could then build wealth through land and property. They could pass this wealth and status to their descendants. This strengthened social divisions between the wealthy and everyone else. When food was plentiful, not everyone had to farm. Some people became artisans or traders. They could generate even more wealth.

Some people specialized so much that they no longer focused on food production at all. They became traders, stoneworkers, religious leaders, and other elites. Those with great wealth could become leaders. They could command armies and make rules. Those without wealth faced hard labor if they were lucky. If they were not lucky, they could face bondage.

Agriculture also created new social divisions based on sex. In many hunter-gatherer societies, women commonly gathered and men commonly hunted. In many farming societies, men typically worked in the fields. The need for strength to control the plow likely helped drive this change. Women were pushed more into domestic work. They prepared food, made pottery, and wove cloth. Because men were less tied to the home, they had more chances for leadership. They also had duties women usually did not, including dangerous work like fighting and dying to defend the settlement.

In the home, women did difficult and time-consuming work like milling grain. At first, people used mortars and pestles. As farming output grew, larger stone tools were used. Using these mills meant long hours kneeling and bending over millstones. In the home, wool from domesticated sheep was also spun into thread and woven into cloth. These tasks came on top of giving birth, raising children, and preparing food.

Agriculture also strongly shaped religion. Greater division of labor and specialization allowed priestly classes to form in many places. These religious elites gained authority by claiming they could interpret the supernatural world. This ability was highly valued. As a result, they could control resources and labor. People used these resources to build elaborate monuments and perform carefully organized rituals.

Religions also became more complex and changed in character. Pre-agricultural societies often practiced forms of animism. They saw spiritual meaning in many ordinary things and animals. They often tried to connect with the supernatural through shamanic and other rituals. Societies shaped by the Neolithic Revolution developed a stronger focus on agricultural fertility. They emphasized deities who could help humans by supporting fertility and maintaining the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.

Like the people of Mesopotamia, Ancient Egyptians were polytheists.  
They worshipped many gods.  
These gods controlled the forces of nature.

Re was the god of the sun.  
Isis was the earth goddess of fertility.  
Osiris was linked to the Nile.

The most important event of the Egyptian year was the Nile’s yearly flood.  
Egyptians explained this flood with the myth of Osiris.

In the myth, Osiris was murdered by his brother Seth.  
Seth was the god of the desert wind.  
Osiris was then brought back to life by his loyal wife, Isis.

This story matched what people saw in nature.

text:
The end of the third millennium BCE was a major turning point in Mesopotamia. It was often chaotic.

Invaders came from the north, east, and west. They put heavy pressure on the rulers of the Third Dynasty of Ur. This was the last Sumerian dynasty.

One of the biggest threats came from nomadic peoples in the deserts of Syria. These people were the Amorites. Their raids were seen as a serious problem.

Around 2034 BCE, Shu-Sin ruled Ur. He built a wall to keep the Amorites out. The wall was about 170 miles long. It ran from the Euphrates River to the Tigris River.

The plan did not work. During the reign of Shu-Sin’s son, Ibbi-Sin, the Amorites broke through the wall. They began attacking cities.

Soon, the Elamites joined the attacks from the east. Raids by the Amorites and Elamites grew more frequent. They also became more intense.

City after city fell. The Third Dynasty of Ur collapsed. By about 2004 BCE, Ibbi-Sin’s empire had shrunk to just one city: Ur.

In 2004 BCE, Ur was also attacked. The Elamites and others sacked the city.

After this, the Amorites spread across Mesopotamia. They founded powerful cities of their own.

They adopted local religious traditions. They also adopted local customs. They used the Akkadian language.

They also accepted the region’s political culture of rivalry. Two Amorite cities became especially important: Isin and Larsa. These cities fought for supremacy.

This struggle for dominance encouraged innovation and expansion. It was similar to the innovation and expansion that had once characterized Ur, the first city.

## The Yayoi Period: Farming and New Society

The next phase of Japan’s prehistory is the move into agriculture.  
This period is called the **Yayoi**.  
It is named after a different people and culture.

### New migrants and new crops
Around **300 BCE**, new migrants arrived.  
They came from groups in **northern Asia**.  
They landed first on **Kyushu**, Japan’s southern island.

They brought farming knowledge.  
They grew **barley** and **buckwheat**.  
Later, they also grew **rice**.

Over time, the Yayoi **overwhelmed and replaced** the **Jōmon**.

### Farming technology and growth
The Yayoi built large **storehouses** for grain.  
They also domesticated **horses** and **dogs**.

As Yayoi culture spread, people changed the land for farming.  
They built **irrigation canals**.  
They dug **wells** and **pits**.

Agriculture brought more stability.  
It also brought population growth.  
By the first centuries of the common era, the Yayoi population may have reached **more than 500,000**.

## More contact with Korea and China
The Yayoi period was a major turning point.  
From this time on, **Korea, China, and Japan** had more regular contact.

One reason was bronze.  
Japan had little **copper**.  
So the Yayoi had to **import** much of it.

This period also begins the **written record** of Japan.

## Trade and the first written descriptions
The **Han** conquered areas and built garrisons on the **Korean peninsula**.  
This helped start trade and exchange.

Through Korea, Japan received:  
- **bronze mirrors**  
- **iron weapons**  
- new **agricultural practices**

The **Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE)** sent envoys to Japan at times.  
Later, the kingdom of **Cao Wei (220–265 CE)** also sent envoys.  
The Han called Japan the **Wa kingdom**.

These envoys wrote the first records about Yayoi life.  
They described slow changes in society and politics.

## From communal life to conflict and states
At first, Yayoi communities were mostly communal.  
People shared **wooden tools** and **public spaces**.

Over time, some places became more valuable for farming.  
This led to competition.  
Competition led to more warfare.

As warfare increased, **states** began to form.  
These states helped organize **defense**.

## Dual rule and Queen Himiko
Chinese records describe a special kind of government.  
Power was shared between **male and female rulers**.  
This appeared in early Japanese states near the end of the Yayoi era.

A famous ruler was **Queen Himiko**.  
She ruled in the **early third century**.

Himiko paid **tribute** to the Chinese emperor.  
In return, China recognized her as an ally.  
She received a **golden seal**.

Himiko ruled with her **younger brother**.  
He managed the administration of her realm.

Cao Wei records say Himiko fought a neighboring king.  
They also say she supported her rule through spiritual authority.  
This included **elaborate burials**, **divination**, and other sacred rituals.

Through this kind of specialization, women held political power.  
This may connect to Jōmon traditions.  
Jōmon **dogu** figurines showed women as deities.  
These deities were linked to fertility and safety.

## A more stratified society and body art
Chinese envoys also described a more stratified society.  
It included:  
- **aristocratic families**  
- **merchants**  
- skilled **divers and fishers**  
- **farmers**  
- other commoners

Warfare was constant.  
Palaces often looked like **garrisons**.

Even so, **granaries** and **markets** were busy and full.

These early Japanese did not yet have a written script.  
But the Yayoi used another kind of “writing.”  
They tattooed patterns on their bodies.  
These tattoos showed **rank**, **status**, and **family**.

They dug wells and storage pits.

Early Yayoi villages were often shared communities.

text:
Records from Queen Himiko’s time show that political power was becoming more concentrated. Control over land was shifting toward a loose confederation of states and powerful families.

This time is called the Yamato era. It was known for building tombs for dead royals, including Himiko. These tombs held many treasures. They also included human sacrifices meant to accompany the dead into the afterlife.

The Yamato era may have begun during a time of climate change and constant turmoil in Japan. Many people lost faith in older deities. They felt these gods had failed to protect them. New gods then rose in importance. These were linked to imported technology, especially mirrors from China and Korea.

Powerful rulers and a new military class, shaped by warfare, connected themselves to these new gods. More importantly, they linked themselves to Amaterasu, the female Sun goddess. Amaterasu soon became the ancestral figurehead of the imperial household.

Yamato kings gained more power in several ways. They brokered alliances. They managed trade. They gave symbolic gifts. They led ceremonies meant to create a shared culture across Japan.

Women still held political influence. They served as co-rulers of kingdoms or as heads of households. They used knowledge of sorcery, often through items like mirrors. They also displayed success through gold jewelry and earrings.

Many spiritual practices came from earlier Chinese dynasties, including the Shang dynasty. During Queen Himiko’s burial, Chinese envoys reported a practice of divination. People heated bones and read the cracks. They used this to predict harvests and the outcomes of wars.

Other burial practices were native to Japan. One example was water purification. These practices later shaped religions such as Shintoism.

Later, new foreign religions also arrived, including Buddhism. Women used these religions in politics. Empress Suiko is one example. She ruled in the early seventh century CE. She tried to preserve women’s political role through piety, serious study of sutras, and building shrines and temples.

Large keyhole-shaped tombs became especially important. Control over burial rituals helped Yamato rulers dominate a wide region. Their power stretched from western Honshu to northern Kyushu.

Building these tombs required many workers and skilled artisans, including blacksmiths. The tombs showed Yamato wealth and strong organization. Yamato leaders later used these skills to build capital cities. These cities had large markets and highways leading to the countryside and coastal ports.

To centralize power, kings began issuing law codes. One major example was Prince Shotoku’s Seventeen Article Constitution in 604. This document emphasized law as the basis of rule. It supported building a bureaucracy to help rulers govern. It also included Confucian values. These features show how much the Yamato drew on Chinese culture for ideas and inspiration.

The Yamato also borrowed Chinese models of imperial statecraft. They strengthened rule through mythology and bejeweled regalia. They raised kings to godlike status. Over time, these kings were transformed into emperors.

Later law codes continued this process. The Kiyomihara Codes of 689 organized monasteries. They created a judiciary. They also managed relations between the king’s advisors and vassals. These changes helped shape Japan’s culture and political system in the later Nara and Heian periods.

North of Yamato lands lived another group. They descended from early Jōmon foragers. These people had lived through, and resisted, the spread of Yayoi settled agriculture. They continued to forage and hunt. They kept their own spiritual beliefs.

They rejected the Yamato cultural sphere. They also rejected Yamato borrowings from China. This included Buddhism, Confucianism, and the idea of large states ruled by kings and emperors.

Later, the imperial courts in Nara and Heian built stronger ties with China’s Tang dynasty. The northern people followed a different path. Their world was shaped by contact with smaller northern Asian cultures. One example was the Satsumon people of Hokkaido.

Over time, relations between north and south worsened. Nara and Heian leaders called the northerners Emishi, meaning “barbarians.” The Emishi survived from the seventh to the eleventh century. They endured repeated efforts by southern emperors and militarists to subjugate them.

They resisted through war. They moved into remote areas. They also used other forms of evasion. Still, southern Japanese culture steadily moved north. By the end of the ninth century, the remaining Emishi groups were subdued.

Religious life in Rome was varied and diverse. In the first century CE, Christians became part of this landscape. Their relationship with traditional Roman religion was often tense.

At first, Christians were not one unified group. Still, they often stood out. They were generally unwilling to take part in some traditional Roman rituals.

Christians usually disapproved of animal sacrifice. They also rejected worship of the emperor. Instead, they focused on prayer. They met in house churches. Purpose-built churches and basilicas appeared in Rome only in the late third and fourth centuries.

Meeting together for worship mattered. It helped Christians form a shared community identity. Christians also held communal meals. They called each other “brother” and “sister.” They also practiced baptism.

Baptism was an initiation ritual. It varied across the empire. It focused on cleansing the spirit. It was performed by church leaders, especially bishops or deacons.

Roman officials were often less worried about Christian beliefs. They were more concerned about Christian practices. Officials saw these practices as a challenge to Roman authority.

For example, officials called Christians “atheists.” They did this because Christians refused to perform animal sacrifice. At times, Christians were singled out for punishment.

The earliest record of this violence comes from the reign of Nero. In 64 CE, a fire broke out in Rome. Nero chose to punish Christians for the fire.

Over the next two centuries, local authorities struggled with how to handle Christian groups. One example comes from Pliny the Younger. He was a provincial governor in Asia Minor in the early second century. He wrote letters to Emperor Trajan asking for advice about local Christians.

Pliny said he arrested and questioned people he suspected were Christian. Trajan replied with instructions. He told Pliny not to search for Christians actively. But he also said to punish those who were caught and who did not renounce their faith.

Later, persecution became more formal. The Edict of Caracalla in 212 extended citizenship across the empire. It also seems to have made everyone responsible for making sacrifices on behalf of the Roman state.

In 250, Emperor Decius called for universal sacrifice. This made refusal a crime. Christians across the empire could be punished for not sacrificing to the emperor. Torture and death were likely punishments.

Persecution under Emperor Diocletian lasted from 303 to 311. It focused on destroying churches. It aimed to restore traditional Roman cults.

This period ended under Emperor Constantine. After a civil war, Constantine won in 312. He said the Christian God gave him victory. He claimed he had seen a vision of a cross in the sky.

In 313, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan. It set a policy of religious toleration. Christianity was no longer illegal. Most traditional Roman religious practices could continue.

Constantine also founded Constantinople as a new imperial capital. He decorated the city with images of himself. He also used religious iconography.

Romans also divided foreigners into different groups.  
One group was free provincials, called *peregrini*.  
They were not Roman citizens.  
Other groups included army recruits.  
Another group included people living beyond the Roman border.

A person could move from one group to another.

Groups that settled in the resource-rich Pacific Northwest formed complex hunter-gatherer societies. They adapted closely to the region’s abundant marine life.

They likely reached the area by following caribou, which they hunted. After settling in the dense forests, they learned to live on many animals. These included beaver, elk, seals, birds, sea lions, and salmon. They also ate many other kinds of fish.

Salmon were a key resource. In the fall, salmon swam upstream to spawn. They were so numerous that people could catch them easily. They used traps, simple dams, or spears. People ate salmon right away or dried it to save for later.

Halibut was also important. Peoples of the Pacific Northwest made it a staple food.

The land provided materials for tools. People used bone to make harpoons. These helped them hunt large marine mammals, including whales. They polished local rocks into woodworking tools. With these tools, they carved dugout canoes from trees.

They also developed advanced woodcarving for art. They made special fishhooks from bone and wood. They used certain tree bark to make cloth and baskets.

Because resources were so abundant, these groups could build wealth more easily than many other hunter-gatherers. Their societies became complex. Wealth and social status were linked.

Burial sites from around 2000 BCE support this idea. In the graves of very wealthy people, archaeologists found carved antler tools. They also found objects made from shells. Over time, wealthy graves included even more items. These objects showed higher social status.

Some areas also had high population density. This was possible because food was plentiful. People could also store and save food supplies.

In the Great Plains, in the center of North America, settlers hunted large herds of bison. The bison grazed on short grasses.

Unlike the animals hunted by the Clovis people, bison could adapt to a warming climate. They survived and spread across the plains.

People who depended on bison lived a seminomadic life. They moved often and owned few belongings. Because of this, their society had less social stratification than societies in the Pacific Northwest.

Bison hunting was dangerous. Hunters had to keep their distance. They did not want to startle the animals. They also did not want bison to become fearful of humans.

Archaeological sites in central Canada, Texas, Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado show an early hunting method. As long ago as 8000 BCE, hunters drove bison herds over cliffs. The bison fell to their deaths.

After the fall, many animals were dead or unable to move. Sometimes there were hundreds. Hunters then processed the carcasses. They used the meat, bones, and hides.

Hunters also used other methods. One method was to corner a herd. This let hunters get close enough to use spears.

Plains peoples hunted more than bison. They also hunted antelope and deer. They hunted small animals too, like rabbits and birds.

Bird hunting sometimes used decoys. Hunters made decoys with feathers. The decoys helped hunters get close enough to kill the birds.

Animal hides were useful for clothing. Soft hides, like rabbit, could be stitched together. People used plant materials for stitching.

People also gathered edible plants. These included seeds, berries, nuts, acorns, and tubers. Tubers included yampa and biscuit-root. People dug them up with digging sticks.

People carried and stored food in containers. They used coiled baskets made from plants. They also used bags made of leather.

East of the Great Plains are the wetter, greener Eastern Woodlands.  
This region stretches from the Mississippi River basin to the Atlantic coast.

People who lived there found many kinds of plants and animals to use for food.  
The region had many rivers and lakes.  
These provided fresh water.  
They also encouraged people to settle along the shores.

Oxbow lakes were also important.  
These are U-shaped pools.  
They formed as river courses stabilized in warmer conditions.  
Oxbow lakes were good places to hunt and fish.  
People caught catfish.  
They also hunted deer, birds, rabbits, and other animals.

People ate many wild plants.  
They gathered nuts from oak, chestnut, and beech trees.  
Near the coast, they could also use saltwater marine life.

Because food and water were easier to find, people did not need to move as much.  
Settlements could last longer.  
Around 6500 BCE, populations began to rise.

People also built large earthworks.  
These were made in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Florida.

The oldest known earthwork is Watson Brake in northern Louisiana.  
It dates to about 3900 BCE.  
It includes several human-made earth mounds.  
Some mounds are as high as twenty-five feet.  
They are set in a circular formation.

Archaeologists think Watson Brake was used by hunter-gatherers.  
They likely used it seasonally.

No burial remains have been found at Watson Brake.  
However, large cemeteries from the same period have been found in other woodland areas.  
These include sites in Illinois and Tennessee.

Some cemeteries contain the remains of more than one hundred people.  
Some individuals were buried with personal items.  
These items include weapons and art.

These sites show that populations were rising.  
They also show that people were living in one place more often.

South and west of the Eastern Woodlands, the climate is much drier. It is also less green. This area is desert scrubland. It stretches down the center of Mexico. It reaches the tip of the Central Mexican Plateau.

Farther south is a region often called Mesoamerica. The environment there is warmer. It is also greener and wetter.

After about 8000 BCE, people who had once hunted large game settled in this region. They did this as large game disappeared. Bison also moved north as grasslands retreated.

Archaeologists have found evidence of Archaic peoples in several places. These include coastal sites along the Gulf of Mexico. They also include coastal sites along the Pacific Ocean. Evidence has also been found in the Tehuacán Valley, south of modern Mexico City.

These people usually lived in small groups. They hunted and gathered across large areas.

In the dry season, they relied mostly on wild game. This included lizards, snakes, and insects. They also ate edible plants, such as agave.

In the rainy season, they ate different foods. They ate avocados and nuts. They ate many kinds of fruit. They also hunted small game, such as rabbits.

Around 8000 BCE, some hunter-gatherer groups began to use a site called El Riego Cave. It is in the Tehuacán Valley. They occupied it at certain times, not all year.

Excavations at the cave have found many stone tools. They have also found woven baskets and blankets. Archaeologists have even found elaborate burial sites.

These burials suggest complex spiritual practices.

Other evidence from the Tehuacán Valley shows a major change by about 5000 BCE. People relied less on wild game. They ate more plants. Their diet included beans, squash, maize (corn), and bottle gourds.

By 2600 BCE, gathering wild plants had decreased a lot. Many groups adopted agriculture. They cultivated maize, beans, and squash.

text:
Far to the west of the mound-building cultures, a very different tradition developed. It formed in the dry landscape of the Southwest.

People there began experimenting with maize very early. This started as early as the third millennium BCE. By then, some groups were planting maize in small plots along riverbanks. They used it to add to a hunter-gatherer way of life.

It is not clear exactly how maize traveled from southern Mexico to the American Southwest. There must have been occasional contact between farmers in the south and hunter-gatherers farther north. For many centuries after maize arrived, people grew only small amounts of it. Hunting and gathering still provided most of their food. The region was very dry. The arid conditions may have required people to stay mobile. That may have made farming less useful at first.

Some of the earliest evidence of maize farming in the Southwest dates to about 2250 BCE. This evidence comes from what is now northwestern New Mexico.

By around 1200 BCE, groups in the Las Capas area made major advances. Las Capas was near the Santa Cruz River, close to modern Tucson, Arizona. These groups built a sophisticated irrigation system to grow maize. They dug a network of canals. The canals carried water from the river into their fields.

Around this farming base, they built oval-shaped homes. They also dug pits to roast the maize they grew. Over time, the homes became more complex. People arranged them in rings around courtyards.

Even at Las Capas, maize was still only a small part of daily life. Most people still lived mainly by hunting and gathering. They gathered goosefoot and piñons. They hunted rabbits, bison, and deer.

By around 500 BCE, people also began cultivating beans. Beans increased the variety of foods in the Southwest. This encouraged greater reliance on maize. Maize and beans work well together nutritionally. Beans provide lysine, an essential amino acid that maize lacks. Growing beans with maize also adds nitrogen to the soil. This helps the soil stay fertile longer.

text:
In the sixth and seventh centuries, the Byzantines and the Sasanians fought their longest period of ongoing conflict. There were some peaceful breaks. There were even times when they were allies. Still, war mostly defined their relationship.

Khosrow I was a skilled military leader. He stopped several invasions by nomadic peoples into the Sasanian Empire. In 532, he made peace with the Byzantines. The peace did not last. Khosrow moved west into Byzantine territory. At the same time, Justinian was busy trying to reconquer Italy. From 541 to 557, the two empires fought a long war. The Sasanians took parts of Byzantine-controlled land. These included Armenia and Syria. A truce was signed in 557. It ended in 565, when Justinian died and fighting began again.

Khosrow II was the last Sasanian king to fight a long war with the Byzantines. At first, he had friendly ties with them. He had regained his throne from a rival with help from the Byzantine emperor Maurice. But Maurice was later murdered. Khosrow used that murder as a reason to invade Byzantine territory in 602. The Sasanians again took Armenia and Syria. This time they went further. They expanded into Palestine and Egypt. By 619, they had even reached Libya. The Byzantines struck back successfully. They recovered all the lost territory. Because of this, Khosrow II was removed from power in 628.

Even with these wars, the two empires shared some court rituals. They also exchanged culture and ideas. People from each empire appeared at the other’s court. They communicated often through embassies. This continued even during conflict. Court life included gift exchanges. It also included processions and games.

Both empires used similar symbols to show power. They treated their capital cities as centers of authority. These were Constantinople and Ctesiphon. They also connected themselves to past imperial glory. They created art to show legitimacy. Each empire accepted the other as a legitimate rival state. At the same time, both competed for universal power.

During this era of near-constant war, both empires used smaller states as proxies. Armenians were Christians and had religious rivalries. Even so, they often asked the Sasanians for help. The Byzantines also played different nomadic groups against each other. Over time, both great empires slowly lost geographic strength. The states on their borders became increasingly important.

From the Arab-Muslim point of view, the conquests were a great success. They saw them as proof of God’s power. They also saw them as proof that God favored their *ummah*.

Many Christians who did not support the Muslims also saw the events as an act of God. They believed God was angry with Christians for their sins. They believed God sent the Arab-Muslims as a punishment.

The phrase “Arab-Muslim conquests” can be misleading. In the early years, there were major battles. These included Yarmuk and Qadisiyya. But most territory came under Islamic control through peace agreements.

Many cities and regions agreed to surrender on set terms. These terms protected residents. They also protected many belongings. They protected the right to practice religion.

Peace agreements often made sense for non-Muslim communities. In the seventh century, Muslims often followed a policy of noninterference in local religious practice. Conquered people could keep practicing their religion with some freedom. They had to pay taxes to the new Muslim government. They also had to accept Muslim rule.

Muslims created a legal category for certain groups under their rule. This included Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians. They called them *ahl al-kitab*, meaning People of the Book. This label recognized them as monotheists. It also recognized that they had received revealed scripture from God in the past. The Islamic state offered them protection if they paid taxes and submitted to Muslim rule.

For many people, this was better than life under earlier rulers. Under Byzantine rule, people who did not follow the empire’s official form of Christianity were often discriminated against. They could be blocked from certain jobs. They could be charged extra taxes. They could be treated as heretics.

For Jewish communities, conditions were often even harsher. Many could not practice their faith openly. Many could not gather outside the synagogue.

Zoroastrians were different in one way. They were not officially seen as monotheists. They were not seen as having a revealed scripture. Even so, Muslims still treated them as People of the Book. This was likely for practical reasons. Zoroastrians had high status among Persian nobles.

The term “Arab-Muslim conquest” has another problem. Not all participants were Arabs. Some came from East Africa. Some came from North Africa. Some were Persians who chose to join Muslim armies.

Some Amazigh (Berber) tribes from North Africa joined. The elite Persian cavalry, the *asawira*, also joined.

Some fighters were Arabs but not necessarily Muslim. Some were Arabs from strongly Christian tribes. One example is the Banu Taghlib.

There were many reasons to join the Muslim effort. Participation could bring a share of the spoils of war. It could also bring status in the new society. Both were very valuable.

In the end, the main status difference in early Islamic society was not Arab versus non-Arab. It was not Muslim versus non-Muslim. The key difference was conqueror versus conquered.

In the first centuries of Islamic history, society was divided in a practical way. Some people paid taxes in exchange for protection and benefits from the state. Other people received those taxes. They provided protection and those benefits.

In the earliest decades, ethnic Arabs often received special advantages in government and society. By the end of the eighth century, this difference weakened. More non-Arabs became involved in running the state.

East Africa was an important part of the Indian Ocean trade network. This network linked East Africa with the Middle East, China, and East and Southeast Asia.

At first, trade in East Africa focused on the Red Sea. Egypt had been ruled by the Hellenistic world and later by Rome. Because of this, trade with Greece and Rome was especially important and profitable.

East Africa traded luxury goods with the Roman Empire. These goods included ivory, furs, and spices such as frankincense and myrrh.

After the Roman Empire collapsed, the trade changed. Other groups, including people from Arabia, began to control more of this trade.

Over time, new trading ports appeared farther down the east coast of Africa. Bantu-speaking Africans also moved into the region. A new and advanced culture developed on the Swahili coast.

The Swahili coast expanded its role in Indian Ocean trade. It built powerful city-states. It also connected to the African interior through trade.

After Mongke Khan died in 1259, a civil war began. Hulagu Khan had to manage several conflicts at the same time.

The biggest danger was war with the Golden Horde. The Golden Horde was led by Berke, Batu’s younger brother. Berke had converted to Islam. He was deeply upset by Hulagu’s destruction of Baghdad. He was also upset by the murder of the caliph.

Hulagu and Berke also argued about tribute. They disagreed about who should receive tribute from areas where Hulagu had restored stability.

Hulagu and Berke supported different sides in the civil war over Mongke’s successor. Their war lasted almost four years. It ended only when both men died in 1265. After that, their successors focused on other goals.

For decades, the Il-Khanate faced repeated conflict. It fought the Golden Horde and the Mamluks of Egypt. Sometimes the Seljuks from Anatolia joined these enemies. Sometimes the Chagatai khans joined them too.

Defending against these attacks used most of the Il-Khanate’s effort and resources. The problem was made worse by periodic civil wars over succession. Because of this, further expansion was not possible.

The Il-Khans struggled to hold the Tigris–Euphrates basin. They could not take the Nile delta. They also could not take the Levant, including lands holy to the Abrahamic religions.

Most people in the Il-Khanate had become Muslim centuries earlier. Because the Il-Khans had to focus on defense, they left much of government to religious scholars. These scholars were called the *ulama*. This strengthened traditional Islamic law and custom.

Ghazan Khan ruled from 1295 to 1304. He strongly favored Islam. His brother Oljaitu took the Muslim name Khodabandeh. Oljaitu promoted Shia Islam. This further strengthened Shia Islam in what is now eastern Iraq and Iran.

Even so, conflict with Muslim neighbors continued. The Il-Khanate still tried to take more resources for itself. It did this at its neighbors’ expense.

The economy recovered slowly from the destruction caused by Hulagu’s attack. Recovery was harder because wars kept damaging irrigation systems and city infrastructure.

There were long-term labor shortages in the first generations after the conquest. Many people had been murdered. Many had been enslaved. Many had been relocated. Many also emigrated to nearby Islamic lands.

Ghazan’s reign created the basis for a generation of prosperity and cultural growth. This was greater than in the unstable periods before and after. The center of this prosperity was east of Baghdad and the Tigris–Euphrates basin. It was focused around Maragha and Tabriz in modern Iran.

Il-Khanate rulers tried to follow the dream of Chinggis and Ogedei Khan. They wanted a world united by trade. They negotiated trade deals, especially with Venice and Genoa in the Italian Peninsula. They also kept secure trade with Mongolian China.

This prosperity did not solve the danger of succession struggles. In 1335, the son of Ghazan died without an heir. The Il-Khanate fell into a civil war. It never recovered from that war.

Afterward, several men claimed to be *il-khan*. None controlled more than a fraction of the lands Hulagu had conquered.

text:
Turan Shah did not live long enough to enjoy his success.

The wandering Turks in his army had become mamluks. They were the backbone of his forces. They believed the ransom money from the crusaders would be used against them. They feared Turan Shah would replace them with more traditional mamluks from Africa.

To protect their position, they overthrew Turan Shah. They also wanted control of the ransom money.

Turan Shah’s stepmother was Shajar al-Durr. She was the surviving widow of al-Salih. She briefly took the throne.

The mamluks did not want to follow a female sultan. They forced Shajar al-Durr to marry their leader, Izz al-Din Aybak. They also forced her to give up the throne in his favor.

Historians see Aybak’s rise as a turning point. It marked the end of the Ayyubid dynasty. It also marked the start of the Egyptian Mamluk dynasty.

The Ayyubids left important marks on the Islamic Levant. They restored Sunni Islam as the leading form of Islam. This came after more than two hundred years of Shia Fatimid rule. They built new madrasas in Aleppo, Cairo, and Damascus. Madrasas were Muslim schools of learning. They often focused on studying the Quran.

While Christians and Muslims fought each other, Hulagu Khan prepared to expand Mongol rule. His troops had looted Baghdad. Their supply routes were secure. They moved north to lands better suited to the huge herds the army needed.

Hulagu chose Syria and Egypt as his next targets. These areas were under Mamluk control. He demanded the Mamluk sultan become his vassal and pay tribute. The sultan refused.

In 1259, Hulagu attacked the Mamluks. First, he secured cooperation, or at least noninterference, from Islamic forces in Anatolia. He also secured cooperation from crusader forces in the region.

At first, Hulagu succeeded. He took Aleppo. Aleppo was destroyed, like Baghdad. He also took Damascus. Damascus surrendered without conditions and was mostly spared.

Hulagu’s direct role did not last long. In early 1260, he learned he was needed at a *kurultai* in Karakorum.

Hulagu seems to have underestimated the Mamluks. He withdrew possibly 90 percent of his forces to return to Karakorum. Even so, he ordered Kitbuqa to invade Egypt. Kitbuqa was one of his top generals. He was also a Nestorian Christian. Hulagu gave him twenty thousand troops.

Kitbuqa’s army was reinforced by Christian Armenians. It also included some remaining crusaders.

In the fall of 1260, the Mamluks met the Mongols at Ain Jalut. The Mamluks won a decisive victory. They killed Kitbuqa and most of his force.

This loss was small compared with Hulagu’s total forces. But it was enough to protect parts of the Islamic world that had not been conquered. It helped stop further Mongol attacks.

Soon Hulagu faced threats from other Mongols. The Golden Horde was a major danger. At the same time, the Mamluks freed Syria and Palestine. They drove out both the Mongols and the remaining crusaders. They also gave some support to the Golden Horde in its conflicts with the Il-Khanate.

Fatimid missionaries worked in Iraq and Syria for many years. This was before they converted the Kutama people in Algeria.

In the 900s (the tenth century), the Fatimids began to capture Muslim strongholds across the Maghreb. By the end of that century, their armies had taken Egypt. They also controlled Palestine, Syria, and parts of the Arabian Peninsula. This included Mecca and Medina.

The Fatimids set up a Shi‘ite caliphate in Cairo. Their main goal was larger. They wanted to defeat the Sunni Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad. They wanted their own caliphate to become the center of the Muslim world.

The founder of the Fatimid Caliphate was Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah. He relied on indigenous African soldiers to conquer the Maghreb. These soldiers were vital in Africa. But they could not match the Abbasid army’s Turkish soldiers. Many of those Turkish soldiers were enslaved captives.

The Fatimids copied the Abbasid approach. They expanded and diversified their army. They recruited both free Turks and enslaved Turks. They kept indigenous African soldiers too. Over time, their tribal army became multiethnic.

This worked well at first. It helped the Fatimids in the short term. But it caused problems later. Different ethnic groups competed for military positions. This competition helped trigger a civil war in Egypt in the 1060s.

The Fatimids had faced persecution and had lived as outsiders. Because of this, they were often religiously tolerant. They did not try to force Christians, Jewish people, or Sunni Muslims to convert.

Coptic Christians still held many top roles. They continued to dominate finance and administration in the Fatimid state.

The Fatimids tried to spread Shia Islam through education. They built many madrasas. They also increased the number of Shia mosques. One major example was the Al-Azhar Mosque in Cairo. text:
Chinese records do not give an exact date for the Black Death’s arrival in China.  
They first mention a deadly epidemic in the years 1331 to 1334.

Accounts from the Chinese Imperial Maritime Customs Service were compiled in the late 1800s.  
These accounts suggest that about thirteen million people died in this outbreak.

For people in China, the disaster may have seemed like a sign.  
It may have suggested that the Yuan dynasty had lost the Mandate of Heaven.  
In this belief system, epidemics, droughts, and other disasters could be seen as warnings.  
They could mean that Heaven no longer supported the ruler.

After devastating China, the plague spread west.  
It moved along trade routes by land and by sea.  
These routes helped it reach and overwhelm much of the Middle East.

The Il-Khanate depended heavily on Silk Road trade networks.  
This made it especially vulnerable when the plague disrupted trade communities.

At the same time, the Il-Khanate faced other crises.  
It was in a long conflict with the Golden Horde, a rival khanate to the north.  
It also suffered from invasion, factional disputes, and the death of its ruler.  
Abu Sa’id Bahadur Khan died in 1335, possibly from plague.

The plague damaged trade and reduced the population.  
This made Mongol rule in the Il-Khanate weaken even more after Abu Sa’id’s death.

Some major trade cities declined sharply.  
Tabriz in Iran had been a thriving trade center for a long time.  
By the 1340s, it was largely abandoned.  
Foreign merchants fled suddenly, and commerce collapsed.

To understand the scale, imagine a modern comparison.  
Imagine New York, Tokyo, London, and Hong Kong suddenly becoming empty ruins.  
That is the kind of shock people felt.

The fall of Tabriz stunned people at the time.  
But few cities were spared.  
Infected fleas traveled with trade caravans.  
They moved across Central Asia and into the Middle East.

Death rates across the Middle East were high.  
Much of what we know comes from records in the Muslim world.  
Many sources focus on the Mamluk Empire (1250–1517).  
The Mamluk Empire lost about one-third of its population.

The Mamluk rulers were based in Cairo.  
Trade routes in the Nile delta were hit especially hard.

In Egypt, the plague was made worse by local famines.  
These famines disrupted agriculture.  
Many rural peasants moved to big cities like Cairo and Alexandria.  
They went looking for work as unskilled wage laborers.  
Crowded cities increased their risk of catching the plague.

Nomads in the region had long avoided settled areas during strange diseases.  
Many escaped by retreating into the desert.

In 1347, some of Cairo’s Mamluk elite fled to rural areas north of the city.  
Most stayed in Cairo.  
They wanted to protect their citadel from attacks by rivals.  
By staying, they exposed themselves to the plague.  
Many of them died.

Islamic scholars wrote treatises in the 1340s.  
These writings help explain how the Muslim world responded.  
They served as plague chronicles.  
They also offered medical guidance and advice on proper behavior.

Doctors could not define the disease or cure it.  
So many texts explained the plague in religious terms.  
They used ideas from the Quran and religious law.

These texts often described the plague as not contagious.  
They told readers not to flee.  
They said the plague could offer martyrdom to faithful Muslims.  
They also described it as a warning from God to infidels.

Other Arab writers described the plague in apocalyptic terms.  
They said it came from a breach in the gate that held back Gog and Magog.  
In tradition, Gog and Magog were evil forces that threatened the faithful.

Even with this dramatic language, the Muslim response was usually different from some other regions.  
It generally did not include the doomsday predictions and persecution of minorities seen elsewhere, such as in Christian Europe.

Many people likely fled anyway, despite the treatises.  
But Muslim writers often stressed a collective and controlled response.  
They emphasized resignation and acceptance of God’s will.

Many industries in Mamluk cities declined sharply during the plague.  
At the same time, construction increased.  
More madrasas, mosques, and tombs were built.  
For survivors, these buildings expressed gratitude.  
Artisans who worked on them were often paid very well.

One other group also did well.  
Spice merchants prospered.  
Egypt remained an important depot in the international spice trade.

Still, agriculture and many other trades collapsed.  
The Mamluks’ golden age ended abruptly in 1341.

The Mamluks continued to rule until 1517.  
But their empire became unstable.  
Fierce clashes and ethnic rivalries increased.  
This instability eventually led to the empire’s collapse.

chapter_key: The Nomadic Culture of the Steppes
text:
The eastern half of the Eurasian Steppe is sometimes called the **Inner Asian Steppe**.  
Today it has wide grasslands, mountains, and deserts.  
Most of this land is not good for farming.  
Few people live there.

Climate change shaped the region’s history.  
In Mongolia, rainfall once supported herds of sheep, camels, goats, and horses.  
When the climate cooled, the grasslands could shrink.  
Nomads then had to travel to find new pastures.  
Drought could also push them into crisis.  
If nearby societies would not trade, nomads often raided farms and cities to survive.

Scholars now think that a colder, drier climate around **1500 BCE** forced many people to stop farming.  
They turned instead to herding livestock.  
Herding required people to move often.  
They had to find fresh grass and protect animals from predators.  
This need led to cultural change.  
People became skilled at horseback riding.

As herders, many steppe peoples ate a lot of meat and dairy.  
They also made goods from animal flesh and furs.  
They traded these goods in farming villages.  
They spoke languages not related to Chinese, such as **Turkic** or **Mongolic**.  
A few groups, such as the **Jie**, may have spoken **Indo-European** languages.

Because climate made pastoral life difficult, steppe peoples stayed in constant contact with farming civilizations.  
This included the Chinese.  
Chinese societies often saw nomads and their herds as a danger to their livelihoods.  
For centuries, Chinese and Koreans tried to build physical and cultural barriers against “foreign” steppe groups.  
Even so, ethnic and ancestral lines were not fixed.  
They were porous between nomads and their neighbors.

During raids, steppe groups took prizes.  
These included silk, lacquerware, grain, and war captives.  
Chieftains gave these prizes to loyal supporters.  
Supporters then honored leaders with titles.  
One title was *chanyu*, or **khan**.  
This meant a supreme leader with spiritual and military authority.

Khans gained more power because they controlled thousands of horses.  
This mattered in an age of cavalry warfare.  
Steppe tribal confederations also controlled parts of the **Silk Roads**.  
The Silk Roads were trade routes for luxury goods.  
They connected China with parts of central Asia, India, and the Middle East.

For mobile societies, manufactured and luxury goods had great value.  
They mattered for daily life, status, and politics.  
Silk was especially prized.  
It was light, which helped in hot summers.  
It was also soft, which made it good for lining beds.  
Generals and khans who collected large amounts of silk used it to show power.  
Other luxury goods, such as wine, worked in a similar way.

Most nomadic groups in Asia lived in small family units.  
Some lived in a **clan**.  
A clan was several families sharing one camp.  
They herded or hunted together.  
Clans followed a chieftain.  
The chieftain was chosen for skill as a mounted warrior.

Compared with many ancient cultures, steppe societies were more egalitarian.  
Differences in role and status between men and women were less strict than in cities or farming settlements.  
Archaeology supports this.  
Female skeletons from the **Xiongnu**, **Xianbei**, and **Turkic** peoples show signs of horseback riding.  
They also show evidence of combat skills, such as archery.  
These women may have inspired later stories.  
One example is the legend of **Mulan**, which began circulating in Chinese society in the **sixth century**.

A mobile life limited how much wealth people could keep.  
It also limited how much they could display wealth through buildings and clothing.  
This may help explain why written scripts were less common.  
At the same time, Inner Asian Steppe cultures often adopted technologies, goods, and ideas from neighbors.

Steppe peoples were pioneers in domesticating the horse.  
This gave them a major military advantage.  
Riding and hunting trained people for war.  
They started both activities at a young age.  
Hunting was central to nomadic life.  
It was also part of rituals.  
These rituals marked movement from child to adult.  
They could also mark a rise in social rank.

The steppes touched both Europe and Asia.  
They formed a bridge for new military developments.  
The chariot and cavalry warfare spread across Asia from this region over time.  
Chariots and mounted warriors helped create large confederations.  
These confederations became serious military threats.

Conquerors from the steppes led major campaigns.  
One was **Modun**, who came to power in **209 BCE**.  
Such campaigns changed relations between the Inner Asian Steppe and China.  
They also shaped the growing Silk Roads as major routes of exchange in the ancient world.

Periods of conquest helped the Roman economy in several ways. Romans wanted to control natural resources. They also wanted wealth from the lands they conquered. Money from conquest helped Rome keep people fed. It also helped Rome pay its troops.

In early Rome, the army was made of volunteers. These volunteers were called up only during war. By the time of the empire, the army had changed. It became a permanent, professional force.

The Roman **legion** was the main unit of the army. Its structure changed over time. A legion had about 5,000 soldiers. It was led by a legate. A legion also included craftspeople. It also included people who helped with building projects.

After Augustus’s reforms, there were 28 legions. They were placed across the provinces and along the frontier. Each legion had a number. Many also had nicknames. The nicknames came from where they were formed or where they served. Legions could move around the empire. For example, the First German legion might be stationed in Spain.

Soldiers served for 16 years. Later, the term was raised to 20 years. Soldiers were paid a set amount at the end of their service. Soldiers and military staff received a large share of wealth taken in war. Sometimes they were also promised land taken during Rome’s conflicts.

Many wars were fought to gain resources and money. Rome’s grain supply grew greatly after it conquered Egypt in the first century BCE. Earlier in Rome’s history, conquest of Sicily and Sardinia also expanded the grain supply. People captured in war were often sold in Roman slave markets. Enslaved and freed people did much of Rome’s work. Their labor was the backbone of Roman industry. Because of this, enslaved people also supported the economy.

There were trade-offs. As the army grew, war became more expensive. As the frontier expanded, conflict became more costly. Earlier, soldiers might fight only part of the year. In the imperial period, conflict on the frontier became regular. Campaigns could last for months. Some wars may have seemed endless.

Distance also raised costs. Campaigns far from the city of Rome were expensive. Paying and supplying the army required a large system. That system pushed Rome toward more conquest. Over time, this situation strained the Roman military.

Continuous war also harmed society. Romans were proud of their military strength. Still, the loss of life and property was a burden for many people. War abroad disrupted regional markets that Italy depended on. For example, in 190 CE, a break in the grain supply caused famine. It also caused riots in the city of Rome. Elites often benefited from conquest. People in the lower classes likely carried more of the negative effects.

After the Carolingian Empire collapsed, Europe became unstable.  
This created tension between secular rulers and the Christian Church.

Under German law, lords controlled everything on their land.  
This control included churches and monasteries.

Lords also controlled church appointments.  
They could choose abbots and bishops.

Many lords wanted church leaders to be loyal to them.  
So they gave church offices to family members.  
Or they sold offices to the highest bidder.

This caused serious problems.  
People with no religious calling could become church leaders.  
Some did not even know Christian teaching.  
Even the pope’s office could be sold.

Many Christians were disgusted by this.  
A reform movement began.  
Its goal was to remove secular control from the church.

This movement is often linked to the monastery of Cluny in France.  
Cluny gained independence from a local aristocrat.  
Other monasteries in France wanted the same rights.  
This became the **Cluniac reform**.

The Cluniac movement spread beyond monasteries.  
More clergy joined it.  
They wanted the church to choose bishops without interference from lords.  
This push for independence reached the top of the church.  
It reached the bishop of Rome, the pope.

Popes and reformers began to change church practices.  
They condemned the sale of church offices.  
They called this sin **simony**.

They also said bishops should be elected by clergy.  
A lord should not choose them.  
Clergy who bought an office, or had one bought for them, could be removed.

Reformers also wanted to stop church offices from becoming family property.  
They did not want offices passed to an officeholder’s children.  
So priests were told to be celibate.  
They were forbidden to marry.

Celibacy was not new in the Catholic Church.  
But reforming monks and popes enforced it more strongly.

These reforms angered many European rulers.  
The church responded with a serious threat.  
A king who tried to appoint a bishop could be excommunicated.  
A king who demanded a bribe could also be excommunicated.

Excommunication meant being placed outside the church.  
It meant losing communion and the sacraments.  
It was meant to pressure the person to change.  
For a king, it could be dangerous.  
It could weaken his rule and trigger rebellions.

Reformers also wanted a more Christian society.  
They tried to define what kinds of war were acceptable.

The church said Christian soldiers, especially knights, should follow a code.  
This code should reflect church values.

For example, knights should not loot monasteries.  
They should not hold clergy for ransom.  
They should protect the church.  
They should protect women and the defenseless.

They should also obey public truces.  
They should not fight on holy days like Easter.

These ideas helped shape **chivalry**.  
Chivalry was a code meant to Christianize knightly violence and behavior.

Chivalry did not stop violence.  
Christianized warfare was only one part of a wider culture of knighthood.  
That culture was also secular.

Still, images of Christian knights were useful to popes.  
They helped popes justify directing Europe’s warriors.  
These warriors were urged to fight people seen as enemies of the church.  
That meant enemies of God.

The reform movement gave the church moral prestige.  
But it also increased the pope’s power.  
This made relations worse between eastern and western Christianity.

In the Middle Ages, five ancient Christian centers were most prestigious:  
Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, Rome, and Constantinople.

Each center was led by a bishop called a “patriarch.”  
By the tenth century, only Rome and Constantinople were not under Muslim rule.

The Golden Horde ruled northwest Asia and the lands of the Rus.  
These regions were less economically developed.  

People there lived in many different ways.  
Power was less centralized than in the Il-Khanate.  
Because of this, the region avoided civil war for a long time.  
It did not break apart until outside forces intervened.  
This happened more than a generation after the Il-Khanate fell.

Batu and Berke were the early leaders of the Golden Horde.  
They set up a capital to store tribute, as their grandfather had done.  
But they mostly traveled with their armies.  
They raided neighbors and defended against attacks.

The Golden Horde ruled many different peoples.  
Some were Turkish peoples, like the Kipchaks.  
The Kipchaks were seminomads, similar to the Mongols.  
Others were settled Slavic peasants.  
Many lived in small towns.

The Mongols ruled the Turks indirectly.  
They let local leaders enforce the *yassa*.  
Local leaders collected taxes.  
They also conscripted labor and soldiers.  
Mongol officials in the capital received and distributed tribute.  
They also heard appeals about local decisions.

The Rus and other Slavic peoples were ruled more directly.  
Mongol overseers were assigned to each local ruler.  
These overseers made sure taxes were paid.  
They also worked to prevent rebellion.

Berke was the first ruler and khan of the Golden Horde to embrace Islam.  
Not all later khans were Muslim.  
Even so, Islam gained more followers among the Horde’s Mongols.

In 1313, Uzbeg made Islam the official religion of the Golden Horde.  
But he did not remove the *yassa*’s tax exemption for other religions.  
Uzbeg’s support of Islam strengthened Islamic communities across Horde lands.

At the same time, Horde rule strengthened the Orthodox Christian church in Slavic regions.  
The church came to represent Rus national identity.  
Many people turned to Christianity to set themselves apart from the Mongols.  
This may also have been a quiet form of resistance.

Under the *yassa*, religious institutions and their leaders had tax and service exemptions.  
These exemptions were greater than what the church received from Rus nobles.  
Church-owned land expanded under the Horde.

This expansion may have happened through donations.  
People may have donated land to support the church’s growing role.  
The church offered spiritual comfort and a sense of identity.

Some expansion may also have come through fraud.  
Elites could avoid Mongol taxes and duties by donating land.  
Then they could become church officials in charge of that land.

By the late fifteenth century, Mongol rule collapsed.  
By then, the Russian Orthodox church held about one-third of the arable land.  
This was in areas once ruled by Rus nobles.

The Golden Horde benefited from the Pax Mongolica.  
It also helped create that prosperity.  
Direct European trade was under Horde control.

Goods entering the Mongol world in the east often passed through the Golden Horde.  
Some goods were produced by the Rus.  
Others were brought by Italian merchants from Europe.  
In either case, they almost certainly entered through Horde territory.  
This gave the Horde the first chance to buy them.

The *yam* system helped goods move across the empire.  
It continued for hundreds of years after Mongol rule faded.

The Chagatai Khanate lay in the middle of Mongol lands.  
It was troubled and unstable.  
Conflict with other Mongol khanates and with Kublai’s Yuan dynasty was unavoidable.

At different times, other Mongol states supported usurpers against Chagatai khans.  
Sometimes they acted alone.  
Sometimes they acted together.  
Most of these usurpers did not succeed in the long term.  
But they kept the khanate in turmoil.

By the mid-fourteenth century, the Chagatai Khanate splintered into small states.

Chagatai khans also fought outside the Mongol world.  
Some raided the Delhi Sultanate.  
On a couple of occasions, they tried to conquer it.  
These efforts failed.  
They also weakened the regime.  
This invited more challenges and more instability.

The most important long-term impact of the Chagatai Khanate was religious.  
It strengthened Islam’s hold over western Central Asia.

Central Asia had long been religiously diverse.  
Merchants of many faiths traveled its trade routes.  
The region helped spread Buddhism from India.  
It also helped spread Islam beyond the caliphate’s borders.  
Asian forms of Christianity also thrived there.  
These differed from Catholic and Orthodox Christianity in Europe.

Tarmashirin was the last ruler of the unified Chagatai Khanate.  
He introduced policies that favored Islam over other faiths.  
He replaced the *yassa* with **sharia**, Islamic religious law.  
Sharia was more restrictive.

This change angered many non-Muslim communities.  
Even so, Islamic law stayed in force in Chagatai lands afterward.  
This continued after the khanate broke into small, warring states.

- service duties

Enslaved people lived very different lives across the empire. Their daily life depended on age and gender. It also depended on whether they lived in the countryside or in a city.

They did many kinds of work. Some were unskilled laborers. Some were artisans. Some assisted merchants and shopkeepers. Many were trained as teachers, doctors, musicians, and actors. Others helped build public works, such as bridges and roads. Some even served as imperial administrators.

City life could be less physically brutal. This was especially true for people working in households. They could avoid the harsh labor required in mines, quarries, and *latifundia* across the empire. On these large estates, more than one hundred enslaved people might work. Their harsh lives showed in their poor clothing. It also showed in cruel treatment. Many could not save money to buy their freedom.

During the early seventh century, the Byzantines and the Sasanians were at war. At the same time, western Arabia became very important. A new world religion began there. It was shaped by the land, the people, and the cultures of the late antique Middle East.

That religion was Islam. The word *Islam* means “submission [to the one God].” Islam is monotheistic. It shares many features with Judaism and Christianity. It also has features that were uniquely Arabian. Over time, Islam brought the culture and traditions of the Arabian Peninsula to greater prominence.

## Why Islam’s early history is hard to study

Islam’s origins and early decades can be difficult to understand. Much of what we know comes from Muslim sources. These sources often assume the reader already believes. Because of that, they may leave out details that outsiders need.

Also, many people at the time could not read or write. They did not write history as events happened. So we have less evidence outside religious scripture.

Arabs strongly valued remembering the past. But they usually passed information on by memory and oral recitation. Poetry was an important memory aid. It helped people preserve and transmit stories across generations. Written history for future readers mattered less than the living “performance” of knowledge through oral tradition.

## Oral tradition was not unique to Arabia

Other societies had been using writing more and more for centuries before the seventh century. Even so, the Arab focus on oral transmission was not unusual in world history.

Early Judaism was also passed down orally before it was written much later. Historians also struggle to reconstruct early Christianity because little writing from the time survives.

Epic poetry was another common way to preserve the past. This happened in the Mediterranean world. Examples include *The Iliad* and *The Odyssey*, linked to the Greek poet Homer. It also happened in the ancient Indian world, as with the *Mahabharata*.

## Core ideas at the center of Islam

Islam began around several key elements. These include the city of Mecca, worship of one God (Allah), and the leadership of prophets.

For Muslims, Allah is not a different god from the God of Judaism and Christianity. *Allah* is simply the Arabic word meaning “the one God.” Today, Arabic-speaking Christians in the Middle East also use the word *Allah* for the God of the Christian Bible.

Belief in the one God and in Muhammad’s message is the first and most important of the Five Pillars of Islam. This pillar is called the *shahada*, the profession of faith. To become Muslim, a person must accept this creed: “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.”

Muslims see Muhammad as the final prophet in a long line. This line includes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Muhammad was chosen by God. Muslims do not worship Muhammad as God. They also do not see him as a relative of God.

## The other pillars of Islam

Other pillars of Islam resemble practices in other religions. These include fasting, charity, and daily prayer.

In Islam, these practices are defined in specific ways:

- **Daily prayer**, performed while facing the direction of the holy mosque in Mecca.  
- **Almsgiving**, meaning donating money and goods to the community and to people in need.  
- **Fasting** (if able) during **Ramadan**. Ramadan is the holy month when the Quran was first revealed to Muhammad.  
- **Pilgrimage to Mecca** at least once (if able). This is the **hajj**. During the hajj, Muslims relive important moments from the life of Abraham and his family’s arrival in Arabia. Pilgrims also circle the Kaaba, the house of God, in prayer.

## Islam as a continuation and correction

Muslims have long believed that Islam is not a new faith invented in the seventh century. Instead, they believe Muhammad brought a correction to earlier monotheistic religions.

From the perspective of most Muslims, Islam is the same faith as Judaism and Christianity. All three worship the same God. All three recognize that God guided humanity through prophets.

Muslims also recognize the Jewish and Christian scriptures as originally given by God. However, they believe these scriptures were corrupted over time. Islam therefore presents itself as a purer form of the same tradition. It also sees itself as directly connected to Judaism and Christianity.

All three traditions share a lineage through Abraham. Each lists Abraham as an ancestor. Because of this shared connection, many modern scholars call Judaism, Christianity, and Islam the **Abrahamic faiths**.

## What was uniquely Arabian about Islam

Islam was influenced by other monotheistic worship in the region. Even so, it also had features that were uniquely Arab or Arabian.

One key feature was the setting. Judaism and Christianity focus heavily on the land of modern Israel and Palestine. In contrast, much of Islam’s formation as a distinct religion took place in western Arabia. This region is called the Hijaz. Islam’s holiest sites are there. The founder of Islam spent almost his entire life there.

Islam is also closely tied to Arabic. Arabic is the indigenous language of the region. It is central to Islam’s holiest scriptures. It is also connected to cultural practices, such as preserving the past through Arabic poetry.

Pre-Islamic Arabian society was organized by tribes. This tribal structure shaped the first decades of Islam and the states it inspired. It created a social hierarchy. For much of Islam’s first century, it was nearly impossible to convert unless a person was first accepted into an Arab tribe.

In this way, conversion was linked to older Arab customs. A convert did not need a specific ethnicity or bloodline. But the convert did need to adopt the cultural traditions and markers of Arabian tribal society.

For early Muslims, it likely seemed that the one God had chosen the peoples of western Arabia and their traditions for special recognition. Accepting these features may have been required to be among the “chosen” people.

Most important of all was belief in Muhammad’s leadership and message. Muslims believed God chose him as the final prophet. He was an Arab man from the Hijaz in western Arabia in the early seventh century.

- daily prayer (facing the holy mosque in mecca)  
- almsgiving (giving money and goods to the community and to people in need)  
- fasting during ramadan (if a person is able)  
- pilgrimage to mecca at least once (if a person is able). this is the hajj  

During the hajj, muslims remember important moments from the life of abraham and his family’s arrival in arabia.

## 6. islam as a continuation and correction

Muslims have long believed that islam was not a new faith invented in the seventh century.

They believe muhammad brought a correction to earlier monotheistic religions.

Many muslims see islam as the same faith as judaism and christianity.

All three worship the same god.

All three teach that god guided humanity through prophets.

Muslims also recognize jewish and christian scriptures as originally given by god.

However, they believe these scriptures changed over time.

So islam presents itself as a purer form of the same tradition.

It also presents itself as closely connected to judaism and christianity.

All three traditions connect themselves to abraham. Each lists abraham as an ancestor.

Because of this shared link, many modern scholars call judaism, christianity, and islam the abrahamic faiths.



## 7. what was uniquely arabian about islam

Islam was influenced by other monotheistic worship in the region.

Even so, it also had features that were uniquely arab or arabian.

### the setting

Judaism and christianity focus heavily on the land of modern israel and palestine.

In contrast, much of islam formed as a distinct religion in western arabia.

This region is called the hijaz.

Islam’s holiest sites are there.

The founder of islam spent almost his entire life there.

### the arabic language

Islam is closely tied to arabic, the local language of the region.

Arabic is central to islam’s holiest scripture.

Arabic also connects to cultural practices, such as using poetry to preserve the past.

### tribal society

Pre-islamic arabian society was organized by tribes.

This tribal structure shaped the first decades of islam and the states it inspired.

It also created a social hierarchy.

For much of islam’s first century, a person often could not convert unless an arab tribe accepted them first.

In this way, conversion connected to older arab customs.

A convert did not need a specific ethnicity or bloodline.

But the convert did need to adopt the cultural traditions and markers of arabian tribal society.

For early muslims, it may have seemed that the one god had chosen the peoples of western arabia and their traditions for special recognition.

Many people may have felt they needed to accept these features to be among the “chosen” people.

### muhammad’s leadership

Most important of all was belief in muhammad’s leadership and message.

Muslims believed god chose him as the final prophet.

He was an arab man from the hijaz in western arabia in the early seventh century.
