- The Nile River in Egypt  
- The eastern Sahara in Sudan  
- The great bend of the Niger River in West Africa  

## Agriculture in Egypt

The oldest evidence of agriculture in Africa is in Egypt. It is found along the Nile River valley.

Sometime after 7000 BCE, farming knowledge reached Egypt. This knowledge likely came from southwest Asia. It included the domestication of:

- wheat  
- barley  
- sheep  
- goats  
- cattle  

These new methods changed the region. They helped set Egypt on the path to greatness.

Over the next few thousand years, these farming practices spread west. They moved across North Africa into:

- Libya  
- Tunisia  
- Algeria  
- Morocco  

## Agriculture south of the Sahara

In the grasslands south of the Sahara, agriculture developed independently.

This process may have started as early as 9000 BCE. The Nilo-Saharan people began using grain-collecting and grinding methods. They learned these methods from northern neighbors. They applied them to local tropical grasses, including:

- sorghum  
- pearl millet  

These changes were possible because of a long wet period. This wet phase began around 11,000 BCE and lasted for millennia.

During this time, monsoon-like weather brought heavy rain. The Sahara had lakes and a lush landscape. It was covered with grasses and acacia forests. Many kinds of wildlife lived there.

By around 8000 BCE, the Nilo-Saharans had domesticated wild cattle. These cattle came from the Red Sea hills.

They also began making pottery. They used pottery to store and cook grains.

By as early as 6000 BCE, gathering wild grains began to change. It started to become deliberate domestication.

Over the next few thousand years, the Nilo-Saharans domesticated more plants. These included:

- watermelons  
- cotton  
- gourds  

## Agriculture in West Africa

Agriculture also developed independently in West Africa. This happened far to the west, in the bend of the Niger River.

There, Niger-Congo peoples gradually domesticated yams. This likely began around the same time that the Nilo-Saharans were adopting agriculture in the eastern Sahara.

By 3000 BCE, Niger-Congo peoples were actively clearing land. They used stone tools. They planted crops such as:

- yams  
- oil palm  
- peas  
- groundnuts  

Over the next couple thousand years, they also domesticated a uniquely African variety of rice. They grew it in the wetlands of the Niger River region.

## Farming and metallurgy

Farming became even more productive because of advances in metallurgy.

Bronze was introduced into Egypt from the Near East and the Eastern Mediterranean. This happened a little before 3000 BCE.

From Egypt, bronze technology spread:

- west across North Africa  
- south up the Nile into sub-Saharan Africa  

Bronze was much harder than earlier farming materials. This made farming more efficient.

Wooden plows could only scratch the surface. Bronze-bladed plows were different. When pulled by oxen, they could dig deep. They could also turn over large amounts of earth.

## Iron in Egypt and the Near East

Iron tools were not unknown in Egypt during the Bronze Age.

An iron dagger was placed in Pharaoh Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1323 BCE. Archaeologists have also found several hundred iron objects in the Near East and Eastern Mediterranean. Some date to centuries before the Iron Age began.

Most early iron objects were ornamental. They included items like iron jewelry.

After about 1000 BCE, iron tools began to outnumber bronze tools across the Near East.

Iron was harder to produce than bronze. Early iron objects were often weaker than bronze. That is why many early iron items were decorative.

During the Late Bronze Age Collapse (1200–1100 BCE), tin became hard to obtain. This pushed people to experiment more seriously with iron.

By about 900 BCE, many blacksmiths in the Near East had learned to make iron tools. These tools were far stronger than bronze.

In Egypt, evidence of sophisticated ironworking dates to the seventh century BCE. This technology was introduced from other parts of the Near East.

## Ironworking in sub-Saharan Africa

For many years, historians thought ironworking spread into Africa from Egypt.

Today, the prevailing consensus is different. Many scholars now think ironworking was developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa.

Most modern scholars agree that iron smelting in sub-Saharan Africa likely existed before it reached Egypt. It may have preexisted it by a few centuries.

The earliest evidence dates to about 1000 BCE. It comes from Central Africa, in areas that are now:

- Chad  
- the Central African Republic  
- South Sudan  

From there, the technology seems to have spread west to the Niger River area. By 500 BCE, it was used by the Nok culture of West Africa.

## The Nok and the spread of iron

The Nok settled near the meeting point of the Benue and Niger Rivers. This is in present-day Nigeria.

At first, the Nok used iron to make jewelry. Later, they used it to make farming tools and weapons.

Iron was useful because it made tougher, more durable tools. These tools helped people:

- clear forests  
- aerate land  
- dig trench-based irrigation systems  

Because of these advantages, more groups adopted iron. Over the next several centuries, ironworking spread across West Africa and then much farther.

Iron was especially important for migrating Bantus. They used iron tools to clear trees. They also expanded prehistoric irrigation systems. They dug deeper furrows and supported them with embankments. This helped create Iron Age farms.

As they moved, they spread ironworking technology throughout equatorial and subequatorial Africa.

text:
The Yuan dynasty kept some Song policies. One example was rotating officeholders.  
But the Yuan ruled very differently from earlier Chinese dynasties.

## A new class system based on ethnicity
Kublai Khan made a major change.  
He replaced the Confucian class system.  
The old system ranked people by economic function.  
Kublai’s new system ranked people by ethnicity.

There were four main classes.

1. **Mongols** were at the top.  
2. **Non-Chinese people** were next.  
   These included Europeans.  
   They also included steppe peoples such as the **Jurchen, Tangut, and Khitan**.  
3. **Han Chinese in the north** came next.  
   These were Han people who had been ruled by the **Jin**.  
4. **Song Chinese in the south** were at the bottom.  

Mongols could not marry people from the bottom two classes.

The government recorded each family’s class in census records.  
The census also listed the head of household’s occupation.  
Sometimes the state assigned an occupation.  
This happened when there was a shortage of certain kinds of labor.

## Different rules for different peoples
The Yuan followed a Khitan idea.  
The idea was to rule different groups in different ways.  
So the Yuan used different types of administration for different peoples.

More Mongols became literate over time.  
Kublai was the first Mongol great khan who could read.  
Even so, the mandarin written exam system fell into disuse.

Mongols were subject to the **yassa**.  
The next two classes were also subject to the yassa.  
They were ruled by administrators.  
These administrators were appointed by the chief local Mongol administrator.  
Sometimes they were appointed by the emperor himself.

The Song Chinese were at the bottom of the system.  
They were governed by two administrators.  
One was Chinese.  
The other was Mongol or non-Chinese.  
Both were appointed by the emperor.  
The Chinese administrator was supervised by the other administrator.  
He was also responsible to him.

Officials in these jobs were rotated regularly.  
This prevented them from building a local power base.

## “Hostage bureaucrats” and Marco Polo
Some non-Chinese administrators over the Song did not plan to work for the Yuan.  
They came to seek favors from the emperor.  
A common favor was the right to trade.  
In exchange, the emperors required them to do administrative work.

Europeans learned about Yuan wealth through one of these officials.  
This was **Marco Polo**.  
He was a young merchant.  
He was part of a Venetian trade caravan.  
He and several family members spent almost **twenty-five years** in Mongol lands.  
He wrote a popular account of their experiences.

The Polos were the most famous of these “hostage bureaucrats.”  
They served for about **twenty years**.  
Most such bureaucrats were not Europeans.  
Most were **Muslim traders** from other parts of the Mongol Empire.

Even if these officials did their jobs well, they had a weakness.  
They were unlikely to bond with the local population.  
So they were unlikely to build a power base.  
This reduced the risk that they could challenge imperial authority.

## The exam system returns, with quotas
After Kublai died in **1294**, problems in his system became clearer.

In **1315**, his great-grandson **Buyantu** brought back the mandarin exam system.  
The exams now reflected the Yuan’s dual administration.

Non-Chinese people took different exams than Chinese people.  
Their exams were also shorter.  
Also, **25 to 50 percent** of those who passed had to be non-Chinese.

This quota mattered even more because of population size.  
Yuan censuses said Song Chinese were **more than 90 percent** of the population.

Because of the different exams and the quota, it was easier for Mongols and non-Chinese to pass.  
It was harder for Chinese people to pass.

## Wealth on the surface, stagnation underneath
Travelers wrote about Yuan China’s great wealth.  
Marco Polo did this.  
The North African Muslim traveler **Ibn Battuta** also did, though less.

But economic growth had, at best, stagnated.  
One reason was inflation.  
Another reason was heavy taxation.  
Inflation and taxes reduced consumer purchasing power.

Paper currency was a major cause of inflation.  
In theory, paper money could be converted into metal or silk.

Guns spread through societies in Europe, Asia, and Africa. This change helped bring an end to some nomadic cultures.

For many centuries before this, nomadic societies played a major role in world history. They often helped drive historical change.

Around 1500 BCE, mounted Indo-Europeans arrived on the Indian subcontinent. Their arrival transformed life there. Their sacred texts, the Vedas, became the foundation for Hinduism. Their social organization helped shape the Hindu caste system. Their language, Sanskrit, became a sacred language in both Hinduism and Buddhism.

Nomadic tribes from central Asia also helped set in motion changes that contributed to the fall of the Roman Empire. In the fourth and fifth centuries CE, the Huns lived in central Asia, the Caucasus, and eastern Europe. They swept westward. They attacked and conquered Germanic tribes living on the borders of the Roman Empire. These tribes included the Goths, the Visigoths, and others. Many fled into Roman territory. This movement destabilized the empire.

In East Asia, mounted nomads had a similar impact on China. Over many centuries, different tribes traded with and attacked Han Chinese settlements. These tribes included the Xiongnu and the Jurchen.

During the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE), China began building a wall. The goal was to protect settled areas from roaming riders. The wall did not fully work. It covered only parts of the border between Chinese-settled lands and nomadic lands. Because of this, some Chinese emperors paid tribute to aggressive tribes. They gave gifts. They also gave Chinese princesses. This showed that women’s status was treated as secondary to the goals and needs of men, even among elites.

In the early modern era, more nomadic societies began to settle down. Firearms used by settled societies threatened the survival of nomadic ways of life. As guns and artillery improved, they became more accurate. They could shoot farther. They could fire faster. Mounted archers could not compete.

Still, guns alone do not fully explain the decline of nomadic life. Early firearms were heavy and awkward. They were hard to use from horseback. Later, firearms became lighter. Nomads could have adopted them. Some did. The Plains Indians of North America, for example, adopted firearms.

Not all nomads were mounted warriors. Some were, including the Mongols and Arab Bedouins. The Huns and the Xiongnu were also mounted warriors, and they troubled the Han dynasty. But many nomadic groups did not ride horses. Many did not form armies. The Sami reindeer herders of Scandinavia and Russia were not traditionally warriors. The Gaddi shepherds of the Himalaya were also not traditionally warriors.

Also, settled societies had mounted warriors too. Medieval Europe had knights. Knights declined after gunpowder and firearms spread widely. Even so, it took centuries after firearms appeared for mounted warriors to disappear from armies. European and U.S. forces used cavalry in World War I.

Because of this, it may be more accurate to say gunpowder made cavalry obsolete. This is different from saying gunpowder made nomads disappear. Today, mounted warriors are largely a thing of the past. But nomadic societies still exist in many regions. Their numbers are much smaller than before. Many modern Mongols and Arab Bedouin, for example, still live nomadically.

Firearms helped force many nomads to adapt to new military, political, and social realities. This pressure often pushed them toward settling down. But guns were mainly a tool. They were a *means* used by modern states to control nomads. Guns were not the main *reason* nomadic groups declined.

Modern states fought nomads for many reasons. Settled people often feared nomads. This was especially true when nomads raided or fought them. Settled people also competed with nomads for natural resources.

The North American Plains Indians are one example. Settlers feared Plains mounted warriors. Settlers also wanted the land the Plains tribes used. As long as Plains tribes controlled large hunting grounds, colonizing farmers, ranchers, and miners could not use the resources of the American West as they wished.

Modern nation-states also created permanent borders. They did not want nomads crossing freely from one country to another. States saw this movement as a threat to national security and sovereignty. Many states forced nomads to settle.

States also found it easier to tax people who stayed in one place. As nations industrialized, nomads faced new problems. Access to grasslands and water became harder. Private lands were fenced. Water sources were polluted. Grasslands were grazed by animals owned by commercial livestock businesses. These businesses produced meat for city populations. At the same time, settled life became more comfortable. Many nomads chose to leave nomadic life behind.

In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, climate change has made nomadic life even harder. Droughts have increased. Severe weather has become more common. Grasslands and water sources for animals are at risk. For nomadic pastoralists, lack of grass is disastrous.

The Battle of Ain Jalut shows how environment can shape outcomes. Soldiers of the Mamluk Sultanate used early cannons in that battle. But cannons were not the main reason they won. The Mongol force was much smaller than Mongol armies usually were. The Levant’s arid climate could not provide enough grass. Mongol warriors traveled with thousands of horses, often five or six per person. With too little grass, the Mongols had to field a smaller army.

Today, more nomad homelands face desertification. Some also face harsher winter temperatures. These changes may be the final blow for the world’s few remaining nomadic societies.

Under Askia the Great, the Songhai Empire flourished. Scholars and poets came to cities like Timbuktu and Djenné. Islam was practiced more widely. The state began major building projects. These included canals to improve farming and increase food production. Trade across the Sahara also grew stronger.

As Askia grew older, his personal power weakened. He depended more on palace officials to run the empire. This upset his family. They became angry about the influence of his head chamberlain, Ali Fulan.

In 1528, Askia’s sons rebelled. They removed him from power. They made one brother, Musa, king. But Musa’s rise was not peaceful. Civil war broke out.

Askia Musa fought his relatives to keep the throne. Dozens of his family members were killed. In 1531, Musa was killed by his brothers. This made the crisis worse. The state became even more unstable.

After that, rulers came and went. Their attempts to govern failed. Political chaos spread through the ruling class and the army. Different groups fought for control. The central government could not manage the empire well. Songhai grew weaker.

Outside powers noticed this weakness. They wanted to take control of the profitable trans-Saharan trade in salt and gold. Morocco’s Saadi dynasty was especially interested.

In 1578, the Saadi stopped an invasion by the Portuguese. But it cost them a great deal. Their treasury was drained. To avoid bankruptcy, Sultan Ahmad I al-Mansur Saadi looked for new sources of wealth.

At the same time, Songhai began to recover. Stability returned under Askia Ishaq II. His reign began in 1588. But this recovery did not last long. In 1591, the Saadi invaded Songhai.

Songhai had more soldiers. But the Saadi had a major advantage. They had many guns, ammunition, and cannons. Queen Elizabeth I of England supplied these weapons. She hoped Morocco would become an ally against Spain.

The Saadi army also included many Spanish Muslims. In 1502, Spain’s monarchs ordered all Muslims in Spain to convert to Christianity. Many Muslims fled Spain as a result.

Songhai’s larger army could not match the Saadi weapons. Songhai was defeated at the Battle of Tondibi. Askia Ishaq II was killed.

After the battle, the Saadi commander moved against key cities and trade centers. He was Judar Pasha, an enslaved Spanish eunuch. The Saadi attacked Djenné, Gao, and Timbuktu. They looted and destroyed these cities. They burned them to the ground.

The invaders also tried to prevent recovery. They filled in water wells. They destroyed crop fields. They spared very few people, including women and children.

After this destruction, Songhai’s power could no longer function. About ten years later, the empire was shattered. Its provinces broke apart into smaller kingdoms and territories.

Europeans had long known about three old trade routes across the Sahara Desert.

- In the western Sahara, one route ran from Taghaza to Timbuktu.  
- Farther east, a second route linked the oasis town of Ghadames with trade centers in Hausaland.  
- A third route connected Tripoli, a major Mediterranean port, with Bornu in Central Africa.

These routes had been used for centuries. They were still very dangerous. The Sahara’s weather could be deadly. Raids were also a threat.

People who knew the routes had a big advantage. They knew where key cities and oases were. They also understood the risks. This knowledge helped them control the trade and make money from it.

Muslim and Arab travelers and caravan leaders often tried to keep this knowledge to themselves. Sharing it would reduce their profits. Because of this, European maps of the African interior stayed unclear. Distances were only rough guesses. The locations of cities like Timbuktu and Kano were uncertain. For Europeans, traveling across the Sahara alone seemed likely to end in disaster. They feared raids and hostile merchants.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, European states felt growing pressure to increase national wealth. This pressure grew after the discovery of the Americas. Colonies there were expensive to reach and build.

European states also wanted to avoid middlemen. These intermediaries controlled trade in luxury goods and raw materials. Important examples were Chinese silk, Indonesian spices, and African gold. Taking control from these merchants was difficult. Their monopolies were often protected by kingdoms and states that benefited from them. The problem was even harder for poorer European states, such as Portugal.

When the Portuguese began sailing along the West African coast, their first goal was not a new route to India. Their goal was West African gold. Europeans had known about West Africa’s goldfields since the fourteenth century. Sudanic gold had been imported into Europe to mint coins.

By the mid-fifteenth century, the Portuguese had pushed into the Senegambian coast. They raided Amazigh settlements on the island of Arguin. Arguin was linked to the trans-Saharan trade routes. The Portuguese took captives there. They enslaved them on plantations in Iberia. The Portuguese also explored the Senegal and Gambia Rivers. They were searching for sources of gold. These actions were among the earliest attempts at direct European involvement in trans-Saharan trade.

The Portuguese monarchy also hired explorers. One was Alvise Cadamosto, a Venetian slaver. He was sent to scout Senegambia. These efforts helped the Portuguese understand trans-Saharan trade more clearly. They learned about trade links in West Africa’s interior. They also saw interactions with the Wolof. The Wolof sold enslaved people along interior trade routes.

A few decades after Cadamosto met the vassal kings of Mali in the Gambia region, the Portuguese built Elmina. Elmina means “the mine.” It was a fort on the coast south of the Akan goldfields. It was in what is now Ghana. Elmina was a fortified trading post. From there, the Portuguese traded copper, brass, and cloth. In return, they received Akan gold.

The Akan mines also depended on enslaved workers. The Portuguese bought enslaved people from Benin. They then sold them to Mande-speaking Dyula traders. By the start of the sixteenth century, the Portuguese also entered the cowrie-shell currency market in West Africa. They supplied cowrie shells and luxury goods. In exchange, they received more gold. Over time, they redirected trade away from the old trans-Saharan routes. More trade moved along the West African coast instead.

The Portuguese first saw São Tomé and Príncipe in the 1470s. These are two islands in the Gulf of Guinea. By 1500, the Portuguese had settled both islands. The islands were valuable for two reasons. They had a strategic location off the West African coast. They also had a tropical climate and volcanic soil. This made them ideal for growing sugar.

Large sugar plantations soon developed on the islands. The Portuguese strengthened their position in the Gulf of Guinea. Sugar production requires intense labor. It needs a very large workforce.

African chiefdoms and coastal middlemen showed the Portuguese that captives could be bought and enslaved as workers. As the plantation economy on São Tomé grew, the demand for enslaved labor increased. By the early sixteenth century, São Tomé was Europe’s largest single supplier of sugar. It also had a huge enslaved workforce. Settlers obtained many of these enslaved people from Elmina.

Less than forty years passed between the settlement of São Tomé and Príncipe and the first trans-Atlantic voyages of African captives. These captives were sold into slavery in the Americas.

African chiefs on the mainland saw a chance to profit. Some carried out raids against neighboring communities. They did this to capture people to sell to Europeans. At first, they sold mainly to the Portuguese. Later, they also sold to the Dutch, Spanish, French, and English.

European competition for trading posts along the West African coast increased. As it grew, tensions rose among African polities. Some took part in the expanding trade in enslaved people. Others resisted it.

In 1591, a major turning point came. Songhai was the largest and most powerful Sudanic kingdom in the sixteenth century. It was defeated by the Moroccan army at the Battle of Tondibi. Songhai was shattered. This permanently changed West Africa.

Without a strong central authority, many smaller states appeared. Their chiefs often preferred to deal directly with wealthy Europeans. They did not want to rely on the older caravan trade system.

These changes greatly expanded the trade in enslaved Africans. In the sixteenth century, the number was a few thousand people. In the seventeenth century, it rose to tens of thousands. For much of the next century, the average was about 45,000 people per year.

Efforts to silence Martin Luther failed.  
A new form of Christianity, called Protestantism, spread through the German-speaking lands.  
By the end of the 1500s, it was firmly established in western and central Europe.  

Many rulers welcomed the new religion.  
It gave them a reason to reject the pope’s authority.  
Luther urged the German princes to do this.  

The Catholic Holy Roman emperor Charles V (also Charles I of Spain) strongly opposed Protestantism.  
Still, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 changed the situation.  
It gave Lutheran rulers in the empire the right to make Lutheranism the official religion in their lands.  
A ruler’s subjects had to follow the church the ruler chose.  
Many rulers in northern Germany became Lutheran.  
In Austria and Bavaria, in the south, the Roman Catholic Church kept its power.  
No other religions were allowed under this agreement.  

In Switzerland, reform ideas were taken up by Ulrich (Huldrych) Zwingli in Zurich.  
Zwingli had been a priest.  
He demanded major changes.  

He rejected the Catholic belief in transubstantiation.  
This belief said Jesus was physically present in the communion wine and wafer during every Mass.  
Even Martin Luther did not reject it that strongly.  

Zwingli also preached against fasting before major religious holidays.  
He wanted religious images removed from churches.  
He banned organs from churches.  
He closed monasteries and convents.  
He had the Bible printed in German instead of Latin.  
He called for an end to clerical celibacy.  
He said the Bible never mentioned purgatory.  
Zwingli was killed in 1531 during conflict between Catholic and Protestant areas of Switzerland.  

Zwingli inspired Konrad Grebel, a Swiss merchant.  
Grebel focused on baptism.  
He believed baptism should be delayed until adulthood.  
He thought only adults could choose to renounce sin.  
Grebel felt Zwingli was reforming Zurich too slowly.  
So Grebel started his own movement in 1524.  
It was called the Swiss Brethren.  

The Swiss Brethren was one of several Anabaptist churches.  
Anabaptists rejected infant baptism.  
They supported adult baptism instead.  
These churches formed in the 1500s, mainly in central Europe and the Low Countries.  

Catholics and most Protestants practiced infant baptism.  
They believed baptism removed the stain of original sin, the sin of Adam and Eve.  
Anabaptists disagreed.  
They believed only adults could truly renounce sin and declare faith.  
So only adults could make a conscious choice to become Christian.  

But baptism was supposed to happen only once.  
So an adult baptism for someone baptized as a baby was seen as rebaptism.  
That violated a Catholic teaching.  

Other Anabaptist movements included the Hutterites, the Mennonites, and the Amish.  
The Amish split from the larger Mennonite movement in the 1600s.  
Anabaptist groups also supported separating church and state.  
They often believed in pacifism.

In 1606, the Virginia Company received a charter.  
It was named for Queen Elizabeth, the “virgin queen,” because she never married.  
The company sent 144 men and boys to North America.

In 1607, they founded Jamestown.  
It was named for the new king, James I.

In England, older brothers inherited most property.

They also faced internal political disputes.

This brought profits to the Virginia Company.

The habit was highly addictive.

They relied heavily on indentured servants.

Indentured servants were European immigrants.  
They usually agreed to work for four to seven years.  
In return, they received transportation to the colony.  
They also hoped for a new life after their service ended.

In the 1600s, up to 100,000 people came as indentured servants.  
Most were poor men in their twenties.  
Many died from disease, exposure, and overwork.  
Those who survived often became comfortable and respected settlers.  
A lucky few became wealthy planters.

In 1619, the first Africans arrived in Virginia.  
At first, they had the same chances as European immigrants.  
They could earn freedom and build wealth.

This was part of a larger trend.  
The Spanish and Portuguese had brought the first Africans to the Americas a century earlier.  
By the mid-1600s, new policies were developing in the Americas.  
These policies bound Africans to servitude for life.

Virginia colonists wanted a permanent labor force.  
This was especially true when it was hard to recruit enough indentured servants from Europe.  
Forcing other Europeans to work would have caused too much resistance.

By 1676, many poor White former servants were angry.  
That year, they tried to overthrow the colony’s government.

Virginia’s elite responded by creating legal differences between Europeans and Africans.  
They gave privileges to Whites that Blacks did not receive.  
They encouraged Europeans to see Africans as inferior and fit only for manual labor.  
At the same time, they took away Africans’ freedom.

In this way, slavery became linked to African ancestry.  
Racial divisions were created that had not existed before.  
Racism became the foundation of the colonial labor system.

This law banned enslaved Africans from carrying weapons.  
It also banned them from gathering in public.  
It banned them from traveling without permission.

They also became central to other English colonies in the South.  
These colonies stretched from Maryland to Georgia.  
Maryland was founded as a haven for English Catholics, just north of Virginia.

Slavery in the United States ended in 1865.  
It ended after a devastating civil war.  
It also ended with the Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

Slavery continued in other parts of the Western Hemisphere.  
Brazil did not abolish slavery until 1888.

text:
Europeans were sometimes hurt by their own success.  
Their economic empires could create colonies that grew strong.  
Some colonies became strong enough to form independent nations.  
In one case, thirteen former colonies formed a new country.  
That country later became richer and more powerful than the empire it left.

## The British colonies in North America

The British colonies in North America began in the early 1600s.  
At first, they were small and struggled to survive.  
By the mid-1700s, they had changed greatly.  
More than two million people lived there.  
The colonists mostly governed themselves.  
They also had a strong commercial economy.

Britain followed mercantilist policies.  
These policies threatened colonial economic growth.  
In the late 1600s, England passed the Navigation Acts.  
These laws aimed to increase profit from the colonies.  
They also aimed to keep colonial resources away from rival European powers.  
They tried to stop smuggling used to avoid trade rules.

### The Navigation Act of 1660

The Navigation Act of 1660 listed certain colonial goods.  
These goods could be sold only in England or to English colonies.  
English merchants decided what they would pay for colonial goods.  
Colonists could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other merchants.  
Those other merchants might have paid more.

The listed products included furs, tobacco, and sugar.  
These were goods wanted across Europe.  
The list also included rice, ginger, cotton, and indigo.  
It included other plants used to make dye.

English textile makers needed cotton and dyestuffs.  
To protect English interests, the Exportation Act of 1660 also banned exporting English wool.

Britain also restricted “naval stores.”  
These were materials used to build and maintain ships for trade and war.  
They could be sent only to England.  
They included masts and hemp (for rope).  
They included pine tree pitch (to seal ships and make them watertight).  
They included pine tree sap (used to make turpentine).

When these colonial goods reached England, they were heavily taxed.  
The tax money went to the English government.  
It did not go to the colonies that produced the goods.

### The Navigation Act of 1663

The Navigation Act of 1663 created another rule.  
Goods coming to the colonies from outside the British Empire had to go to England first.  
In England, they were taxed.  
Only then could they be shipped to the colonies.

This raised prices in the colonies.  
Foreign shippers passed the cost of English taxes on to colonists.

### Limits on colonial manufacturing

By the end of the 1600s, Parliament added more restrictions.  
It began to block colonists from making certain goods.  
These were goods also made in England.  
The goal was to stop colonists from underselling English merchants.

Colonists could not sell goods made from wool or iron.  
They could not sell them in England.  
They also could not sell them to other English colonies.

By the mid-1700s, colonists also could not export beaver hats.  
Beaver hats were a popular fashion in Europe.  
The English colonies were active in the fur trade.

Parliament allowed colonists to export only unfinished furs.  
Colonists could not export the finished hats.  
Finished hats would have sold for higher prices.  
This limited how much wealth colonial settlers could gain.

## After the French and Indian War

After the French and Indian War, tensions grew.  
British colonists reacted with hostility to new actions by Parliament.  
They believed these actions unfairly limited their economic opportunities.

Many colonists wanted to move west of the Appalachian Mountains.  
They wanted farms on the rich land of the Ohio Valley.

In New England, families were large.  
Over time, parents struggled to provide enough land for their children.

In the southern colonies, tobacco farming created constant demand for new fertile land.

Many colonies claimed land west of the Appalachians.  
But the French had taken this land.  
It was also home to many Native American allies of the French.

After Britain defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, colonists expected to take the land.  
The British government did not allow this.  
It wanted to avoid angering the tribes of the Ohio Valley.  
It also wanted to avoid expensive new wars.  
So it quickly banned settlement west of the Appalachians.

Many colonists were dismayed and angry.  
Many had fought alongside British troops in the war.

## Troops, taxes, and courts

Britain also kept troops in North America.  
Britain said this would keep peace with Native Americans.  
Britain also needed to repay war debts.

These troops policed the frontier.  
They regulated colonial trade.  
They collected taxes.

Paying for the army led Britain to seek more money.  
It tried to impose new taxes on colonists.  
It also tried to enforce existing taxes more strictly.

Colonists often used smuggling to avoid trade restrictions.  
Britain responded with new legal rules.  
Smugglers had to be tried in admiralty courts.  
These courts did not use juries.  
Many colonists believed this violated the English Bill of Rights.

## Quebec and rising anger

In 1774, Parliament made a decision that angered many colonists.  
It gave control of the Ohio Valley to the French province of Quebec.  
It allowed Quebec to keep French civil law.  
It also extended religious toleration to Roman Catholics there.

Most British colonists were Protestant.  
Many were outraged by these changes.

Conversation and debate in public life were closely tied to the growth of print culture during the Enlightenment.

In late-seventeenth-century French cities, literacy was about 30 percent for men and 14 percent for women. By the mid-eighteenth century, it had risen to 48 percent for men and 27 percent for women.

As literacy rose, printed material spread quickly. More books, pamphlets, newspapers, and political cartoons appeared. Print helped standardize spelling and shared systems of knowledge. It also allowed news, opinions, poetry, political philosophy, scientific writing, and many other kinds of information to reach far more people than speech alone.

The “Republic of Letters” was a long-distance community of writers. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, they exchanged ideas across Europe and the Atlantic. They sent handwritten letters and published works of many kinds. This created an important international network for sharing and spreading ideas.

The Republic of Letters was like a republic based on ideas, not geography. Its “citizens” did not live in one place. They were connected through print. In theory, any literate person in Europe or the Atlantic world could belong. Members treated each other as intellectual equals. They exchanged ideas freely, like citizens of a political republic who were, in theory, free and equal.

Famous members included Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin, and Catherine the Great.

Because members came from many countries and spoke many languages, they faced a language barrier. Much of their writing was in Latin, which was the common language of scholarship in multilingual Europe. Otherwise, they needed skilled translators. This made it hard for most people to take part directly in Enlightenment print culture.

Even with the strong influence of print, Enlightenment texts reached the general public in limited ways. Many artisans, peasants, and tradespeople could not read. Literacy was rising quickly among the urban elite, especially wealthy merchants and aristocrats. But for people lower on the social and economic ladder, literacy stayed well below 20 percent. This was especially true in rural areas.

The Enlightenment supported, in theory, more democratic sharing of knowledge. In practice, participation depended on wealth and free time. Books were extremely expensive. Most people could not afford them. Even cheap pamphlets cost too much for many eighteenth-century laborers and peasants.

In the second half of the eighteenth century, lending libraries appeared. They increased access to printed materials. However, only certain academics and government officials could borrow books.

By the end of the century, reading clubs became more common. Members paid an annual fee to use books and periodicals. These clubs helped expand the reading public. They also helped raise literacy among the middle class.

By the mid eighteenth century, literacy had risen to:

- **Men:** **48%**  
- **Women:** **27%**

## 3. How print spread ideas

As literacy rose, printed material spread quickly.

More of these appeared:

- **Books**  
- **Pamphlets**  
- **Newspapers**  
- **Political cartoons**

Print helped in key ways:

- It **standardized spelling**.  
- It spread **shared knowledge**.  
- It helped ideas travel farther than speech alone.

Print also made it easier for many kinds of writing to reach more people, including:

- News and opinions  
- Poetry  
- Political philosophy  
- Scientific writing  

---

## 4. The Republic of Letters

The **Republic of Letters** was a long-distance community of writers.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, they shared ideas across:

- Europe  
- The Atlantic world  

They did this by:

1. Sending handwritten letters  
2. Publishing many kinds of works  

This created an international network for sharing and spreading ideas.

### A republic based on ideas

The Republic of Letters was like a republic based on **ideas**, not geography.

Key points:

- Its “citizens” did not live in one place.  
- They were connected through **print**.  
- In theory, any **literate** person in Europe or the Atlantic world could belong.  
- Members tried to treat each other as **intellectual equals**.  
- They exchanged ideas freely, like citizens in a political republic who were, in theory, **free and equal**.

Famous members included:

- **Voltaire**  
- **Benjamin Franklin**  
- **Catherine the Great**  

---

## 5. Language barriers

Members came from many countries and spoke many languages. This created a **language barrier**.

To deal with this:

- Much writing was in **Latin**, the common language of scholarship in multilingual Europe.  
- Otherwise, they needed **skilled translators**.

Because of this, it was hard for most people to take part directly in Enlightenment print culture.

---

## 6. Who could (and could not) take part

Even with the strong influence of print, Enlightenment texts reached the general public in limited ways.

Many people could not read, including:

- Artisans  
- Peasants  
- Tradespeople  

Literacy rose quickly among the **urban elite**, especially:

- Wealthy merchants  
- Aristocrats  

But for people lower on the social and economic ladder, literacy often stayed:

- **Below 20%**

This was especially true in **rural areas**.

---

## 7. Cost and access to books

The Enlightenment supported, in theory, more democratic sharing of knowledge.

In practice, participation depended on:

- **Wealth**  
- **Free time**

Books were **extremely expensive**, so most people could not afford them.

Even cheap pamphlets often cost too much for many:

- Laborers  
- Peasants  

---

## 8. Lending libraries and reading clubs

### Lending libraries

In the second half of the eighteenth century, **lending libraries** appeared.

What they did:

- They increased access to printed materials.  

Limits:

- Only certain people could borrow books, such as:  
  - Academics  
  - Government officials  

### Reading clubs

By the end of the century, **reading clubs** became more common.

How they worked:

- Members paid an **annual fee**.  
- They could use books and periodicals.

These clubs helped:

- Expand the reading public  
- Raise literacy among the **middle class**

Saint-Domingue was a French colony.  
It was on the western side of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola.  
France founded it in the mid-1600s.

Soon it became the most profitable colony in the Americas.  
This wealth came mostly from the labor of enslaved Africans.  
They were forced to work on sugar, coffee, and indigo plantations.

In 1791, freed and enslaved Africans rebelled.  
Other islanders of African descent also joined.  
Two key leaders were Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines.  
Both men had been born enslaved on local plantations.

The revolt grew into a full revolution.  
It led to independence.  
It also led to the creation of the free republic of Haiti in 1804.

The Haitian Revolution was unique.  
It was not led by White colonists of European descent seeking political representation and more economic freedom.  
That had been the pattern in the British colonies of North America.  
In Saint-Domingue, the fight was led by people at the lowest levels of the social hierarchy.

The rebellion in Haiti had two main goals.  
It also aimed at two kinds of liberation.

For free Blacks and mixed-race elites, freedom meant ending colonial rule.  
It meant independence from France.

For enslaved Blacks, liberation was more basic.  
It meant an end to plantation abuse.  
It meant an end to slavery.

By January 1804, Black revolutionaries had defeated the French.  
They used successful guerrilla tactics.  
The French army was also weakened by a yellow fever outbreak.  
These factors helped create the Haitian nation.

Haiti became the second liberated territory in the Western Hemisphere.  
It also became the second republican system there.

They worried it would inspire other slave rebellions.  
They feared that American Indians, free and enslaved Africans, and people of mixed ancestry might fight violently for independence.

Because of this fear, the creole aristocracy hesitated.  
They were less willing to copy the liberty-seeking Anglo-American colonists.  
Support for independence from their parent countries weakened instead of growing.

Instead, events in the Iberian Peninsula led to change.  
Upheavals there would break the ties between Spain and Portugal and their colonies.

During the Napoleonic Era (1803–1814), Portugal and Spain took different sides.  
Europe was at war with Napoléon Bonaparte, the emperor of the French.

Portugal kept its long-standing alliance with Great Britain.  
Britain was an enemy of Napoléon.  
Spain, in contrast, was allied with France.

Since the War of Spanish Succession (1701–1714), Spain had been ruled by the House of Bourbon.  
The king at this time was Carlos IV.  
He followed a disastrous policy of war with England.

British naval blockades disrupted trade between Spain and its colonies.  
In 1806, British soldiers attacked Buenos Aires.  
Buenos Aires was in the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata (present-day Argentina).

Local forces defeated the British.  
But the attack revealed something important.  
Spanish American colonists saw how vulnerable Spain was.  
They also saw that Spain could not protect them well.

In 1807, Napoléon created the Continental System.  
It was also called the Continental Blockade.  
It required all European ports to close to English shipping.

Portugal did not follow this policy.  
Portugal kept trading with Britain, one of its oldest allies.  
Britain could not be defeated if it could still trade through Portugal.

To force Portugal to comply, France would need to invade it.  
But France could only reach Portugal by marching through Spain.

By then, Spain was a weak French satellite.  
Napoléon easily got permission from the Spanish Crown to invade Portugal by land.  
As a result, Spanish subjects suffered.  
They faced heavy taxes, war, and occupation.

Popular anger grew against these pro-French policies.  
Carlos IV felt pressure to step down.  
He abdicated in favor of his son, Fernando.

Napoléon then intervened.  
He detained both Carlos IV and Fernando.  
He forced both men to give up their claims to the Spanish throne.  
He installed his brother, Joseph Bonaparte, as king of Spain.

Napoléon’s plan still did not fully work.  
In early 1808, most people in Spain rejected Joseph Bonaparte.  
Creole royalists in the colonies also rebelled.  
Some republicans in the colonies rebelled as well.

The rebellion began in Madrid.  
It quickly spread to other cities across the Iberian Peninsula.

Eventually, the Peninsular War (1808–1814) followed.  
British, Spanish, and Portuguese forces fought together.  
They fought against the French.

As the United States and many European nations industrialized, most nations in Africa, Latin America, and Asia did not. Japan was the main exception.

This created a gap. These regions fell behind in the economy, technology, and military power. They were at a disadvantage compared to industrialized countries.

Historians disagree about why this “Great Divergence” happened.

Some historians say natural resources mattered. They argue that many of these nations did not have key resources. One example is abundant coal. Many European nations did have large coal supplies.

Other historians focus on colonies. They note that European countries built colonies in the Americas and Asia. Colonies helped countries like Britain and France gain capital. Colonies also provided resources and new markets. These advantages supported industrial growth in Europe.

As a result, Africa, Asia, and Latin America were often forced into unequal treaties. Europeans imposed these treaties using deadlier weapons.

Another argument offers a different view. It says some countries made a practical choice. Countries such as Egypt and many Latin American nations saw their strengths in producing raw materials. They supplied agricultural goods and other raw materials to industrializing nations.

Several factors supported this path. These included history, geography, climate, and the nature of local labor forces. In many places, these conditions made raw material production easier than widespread industrialization.

Each nation followed its own path. A unique set of circumstances shaped the choices and outcomes in each place.

Latin American nations also became export economies. They were no longer under Spanish or Portuguese control. Many leaders wanted to industrialize. But they faced many obstacles.

Wealthy plantation owners and urban professionals could afford factory-made goods. Agricultural laborers could not. This widened the class divide.

By the start of the Second Industrial Revolution, new inventions and factory methods needed new raw materials.  

Industries needed petroleum to fuel engines.  
They needed natural rubber for valves and tires.  
They needed palm oil to lubricate machines.  
They needed copper to conduct heat and electricity.  
They needed silver for medicine and photography.  
They needed lead for pipes.  

Coal was also in high demand.  
Coal helped turn iron into steel.  
Coal was used to make gas that heated homes.  
Coal was used to generate electricity.  
That electricity powered machines and lit streets and buildings.  

Not every industrial nation could produce enough of these materials.  
Many could not meet their growing needs on their own.  

New fashions and tastes also increased demand for imports.  
Middle-class families in Europe and the United States wanted their daughters to play the piano.  
This created a market for ivory, which was once used to make piano keys.  

Industrial workers needed quick energy.  
This increased demand for coffee, tea, and sugar.  

Elites and people trying to join the middle class wanted expensive furniture.  
They bought furniture made from mahogany, rosewood, and ebony.  

Cotton textiles stayed popular.  
But after slavery ended in the United States, cloth makers could not rely on cheap raw cotton.  

Industrial powers tried to meet their needs by looking beyond their borders.  
They turned to Africa, Asia, and the Pacific Ocean for raw materials and new markets.  

To make large profits, they wanted to buy raw materials at very low prices.  
Africans, Asians, and Pacific Islanders were unlikely to agree to such low prices.  

These regions would also have to buy manufactured goods from industrial nations.  
This was also unlikely.  
Many could make some of these goods themselves.  

Because of this, many business owners and politicians believed they needed control.  
They wanted to control distant countries and rule them as empires.  
Often, they used military conquest to do this.  

After taking territory, imperial powers set up markets and invested money there.  
Then they tried to stop other industrial powers from taking their colonies.  
This led them to tighten control over colonies.  
It also led them to try to conquer nearby regions.  

Great Britain, for example, competed with Russia for control of Afghanistan.  
Britain did this mainly to limit Russian access to India.  
India was Britain’s most valuable colony.  

These new colonies were different from earlier European colonies.  
In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Europeans often created “settler colonies.”  
Large numbers of Europeans moved there and made permanent homes.  

In the newer colonies, this was not usually expected.  
Most Europeans were not expected to relocate to Africa or Asia in large numbers.  
The colonies were not meant to have the same relationship to the home country.  

For example, U.S. rule of the Philippines and Filipinos was very different.  
It was different from what North American colonists had experienced under Great Britain.  

Industrial nations mainly wanted to exploit colonial resources and labor.  
They did not mainly want to settle these colonies.  

There were some exceptions.  
France took control of Algeria in 1830.  
In 1848, France made Algeria part of France.  

In the nineteenth century, the government encouraged immigration to North Africa.  
Many French people and other Europeans moved to coastal Algeria and Tunisia.  

Many Europeans also settled in southern Africa.  
This happened in British and Dutch colonies.  

Even so, this was not the usual pattern of imperialism.

The Cold War between the West and the East was fought in many ways.  
Both sides used many strategies.

## Aid and influence
The United States and the Soviet Union both gave aid and technical help.  
They focused on countries in Latin America, Asia, and Africa.  
Many of these countries had been European colonies until the end of World War II.

The United States hoped this aid would stop communism from spreading.  
The goal was to remove economic reasons for countries to side with the Soviet Union.

Communism appealed to many poor people.  
It promised that a nation’s wealth would support all citizens.  
In the Soviet system, people were provided with jobs, housing, education, health care, and public transportation.  
The standard of living was lower than in the West.  
But for people facing hunger and homelessness, and with little hope of improvement, communism seemed like a good alternative.

## Propaganda and media
Both sides used propaganda.  
They used books and pamphlets, images, and films.  
They used propaganda to build support for their own policies and beliefs.  
They also used it to damage the other side’s reputation.

In 1950, the United States funded Radio Free Europe.  
It broadcast news to countries in the Eastern Bloc.  
In 1953, Radio Liberty began broadcasting to the Soviet Union.

Radio Free Europe and the Free Europe Committee also printed leaflets and posters.  
The Free Europe Committee was an organization of American business executives and lawyers.  
It was established by the U.S. government.  
These materials praised life in democratic, capitalist countries.  
They were dropped from weather balloons over East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary.

## Soviet messages and their appeal
Soviet propaganda emphasized the USSR’s desire for world peace.  
It praised communist ideals.  
It promoted a classless society where people were treated equally, regardless of race or gender.

This message appealed strongly in Latin America, Africa, and Asia.  
Some African Americans were also attracted to these promises.  
They faced racism and segregation in the United States.  
Opponents of the U.S. civil rights movement often called it communist.

## Sports and culture
Propaganda sometimes appeared through sports.  
Each side used athletes to show that its system was better.  
Swimmers, runners, weightlifters, and gymnasts were part of this effort.  
People closely tracked Olympic medal counts for the United States and the Soviet Union.

There were also cultural exchanges.  
Soviet ballet dancers toured the United States.  
American jazz musicians and symphony orchestras visited Eastern Bloc countries.

## Technology and the space race
Both sides highlighted their technology and creativity.

In 1959, there was an exhibition in Moscow.  
U.S. vice president Richard Nixon showed Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev American technology.  
He used a model kitchen to do this.  
Khrushchev mocked the labor-saving devices.  
He asked if Americans also had machines to put food in their mouths and swallow it.

The two countries also competed in space.  
In 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite.  
This was a major blow to U.S. pride.  
In response, in 1958 President Dwight D. Eisenhower asked Congress to create a space agency.  
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was created that year.

In 1961, the Soviet Union sent the first astronaut into space.  
In 1969, the United States put the first humans on the moon.

## Espionage and covert action
Espionage was another major tool.

The United States used the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).  
The CIA was formed in 1947.  
The USSR used the KGB.

These agencies watched the other side.  
They also planned and carried out sabotage.  
They also supported assassinations of people seen as enemies.

Both agencies also stirred unrest in other countries.  
They trained fighting forces.  
They encouraged revolutions and insurgencies.  
Their goal was to overthrow foreign governments.  
They wanted to install leaders friendly to their own side.

For example, the CIA trained Cuban insurgents in 1961.  
The goal was to overthrow Cuba’s communist government under Fidel Castro.  
Similarly, the KGB helped Vietnamese communists.  
These communists tried to defeat the government of South Vietnam during the Vietnam War.

## Nuclear weapons and deterrence
The most dangerous competition was nuclear weapons.  
This was also the main way each side tried to restrain the other.

In 1949, the Soviet Union detonated an atomic bomb.  
This ended the U.S. monopoly on nuclear weapons.

In 1952, the United States developed the hydrogen bomb.  
Some atomic scientists who had worked on the Manhattan Project opposed this step.  
The United States tested the hydrogen bomb at the Pacific atoll of Eniwetok in 1952.  
This weapon was one thousand times more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.  
After this, the Soviet Union also needed to develop the same kind of weapon.

## Missiles and “mutually assured destruction”
In the 1950s, both countries developed intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs).  
These missiles could carry nuclear warheads.  
They could be launched from the home country.  
They could also be launched from satellite nations.

Because of this, air defenses were no longer enough.  
Intercepting bombers could not fully prevent nuclear attack.

Both the Western and Eastern Blocs built shelters for civilians.  
They prepared for the possibility of nuclear war.  
But neither side believed it could truly win.

Both countries came to believe survival depended on retaliation.  
They wanted the ability to strike back with overwhelming force.  
The idea was to make the other side afraid to strike first.  
In the United States, this policy was called “mutually assured destruction” (MAD).

If nuclear weapons failed to prevent war, both sides were still prepared.  
They built large military forces during the Cold War.  
They also spent billions on battleships, submarines, and fighter jets.  
This gave them the ability to fight a conventional war too.

Germany joined the scramble for colonies later than other European powers.

None of them was rich or powerful enough to build colonies.

It needed this navy to trade with colonies and defend them.

He was in office from 1871 to 1890.  
At first, he had no interest in an overseas empire.

Bismarck first thought building an empire was foolish.  
He believed it cost more than it returned.  
But in the 1880s, he changed his mind.

He may have been influenced by German merchants.  
They wanted trade and investment opportunities overseas.  
He may also have been influenced by public pressure.  
Many people wanted Germany to gain prestige by claiming colonies.

These areas were scattered across the continent.

In West Africa, Germany claimed Togoland.  
This is today Togo and part of Ghana.  
Germany also claimed German Cameroon.  
This is now parts of Cameroon, Chad, the Central African Republic, and Gabon.

In southern Africa, Germany claimed German South-West Africa.  
This is now Namibia.

In East Africa, Germany claimed German East Africa.  
This is today Rwanda, Burundi, and parts of Tanzania.

In the decades before the Great War (later called World War I), Europe was mostly stable.

In 1815, after the Napoleonic Wars, European leaders worked to create a balance of power.  
This system was largely successful.

An informal agreement called the Concert of Europe aimed to keep the status quo.  
It helped Europe handle some internal conflicts.  
It also absorbed the spread of more liberal political ideas.  
It did this without causing major political or territorial instability.

There were some wars.  
Most were short.  
Most were limited in size.

Prussia was different in one key way.  
Prussia had a strongly militarized culture.  
Its leaders still saw war as a way to achieve national goals.  
France also sometimes saw war this way.

In 1866, Austria-Hungary and Prussia went to war.  
The war lasted about seven weeks.  
Prussia won clearly.

Prussia had invested in better military technology and weapons.  
After the war, Prussia annexed several German states.  
Austria was effectively shut out of German affairs from then on.  
Prussia became the leading German state.

The war also pushed Austria into a new political system.  
Austria accepted a dual monarchy with Hungary.  
This created Austria-Hungary.

Austria agreed because it needed allies after being pushed out of German affairs.  
But the system was awkward.  
Austria and Hungary had separate national governments.  
They also had separate parliaments.  
They often had different goals, even though they were in the same empire.

Another short war followed in 1870–1871.  
This was the Franco-Prussian War.

France declared war on Prussia.  
The immediate cause was a dispute over who would inherit the Spanish throne.

The fighting lasted only a few months.  
Prussian forces besieged Paris.  
Napoléon III was captured.

The peace treaty forced France to pay a large war indemnity to Prussia.  
France also had to pay for the occupation forces.  
France also lost Alsace and Lorraine.  
These territories changed hands several times again in the first half of the twentieth century.

The defeat was humiliating for France.  
But it helped clear the way for German unification.

The treaty was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.  
This confirmed Prussia’s leadership in the new German Empire.  
It also completed what the revolutions of 1848 had not achieved.  
Germany emerged as a major European power.

These wars were mostly local.  
Because they were short, they did not require full economic mobilization.  
They did not involve many countries.  
Fighting rarely spread into other nations’ territory.

Except for the Franco-Prussian War, the effect on civilians was small.  
There was little civilian death.  
There was little property destruction.

Because of this pattern, many Europeans came to expect a certain kind of war.  
They assumed future wars would also be short and limited.

World War I devastated the world’s economies. The war lasted four long years. It caused huge losses. It also disrupted the labor force across Europe. Governments’ budget plans were thrown off.

## Africa after World War I

Before the war, many African nations traded heavily with Europe. Germany was especially important. It accounted for most European trade with sub-Saharan Africa.

When the war began, trade with countries at war became difficult. Many European goods became more expensive. Many Africans could no longer afford them.

After the war, Britain and France looked to Africa for financial recovery. They relied on their African colonies. They also relied on Germany’s former colonies.

Both countries focused on agricultural development. This often increased opportunities for White settlers. It increased profits for settlers and for the home country. At the same time, it limited opportunities for Black Africans.

In the part of Cameroon that France administered after the war, French officials encouraged coffee farming for export. But they gave licenses mainly to Europeans. They also restricted how many acres Black Africans could grow. Because Black Africans had fewer opportunities, White coffee growers had many workers available. These workers were forced to accept low wages.

In British Tanganyika (present-day Tanzania), Europeans had special rights too. The right to cut and sell timber was reserved for Europeans.

## East Asia after World War I

East Asian countries were also affected by the war. After the war ended, some economies grew. China and Japan are examples.

China was not yet heavily industrialized. Still, China benefited from Europe’s economic problems. Global competition decreased, and that helped China.

In Japan, the 1920s were the Taisho period. Japan’s economy faced many shocks. There were booms and recessions. There was the Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923. There was inflation. There was also a serious banking crisis in 1927.

Japan became heavily dependent on trade with the United States. But Japan’s urban economy was hurt by protectionism. The United States and European countries used tariffs on foreign imports.

Even so, Japan’s economy kept growing in the 1920s. Japan increased military production. Japan also began investing in China.

Japan increased its exports after the war. It increased them even more than China did. Trade with the United States grew a great deal.

Latin American countries saw little real economic change after the war. Many had few industries. Many still depended on agricultural exports for growth.

Some countries faced more competition. Other regions began exporting more commodities, such as rubber.

In August 1941, the United States tried to pressure Japan to stop its aggression.  
The United States imposed sanctions.  
These included an embargo on oil and gas sales to Japan.

This embargo strengthened Japan’s plan to move into the South Pacific.  
Japan wanted to take natural resources from weakening European empires.  
Japan also looked toward the Philippines, which was a U.S. colony.

Japan saw the United States as a “soft” enemy.  
Japan believed the United States would not make the sacrifices needed to win a war.  
Japan planned a surprise attack on the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.  
At the same time, Tokyo and Washington were still trying for a last-minute diplomatic settlement.

The United States wanted Japan to withdraw from China.  
Japan would not agree to this.  
Japan also believed the United States would not accept further negotiations.  
Japan’s leaders decided they had to act against the United States while they still could.

U.S. intelligence services had broken several Japanese codes.  
By late November 1941, the United States sent warnings to its forces.  
The warnings said war with Japan was likely.  
They said the Philippines was the most likely target.

Early on the morning of December 7, 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.  
A Japanese task force avoided detection.  
The surprise attack devastated the U.S. fleet.

Japan sank or damaged eight battleships.  
It also damaged smaller ships.  
About three hundred aircraft were destroyed or damaged.  
More than two thousand people were killed.  
More than one thousand others were injured.

Japan launched near-simultaneous attacks on U.S. bases.

After World War II, most European nations quickly chose a side. They joined either the Western Bloc or the Eastern Bloc. One country was different: Yugoslavia.

In 1942, communist partisans fought the Axis powers. They fought as part of the People’s Liberation Front. That same year, they formed a government. It was called the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ).

In 1943, Italian forces left Yugoslavia. AVNOJ then took control of the territory. It created a new state called Democratic Federal Yugoslavia. The partisan leader, Josip Broz Tito, became prime minister.

In 1945, Yugoslavia ended its monarchy. Tito was recognized as the country’s leader. A nationwide election soon confirmed this result.

Yugoslavia was communist from the start. In 1947, it helped found Cominform. Cominform was the Information Bureau of the Communist and Workers’ Parties.

Cominform’s goal was to guide communist governments in Europe after the war. It aimed to help them coordinate against anti-communist activity in the rest of Europe. The Soviet Union would lead and advise the others.

Tito and Joseph Stalin clashed early. Tito wanted Yugoslavia to include Bulgaria and Albania. He also wanted parts of Greece, Italy, and Austria. Stalin rejected these claims. He thought they were unreasonable. He also feared they would cause conflict with Western Europe.

Yugoslavia also supported Greek communists in the Greek civil war. Stalin opposed this too. Again, he believed it would anger the West.

Tito refused to accept a lesser role for Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia had freed itself from the Axis without Soviet help. Tito believed the Soviet Union should treat Yugoslavia as an equal. He did not want Yugoslavia to be a satellite state that took orders.

In 1948, Cominform expelled Yugoslavia. Tito then sought help from the United States. The United States helped Yugoslavia survive. This was important because Yugoslavia could not trade with its Eastern Bloc neighbors.

Tito also worried about becoming a puppet of the United States. During the 1950s and 1960s, Yugoslavia became economically self-sufficient. It also traded with countries in both the Western and Eastern Blocs.

In 1960, Tito spoke to the United Nations General Assembly. He called on “non-bloc countries” to unite. He urged them to work for shared goals. These goals included decolonization and disarmament. They also included bans on nuclear testing. Another goal was equal economic development.

Joseph Stalin died in 1953.

In February 1956, Khrushchev spoke at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party.  
He denounced the late Stalin.  
He accused Stalin of crimes against the Soviet people.

Khrushchev then began de-Stalinization.  
He changed many Stalin-era policies.  
He reduced censorship of the arts.  
He released many people jailed for political reasons.  
He dissolved the special tribunals that had convicted them.  
He removed Stalin’s name from public buildings.  
He also took down monuments to Stalin.

## Poland, 1956

In the Eastern Bloc, these changes signaled a political thaw.

In June 1956, workers in Poznan, Poland, rioted.  
They protested food shortages.  
They protested poor housing.  
They also protested other grievances.

In the autumn, protests spread to other cities.  
These protests were strongly nationalistic.  
People demanded the Soviet army leave Poland.  
They also demanded Russian language classes be removed from Polish school curricula.

In October, Władysław Gomułka became leader of the Polish Communist Party.  
This made him the leader of Poland.  
He called for government reforms.

Khrushchev feared Poland might leave the Eastern Bloc.  
He mobilized Soviet troops in Poland.  
He moved them toward Warsaw.  
He also flew to Warsaw in person.

Gomułka assured Khrushchev of two things.  
He would not end communism.  
He would not end Poland’s relationship with the Soviet Union.

After this, Khrushchev agreed that reforms could happen.

Poland then made several changes.  
It ended the collectivization of Polish agriculture.  
Soviet advisers were sent home.  
Political prisoners were released.

They wanted to read their demands on the air.  
The State Security Police opened fire.  
Several students were killed.

An uprising began.  
Citizens fought the police.  
They also fought Soviet troops.

Protesters attacked the parliament building.  
Ernő Gerő was the head of the ruling Hungarian Working People’s Party.  
He was also the leader of the country.  
He fled.  
His prime minister, András Hegedüs, also fled.

Imre Nagy became prime minister.  
Nagy was a reformer.

He dissolved the State Security Police.  
He demanded Soviet troops leave Budapest.

He said Hungary was no longer a member of the Warsaw Pact.  
He said Hungary would remain neutral in international affairs.

European ship captains bought captives from African sellers.  
Europeans did not introduce slavery to Africa.  
Slavery had existed in Africa for centuries before the triangular trade.  

But African slavery was different from the slavery many Africans faced in the Americas.

## Slavery in African societies
Slavery existed in many African societies.  
People could become enslaved in several ways.

- In some places, slavery was a punishment for a crime.  
- In other places, people were enslaved to pay a debt.  
- Some parents sold children into slavery to pay a debt.  
- During famine or other hardship, parents might sell children to wealthier people.  
  This could bring money to the parents and food for the children.  
- Many enslaved people were prisoners of war.

Africans often enslaved people to enlarge their households.  
Households were the basic economic units of society.  
Families suffered if they lacked enough workers.  
They needed people to farm or to tend herds.  
Slavery was one way to solve this problem.

Some enslaved people stayed with the slaveholder for life.  
Others expected to regain freedom.  
For example, a person enslaved for a debt could be freed after the debt was paid.

Even people enslaved for life could sometimes take part in community life.  
They could marry.  
A spouse might be free.  
Their children would be free.  
They might own property.  
This could include enslaved people of their own.  
They were sometimes respected, especially if they had important skills or knowledge.

In many African societies, slavery was seen as a misfortune that could happen to anyone.  
It did not mean a person was naturally inferior.  
Life as an enslaved person was not easy.  
But it was often not like Atlantic plantation slavery.

## Slavery in the Americas
Slavery in the Americas was different.  
It was **chattel slavery**.  
In chattel slavery, a person is owned as property, like an object.

Enslaved people had no legal rights as persons.  
They could be bought, sold, inherited, or given away.  
They had no right to control their bodies or their labor.  
They could be forced to do whatever the slaveholder wanted.

Their status could pass to their children.  
In every European colony in the Americas, a child born to an enslaved woman was born enslaved.

Chattel slavery also existed in Africa.  
But in the Americas, it was the only form of slavery.

## How the Atlantic trade changed slavery in Africa
For centuries, Africans took part in the trans-Saharan slave trade.  
They sold prisoners in North Africa and on the Swahili Coast.  
These captives were transported to the Mediterranean or the Middle East.

Then Europeans arrived and paid large sums.  
This changed the focus of the slave trade.  
Africans began capturing and enslaving many more Africans to sell to Europeans.  
The goal was transport across the Atlantic.

Wars were started against rival peoples to take captives.  
Slave traders led expeditions into the interior to kidnap people far from the coast.  
People were not safe even in their own homes.

In the 1700s, slave traders kidnapped Olaudah Equiano and his sister.  
They were playing at home.  
Their parents were away.  
Strangers climbed over a wall into the courtyard and carried the children away.  
Some people were also tricked and sold by their own relatives.

## The march to the coast
After capture, people were marched for days to coastal trading places.  
Europeans traded goods there for human beings.  
Many captives died on the way.

Traders often chained captives together.  
Sometimes devices were fixed to captives’ necks.  
If someone escaped, the device could prevent them from lowering their head to drink.  
They could die of thirst.

At the coast, traders stripped captives naked.  
They shaved their heads to reduce lice.  
They greased bodies with palm oil.  
This was meant to make captives look fit and healthy to buyers.

## Slave trading ports and European buyers
Many slave trading ports grew on the west coast of Africa.  
This happened from the 1400s through the 1700s.

Ports included:  
- Ouidah (Whydah), Grand-Popo, Jaquim, and Porto-Novo (in modern Benin)  
- Badagry (in Nigeria)  
- Little Popo (in Togo)

In these ports, European traders bargained with African slave traders.  
The Europeans included English, Dutch, French, Portuguese, Spanish, Danish, and Swedish traders and sea captains.
