Liberalism aims for freedom from restraint. It supports freedom of expression. It supports popular sovereignty. It supports representative government. It supports the protection of private property and civil rights.

The meaning of “liberalism” has changed over time. Nineteenth-century liberalism was not the same as liberalism in the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries. In the twenty-first-century United States, people called liberals often support government help for the poor. They also often support government action to promote equality. In the nineteenth century, liberals usually opposed government intervention.

Liberalism and nationalism can exist together. They are not mutually exclusive. For example, nationalist leaders like Mazzini also adopted many liberal principles.

Over time, people began to separate **political liberalism** from **economic liberalism**. This distinction grew from Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke and Adam Smith.

## Political liberalism

Political liberalism is based on John Locke’s ideas. Locke emphasized the **consent of the governed**. He also argued that people have natural rights to **life, liberty, and property**.

Political liberalism supports limited government. It also supports the right to oppose political authority that does not have the people’s consent.

Liberals believed these goals could be protected in specific ways. Government power should have clear limits. Rights should be guaranteed to all citizens. These rights should be written into a constitution.

In the eighteenth century, liberalism also supported religious toleration. It supported the separation of church and state.

These ideas shaped several revolutionary movements. They influenced revolutions in Britain’s North American colonies, Haiti, and France. Each of these revolutions produced written constitutions. These constitutions claimed that the people are sovereign.

Enlightenment ideas about natural rights were tested through these revolutions. In the nineteenth century, liberal political thought developed a lasting commitment to consent of the governed. It also developed a lasting commitment to equality before the law.

## John Stuart Mill and individual rights

One of the most famous nineteenth-century liberals was the English philosopher John Stuart Mill. He argued that individual rights must be protected from censorship and tyranny.

His book *On Liberty* was published in 1859. It emphasized toleration. It argued that different ethical codes can exist peacefully in the same society.

Mill said people should be free to make ethical choices about their own lives. He believed the government should not intrude or obstruct those choices.

Mill also supported equality. He was an important supporter of women’s rights. His essay *On the Subjection of Women* influenced the nineteenth-century women’s rights movement.

## Economic liberalism

Locke and Mill focused on natural rights and equality. **Economic liberalism** came from the ideas of the Scottish economist Adam Smith.

Smith’s theories influenced the growing capitalism of the period. He supported **laissez-faire**. This is the idea that the economy should be free from government interference.

In *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759), Smith argued that self-interest in a free market is regulated by unseen forces. He called this the “invisible hand.” He believed government interference would disrupt these forces.

Smith argued that people should be allowed to seek financial success without government restraint. He believed this would increase prosperity. He believed others would benefit from that greater prosperity.

Smith’s laissez-faire theory focused mainly on economics. Still, like Mill and Locke, he supported freedom from government restraint. He also supported the protection of natural rights as key principles of good government.

chapter_key: Cultural Movements of the Second Industrial Revolution
text:
The industrial city was more than a place to live, work, and have fun.  
It also became a subject in late nineteenth-century art and literature.  
Industrialization shaped culture as much as it shaped production and travel.

## Romanticism

The first major cultural response to industrialization was **romanticism**.  
It began in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.  

Romanticism valued emotion and imagination.  
It often focused on nature.  
It also focused on ordinary people, the exotic, the ancient, and the supernatural.  

Romantic writers and artists praised the beauty and power of nature.  
They criticized how cities and industrial growth harmed people and the environment.  
William Blake called England’s factories “dark satanic mills.”  
This phrase captured the romantic view of modern life.

## Realism

Another major nineteenth-century movement was **realism**.  
Realism focused on everyday life in the modern world.  
It did not focus on the exotic, the ancient, or the faraway, as romanticism did.  

Realists showed life as it was.  
This included life’s ugly side.  

Some realist painters chose rural subjects.  
Rosa Bonheur and Jean-François Millet painted the countryside.  
They showed rural horse fairs.  
They showed oxen pulling plows.  
They showed men sowing fields.  

Other realists focused on modern cities and city people.  
John Sloan and George Luks painted barrooms.  
They also painted crowded streets in working-class neighborhoods.

## Realist writers and the city

Writers also made the city a main subject.  
One of the greatest realist writers was Britain’s Charles Dickens.  

In many popular novels, Dickens described the hard lives of urban people.  
He wrote about poor, working-class, and middle-class city dwellers.  
He set scenes in foundling homes, prisons, poor neighborhoods, and dark streets.  

Some critics said he was unrealistic about the “virtuous poor.”  
Even so, his writing and his activism raised awareness.  
This was especially true about the suffering of children.  
His work helped bring some social change.

Other writers focused even more on harsh and shabby life.  
In Russia, Fyodor Dostoyevsky described St. Petersburg streets.  
He wrote about rundown areas where the poor were forced to live.  
He also wrote about cheap saloons where they looked for relief.  

In France, Honoré de Balzac showed the seedy side of city life.  
He often told stories about crime.  

Another French novelist, Gustave Flaubert, wrote *Madame Bovary*.  
It is about a rural doctor’s young wife.  
Her desire for consumer goods and city pleasures leads to her ruin.  

In the United States, Kate Chopin wrote about women who felt trapped.  
They felt stifled by marriage and by social rules of the time.

## Naturalism

In the late nineteenth century, realism was joined and surpassed by **naturalism**.  
Naturalism used a detached and impersonal style.  
It showed characters shaped by their environment.  
Often, they could not control what happened to them.

The French novelist Émile Zola created naturalism.  
His many works show people trapped by environment or heredity.  
They act in ways for which they cannot be held fully responsible.

One example is *Thérèse Raquin*.  
It was Zola’s first naturalistic novel.  
He published it in installments in the magazine *L’Artiste* in 1867.  

Thérèse is an orphan.  
The woman who raised her forces her to marry her sickly son.  
Thérèse does not love him.  
She later murders him.  
She does this with help from a brutish man.  
She feels drawn to him by irresistible sexual impulses.  

Critics were shocked by *Thérèse Raquin*.  
They were also shocked by later naturalist works.  
They called the book immoral.

## Naturalism in the United States: *McTeague*

American readers were also shocked by *McTeague*.  
It is an 1899 novel by Frank Norris.  

In the story, McTeague is a dentist.  
He marries Trina.  
His friend had been in love with Trina.  

The friend takes revenge.  
He ruins McTeague’s dental practice.  
McTeague steals money from Trina and runs away.  

He later returns.  
He has spent all the stolen money.  
Trina refuses to help him.  
McTeague beats her to death.  

He then runs from the law.  
His former friend chases him.  
The novel ends in the desert.  
McTeague is stranded there.  
He is handcuffed to the body of his friend, whom he has killed.  

In *McTeague*, people are greedy, unfaithful, and violent.  
There is no escape from life’s horrors.

Slavery and serfdom disappeared from the industrialized world in the nineteenth century.  
But other systems still kept people working for a long time.  
Two of these systems were **contract labor** and **debt bondage**.

**Contract labor** is when people sign a contract.  
The contract promises they will work in exchange for a fee.  
Contract labor still exists today.

**Indentured servitude** is one type of contract labor.  
People agree to work for a set period of time.  
They also agree to a set form of compensation.  
Indentured servants are not enslaved.  
However, while the contract lasts, employers have almost total control.  
Workers are not allowed to leave.

**Debt bondage** is different.  
A person who owes money works for the creditor until the debt is repaid.  
Sometimes the person provides someone else to work instead.

Indentured servitude and debt bondage are similar.  
Both were common in the later nineteenth century.  
They differ from slavery in one key way.  
In theory, the bondage ends at some point.

## Contract labor in the United States and Hawaii

In the United States, indentured servitude was common during the colonial period.  
Many Europeans used it to pay for passage to North America.  
By the middle of the nineteenth century, it had mostly died out.  
But it still existed in a few places.

In Hawaii, plantation owners used contract labor to grow crops.  
Sugarcane was especially important.  
Workers came from Portugal, China, Korea, Japan, and the Philippines.

Many Chinese immigrants also came to the United States as contract laborers.  
Often, they did not have a contract with their employer.  
Instead, they agreed to work for a compatriot.  
This work paid back the cost of their passage to the United States.

Many Chinese workers were taken abroad by the Six Companies.  
The Six Companies was a Chinese-owned business.  
It was formed to transport Chinese immigrants to North America.  
Workers had to repay their debt to the company.  
Only then were they allowed to return home.

## Contract labor in other parts of the world

After slavery was abolished, other regions also relied on contract labor.  
During the nineteenth century, Australia depended on indentured laborers.  
Many came from Pacific islands.  
These included the Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, Samoa, and the Gilbert Islands.  
The Gilbert Islands are now called Kiribati.

A large trade also sent Chinese and Indian laborers to other regions.  
They worked in Latin America, the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and European colonies in Africa.

These laborers were often treated very badly.  
They were underpaid.  
They were overworked.  
They faced brutal discipline.  
They were given only enough food to keep working.

Reports of this treatment changed policy.  
Many industrialized countries ended their participation in the trade.

Britain banned its ships from carrying Asian laborers to Cuba and Peru.  
These were two main destinations.

In 1874, Portugal followed Britain’s example.  
Portugal stopped the trade in Macao.  
Macao was a Portuguese colony in Asia.  
Many Chinese laborers had been shipped through Macao to other parts of the world.

## Debt bondage in the late nineteenth century

Debt bondage was also common in the late nineteenth century.

In Japan in the 1880s, the country faced an economic depression.  
Many people faced bankruptcy and starvation.  
Some parents “rented” their children to factories.  
This happened especially to daughters.  
The girls received food and shelter.  
The money they earned was sent to their parents.

Some daughters were also hired out to brothels.  
Some dutiful daughters chose this themselves.  
They did it to spare their parents pain.

In the United States, debt bondage was common in the South.  
Southern farmers used it to keep a labor force available.  
This included African American people and poor White people.

Debt bondage also trapped many Asian laborers in South America.  
This could happen even after their contracts ended.

## Why debt bondage was hard to escape

In some places, debt bondage was almost impossible to escape.

Sharecroppers and tenant farmers worked on land owned by others.  
They depended on the harvest for income.

Before the harvest, they needed food and other necessities.  
They bought these items on credit from a local store.  
The store was usually owned by the landlord.

They also often had to buy seed.  
They also had to use equipment owned by the landlord.

After the harvest, they sold their crops.  
Then they repaid their debts.

Often, the system kept them in debt.  
Store prices were very high.  
Interest rates were also very high.  
Harvest income was not enough to pay what they owed.  
The unpaid amount was added to the next year’s debt.

Some employers paid workers with **scrip** instead of money.  
Scrip could be used only at the employer’s store.  
Workers could not shop elsewhere.  
This left them with little choice and often forced them into debt.

In Japanese brothels, women were not paid in scrip.  
But every cost was recorded.  
This included clothing and food.  
The women could not leave until they repaid two things:  
1) the original sum exchanged for them, and  
2) the total cost of their upkeep.

During the nineteenth century and the first decades of the twentieth century, about 60 million Europeans left home. They wanted better economic opportunities on other continents.

Most came from places that were not very industrialized. Many came from farming regions. Examples include southern Italy and Sicily.

About 28 million Europeans and Canadians moved to the United States during this period. Most arrived between 1890 and 1914. Many were peasant farmers from southern and eastern Europe. Many also still came from Germany and Ireland. In the first half of the nineteenth century, Germany and Ireland had sent the largest numbers of immigrants.

Not everyone left only because of poverty. Some fled religious persecution. This was especially true for Jewish people from the Russian Empire. They faced discrimination and anti-Semitism. This sometimes led to violent attacks called **pogroms**. Pogroms killed people and destroyed property.

Others who migrated included political dissidents. Some were craftspeople who lost work because of industrialization.

After the United States, the largest numbers went to Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay. About 4.5 million emigrants went to Argentina. At one point, immigrants made up 30 percent of Argentina’s population.

Latin America attracted many Italians and Germans. It also attracted Spanish and Portuguese settlers.

Canada received about 5.1 million people between the 1850s and the 1920s. Other common destinations were Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa. Australia became especially attractive after gold was discovered there in 1851. South Africa became especially attractive after gold was discovered there in 1886.

In their new homes, European immigrants did many kinds of work.

Many worked in factories. Jewish people were especially active in the garment industry. This was true in places like New York City.

In the United States, Polish people and other eastern Europeans worked in the steel industry in Pittsburgh. They also worked in Chicago’s stockyards.

Portuguese immigrants often worked in fishing. In New England, they also worked in textile mills. There they worked alongside French Canadians.

Italian immigrants did many kinds of work. They worked in agriculture, mining, and the building trades.

Welsh immigrants often found jobs as miners in the West. Irish immigrants worked in mines, built railroads, and worked in factories across the United States.

Women from all these ethnic groups often worked in domestic service.

The reaction in the countries where immigrants settled often depended on ethnicity.

In the United States, people sometimes mocked Germans and eastern European Christians for their “foreign” ways. But these groups were mostly accepted.

Irish immigrants were different at first. Most were Roman Catholics. They faced rejection when they arrived in large numbers in the 1840s and 1850s. But by the second half of the nineteenth century, many Irish people and their children had become established. They became politicians, business owners, and police officers.

Jewish people and Italians were more recent immigrants. They often faced discrimination. Anti-Semitism was common.

By the end of the nineteenth century, many native-born Protestants in the United States called for stricter immigration laws. Many were of northern European ancestry.

In 1924, the United States passed the Johnson-Reed Act. This law set a quota for the total number of immigrants allowed to enter from outside the Western Hemisphere.

The law also set limits by nationality. Each nationality could send only 2 percent of the number of people from that nationality who were already living in the United States in 1890.

This created a second barrier. A person could be turned away if the quota for their nationality was already full. This could happen even if the overall total quota was not yet full.

Before 1890, most immigrants had come from northern and western Europe. Fewer had come from southern or eastern Europe. Because of this, the 2 percent rule allowed many more English, Irish, and German immigrants than Italian, Polish, or Russian Jewish immigrants.

Immigration from Asia was banned. The only exception was the U.S. territory of the Philippines.

In Latin America, the situation was different.

Argentina and Uruguay had never had large populations. They lacked their neighbors’ mineral wealth. They also lacked climates that were good for growing sugar and coffee. Because of this, European immigration was seen as a welcome boost.

Brazil and Venezuela actively sought European immigrants. They wanted to make their populations more White. At the time, their populations were mostly African, Native American, and biracial.

In Britain and the United States, unions developed mostly separate from politics.  
In Germany, France, and Russia, politics helped drive union growth.  
The main political influence was socialism.

Today, socialism is a political theory.  
It supports government ownership of the means of production.  
In the nineteenth century, socialism was different.  
It took many forms.

Socialists in that era shared a few key beliefs.  
They disliked laissez-faire capitalism.  
They wanted to improve the lives of the poor.  
They believed government should solve problems caused by capitalism and industrialization.

## Utopian socialism

In the early nineteenth century, **utopian socialism** was most common.  
It focused on creating a perfect society.

French thinkers such as Henri de Saint-Simon and Charles Fourier described ideal societies.  
These societies were based on sharing and cooperation.  
They wanted to remake society completely.

They often supported ideas seen as radical at the time.  
These included communal housing, free love, and women’s rights.

Some reformers tried to build real utopian communities.  
One example was Robert Owen, a British textile manufacturer.  
He tried these ideas in New Lanark, a village in Britain.  
Workers there lived near his father-in-law’s textile mill.  
Owen also tried them in New Harmony, Indiana.

In these communities, people worked an eight-hour day.  
They lived in decent housing.  
They raised children communally.

## Scientific socialism and Marxism

By the middle of the nineteenth century, **utopian socialism** was mostly replaced by **scientific socialism**.  
“Scientific socialism” meant organizing society according to reason.

French economist and philosopher Pierre-Joseph Proudhon first used the term.  
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels later made it widely known.

Marx and Engels published *The Communist Manifesto* in 1848.  
That year, political revolutions spread across Europe.

Because of these revolutions, voting rights for men were created or expanded in France and Prussia.  
By the end of the nineteenth century, men in France and Germany used voting to change their countries.  
Germany united with Prussia in 1871.  
This created the most powerful German-speaking state.  
Many voters supported the socialist ideas described by Marx and Engels.

Marx and Engels said history changes through conflict between social classes.  
In the industrial age, they said the main conflict was between two groups.

One group was the **bourgeoisie**.  
They owned the means of industrial production.  
This included factories, mines, and railroads.  
These were the tools that generated wealth.

The other group was the **proletariat**.  
They were underpaid workers.  
Marx and Engels said the bourgeoisie exploited their labor.

Marx and Engels believed capitalism would end through revolution.  
They believed the have-nots would rise up and overthrow the bourgeoisie.  
After that, all people would be equal.  
Property would be held in common.  
Class divisions and class conflict would disappear.

This set of ideas became known as **Marxism**.  
It became the main ideology for many people who called themselves socialists in the late nineteenth century.

## Socialism, unions, and political parties

Marx did not try to put his ideas into practice.  
During the Second Industrial Revolution, many workers used his ideas to organize.  
They formed unions and political parties.

In 1864, socialists founded the International Workingmen’s Association (IWA) in London.  
The IWA included many kinds of socialists, including Marx.  
Disagreements soon appeared.

Some socialists supported violence to create change.  
Others supported peaceful and democratic methods.  
Those who supported peaceful methods are often called **social democrats**.

One major social democratic party was the German Social Democratic Party.  
It formed in 1875.  
It supported laws to improve working-class conditions.  
Many of its members won seats in the German parliament.

A key goal was to reduce working hours.  
The party helped create trade unions.  
It also helped pass laws to protect workers.

Similar parties formed elsewhere.  
The Federation of the Socialist Workers of France (FSWF) began in 1879.  
The Social Democratic Party of Austria began in 1889.

## Revolutionary socialist movements

Social democratic parties competed with groups that wanted revolution.

In France, the French Workers’ Party formed in 1880.  
It offered an alternative to the slower approach favored by the FSWF.

In Russia, the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party formed in 1898.  
It united many smaller socialist groups.

Another Russian group was the Socialist Revolutionary Party.  
It formed in 1902.  
It assassinated government officials.  
It did not follow Marx’s focus on industrial workers.  
It also tried to organize peasants.

Many Russian groups that followed a more orthodox Marxist approach joined the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party in 1898.  
A faction of this party was the **Bolsheviks**.  
They supported revolution.  
They took control of the Russian government in 1917.

## Anarchism and the role of government

Socialists also disagreed about government.

Marx said government would eventually disappear.  
He believed it would fade once class divisions ended and equality was achieved.  
But he also said that, before that, workers would need their own government to manage society.

Some socialists feared this would create a new ruling group.  
They thought it would become another form of oppression.  
They believed government should be abolished.  
This belief is called **anarchism**.

A leading anarchist in the nineteenth century was Mikhail Bakunin.  
He was a Russian revolutionary.  
He joined the IWA in 1868.

Bakunin argued with Marx about government’s role in creating socialism.  
In 1872, at the Fifth Congress of the IWA, this conflict led to Bakunin’s expulsion.

## Opposition to socialism and anarchism

Many business owners and many middle- and upper-class people opposed socialism and anarchism.  
They feared these movements.

They believed business owners provided important benefits.  
They said owners supplied goods and services at reasonable prices.  
They said owners helped the economy grow.  
They said owners helped keep their countries strong and competitive.

They also believed owners deserved a fair profit.  
They said profit was fair because owners took financial risks.  
They argued that, to keep prices low, owners could not pay the high wages workers wanted.

Opponents also argued that workers had a choice.  
They said workers could accept a job’s terms or leave.

They argued that if owners could not earn profits, they would not take risks.  
They said the economy depended on those risks.

They also argued that private property encouraged people to work.  
They said without the ability to build private property, people would lose motivation.

They argued that violence and destroying property helped no one.

They said workers should improve their lives in other ways.  
They recommended education, thrift, and self-discipline.  
They warned against demagogues.  
They said demagogues encouraged disloyalty to employers.  
They said demagogues promised unrealistic “workers’ paradises.”

## 1. Unions and Politics

- In **Britain** and the **United States**, unions grew mostly **apart from politics**.  
- In **Germany**, **France**, and **Russia**, **politics helped unions grow**.  
- One of the biggest political influences was **socialism**.

---

## 2. Socialism in the 1800s

Today, **socialism** is a political idea.

- It supports **government ownership of the means of production**.  
  - This includes things like **factories, mines, and railroads**.

In the **nineteenth century**, socialism was not one single idea. It came in many forms.

Many socialists shared these beliefs:

- They did not like **laissez-faire capitalism**.  
  - This means very little government control of business.  
- They wanted to improve life for **poor people**.  
- They believed government should fix problems caused by **capitalism** and **industrial growth**.

---

## 3. Utopian Socialism

In the early **nineteenth century**, **utopian socialism** was the most common kind.

Main idea:

- Build a **perfect society**.

French writers such as **Henri de Saint-Simon** and **Charles Fourier** described ideal societies.

These ideal societies were based on:

- Sharing  
- Cooperation  
- A complete remake of society  

Some ideas were seen as very radical at the time, such as:

- Communal housing  
- Free love  
- Women’s rights  

Some reformers tried to build real utopian communities.

Example: **Robert Owen**

- He was a **British textile manufacturer**.  
- He tried these ideas in:  
  - **New Lanark** (a village in Britain)  
  - **New Harmony, Indiana** (in the United States)

In these communities, people often had:

- An **eight-hour work day**  
- Decent housing  
- Shared child care, with children raised communally  

---

## 4. Scientific Socialism and Marxism

By the middle of the **nineteenth century**, utopian socialism was mostly replaced by **scientific socialism**.

Scientific socialism meant:

- Organizing society using **reason** and **clear rules**

**Pierre-Joseph Proudhon** (a French economist and philosopher) first used the term.  
**Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** later made it widely known.

### Key event
- In **1848**, Marx and Engels published **The Communist Manifesto**.  
- In the same year, revolutions spread across **Europe**.

### Political change in Europe
Because of these revolutions, voting rights for men were created or expanded in places like:

- **France**  
- **Prussia**

By the end of the **nineteenth century**:

- Men in **France** and **Germany** used voting to push for change.  
- **Germany** united under **Prussia** in **1871**.  
  - This created the most powerful German-speaking state.  
- Many voters supported socialist ideas linked to Marx and Engels.

### Marx and Engels: class conflict
Marx and Engels said history changes through conflict between social classes.

In the industrial age, they said the main conflict was between:

1. **The bourgeoisie**  
   - People who owned the means of industrial production  
   - Examples: factories, mines, railroads  
   - These were the tools that created wealth  

2. **The proletariat**  
   - Underpaid workers  
   - Marx and Engels said the bourgeoisie exploited their labor  

### Marx and Engels: revolution
They believed capitalism would end through revolution.

They believed:

- The have-nots would rise up and overthrow the bourgeoisie.  
- After that:  
  - People would be equal  
  - Property would be held in common  
  - Class divisions would disappear  

These ideas became known as **Marxism**.

By the late **nineteenth century**, Marxism became the main set of ideas for many people who called themselves socialists.

---

## 5. Socialism, Unions, and Political Parties

Marx did not try to put his ideas into practice himself.

During the **Second Industrial Revolution**, many workers used his ideas to organize.

They formed:

- Unions  
- Political parties  

### The International Workingmen’s Association
- In **1864**, socialists founded the **International Workingmen’s Association** in **London**.  
- It included many kinds of socialists, including Marx.  
- Disagreements soon appeared.

### Two main approaches
Some socialists supported violence to create change.  
Others supported peaceful and democratic methods.

- People who supported peaceful methods are often called **social democrats**.

### A major social democratic party: the German Social Democratic Party
- Formed in **1875**  
- Supported laws to improve working-class life  
- Many members won seats in the German parliament  

Key goals and actions included:

- Reducing working hours  
- Helping create trade unions  
- Helping pass laws to protect workers  

Similar parties formed in other countries, including:

- The **Federation of the Socialist Workers of France** (formed in **1879**)  
- The **Social Democratic Party of Austria** (formed in **1889**)  

---

## 6. Revolutionary Socialist Movements

Social democratic parties competed with groups that wanted faster change through revolution.

### France
- The **French Workers’ Party** formed in **1880**.  
- It offered an alternative to the slower approach favored by the **Federation of the Socialist Workers of France**.

### Russia
- The **Russian Social Democratic Labor Party** formed in **1898**.  
- It brought together many smaller socialist groups.

Another Russian group was the **Socialist Revolutionary Party**:

- Formed in **1902**  
- It assassinated government officials  
- It did not follow Marx’s focus on industrial workers  
- It also tried to organize peasants  

### The Bolsheviks
Many Russian groups that followed a more traditional Marxist approach joined the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party.

One faction was the **Bolsheviks**.

- They supported revolution.  
- They took control of the Russian government in **1917**.

---

## 7. Anarchism and the Role of Government

Socialists also disagreed about the role of government.

### Marx’s view
Marx said government would eventually disappear.

- He believed it would fade away after class divisions ended.

But he also said that, before that happened:

- Workers would need their own government to manage society.

### The anarchist view
Some socialists feared a workers’ government would become a new ruling group.  
They believed it could turn into another kind of oppression.

They argued that:

- Government should be abolished.

This belief is called **anarchism**.

### A leading anarchist: Mikhail Bakunin
- A Russian revolutionary  
- Joined the International Workingmen’s Association in **1868**

Bakunin argued with Marx about government’s role.

In **1872**, at the fifth congress of the International Workingmen’s Association:

- This conflict led to Bakunin being expelled.

---

## 8. Opposition to Socialism and Anarchism

Many business owners, and many middle- and upper-class people, opposed socialism and anarchism.

They feared these movements.

### Why they supported business owners
They argued that business owners:

- Provided goods and services at reasonable prices  
- Helped the economy grow  
- Helped keep their countries strong and competitive  

They also argued that owners deserved profit because:

- Owners took financial risks  

They said that to keep prices low:

- Owners could not pay the high wages workers wanted  

### Arguments about worker choice
Opponents also argued that workers had a choice:

- Accept a job’s terms  
- Or leave and find other work  

### Arguments about profit and risk
They argued that if owners could not earn profits:

- Owners would not take risks  
- The economy would suffer because it depended on those risks  

### Arguments about private property
They argued that private property encouraged people to work.

They said that without the chance to build private property:

- People would lose motivation  

### Arguments against violence
They argued that:

- Violence and destroying property helped no one  

### Other ways to improve life
They said workers should improve their lives through:

- Education  
- Thrift  
- Self-discipline  

They warned against demagogues.

They said demagogues:

- Encouraged disloyalty to employers  
- Promised unrealistic “workers’ paradises”

text:
Tensions between Germany and the United States grew worse on March 1, 1917. That day, the **Zimmermann Telegram** was published.

The telegram was a message from Germany to Mexico. It was sent by Germany’s foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann. It offered Mexico a deal.

Germany wanted Mexico to help if Germany went to war with the United States. Germany wanted Mexico to create more trouble along the U.S.–Mexico border. This would force the United States to keep more troops at the border. Those troops would not be available to fight in Europe.

In return, Germany promised Mexico land. Germany said that after a German victory, Mexico would receive **Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona**. Mexico had lost this territory in **1848** after war with the United States.

In reality, Mexico was unlikely to join this plan. Even if Mexico had wanted to, it probably could not. In 1917, Mexico was in the middle of violent conflict. Many revolutionary groups were fighting each other. Pancho Villa’s forces were one of these groups.

The conflict began in 1910. A liberal politician, **Francisco Madero**, announced he would run for president. The presidency had been held since 1884 by **Porfirio Díaz**, a dictator. Díaz’s government favored wealthy landowners and business owners.

Díaz won the election through fraud. He had Madero arrested. This led to uprisings across Mexico. In 1911, Díaz resigned and went into exile.

Madero became president. But he did not deliver the reforms many people expected. Revolt then broke out against Madero as well. In 1913, he was forced to give up office. He was replaced by **Victoriano Huerta**, a general who led rebellious forces in the Mexican army. Madero was executed soon after.

Huerta tried to rule as a dictator. Opposition quickly formed. In the south, **Emiliano Zapata** led a rebellion. His supporters were Indigenous peasants who wanted land reform. In the north, the revolution was led by **Venustiano Carranza**, **Alvaro Obregon**, and **Pancho Villa**.

U.S. president **Woodrow Wilson** supported Carranza. He supplied Carranza’s forces with munitions. Wilson also ordered U.S. marines to invade Mexico. He said this was to prevent damage to U.S.-owned property.

In April 1914, the U.S. Navy took control of the Mexican port of **Veracruz**.

During the summer of 1914, rebel factions fought each other. Each leader wanted to replace Huerta. Huerta fled into exile in July.

Carranza declared himself president. Villa and Zapata objected. The United States supported Carranza, and Villa retaliated. In March 1916, Villa attacked **Columbus, New Mexico**.

Wilson responded by sending **five thousand** troops into Mexico to capture Villa. Villa escaped. Within a year, the troops withdrew.

The U.S. invasion harmed relations with Carranza. Carranza saw it as an insult to Mexican sovereignty. By 1917, Carranza was firmly in power. But rebellion continued. Villa fought in the northern state of **Chihuahua**. Zapata fought in **Morelos** in the south.

Because of this situation, Carranza was not in a position to accept Germany’s offer. This was true even if he had wanted to.

Still, when the Zimmermann offer became public, the United States was furious. The United States was not yet a combatant. But Germany was already planning how to break it apart.

U.S. banks also supported entering the war. They feared that loans to the European Allies would not be repaid if Germany won. Some businesses supported war as well. They hoped U.S. help would lead the Allies to give them greater access to global markets.

Public support for war against Germany grew quickly. In April 1917, the United States entered the war on the side of the Allied powers. The United States was already angry about the sinking of the **Lusitania** and the **Sussex**.

- Those troops would not be available to fight in Europe.

In return, Germany promised Mexico land.  
Germany said that after a German victory, Mexico would receive:

- **Texas**  
- **New Mexico**  
- **Arizona**

Mexico had lost this territory in **1848** after war with the United States.

---

## 3. Why Mexico was unlikely to agree

In reality, Mexico was unlikely to join this plan.

Even if Mexico had wanted to, it probably could not.  
In **1917**, Mexico was in the middle of violent conflict.

Many revolutionary groups were fighting each other.  
**Pancho Villa’s** forces were one of these groups.

---

## 4. The Mexican Revolution (1910–1917)

The conflict began in **1910**.

- **Francisco Madero**, a liberal politician, announced he would run for president.  
- **Porfirio Díaz** had held the presidency since **1884**.  
- Díaz ruled as a dictator.  
- His government favored wealthy landowners and business owners.

Díaz won the election through fraud and had Madero arrested.  
This led to uprisings across Mexico.

In **1911**:

- Díaz resigned.  
- Díaz went into exile.  
- Madero became president.

But Madero did not deliver the reforms many people expected.  
Revolt then broke out against him.

In **1913**:

- Madero was forced to give up office.  
- **Victoriano Huerta**, a general, took power.  
- Madero was executed soon after.

Huerta tried to rule as a dictator.  
Opposition quickly formed.

Key rebel leaders included:

- In the south: **Emiliano Zapata**  
  - His supporters were indigenous peasants who wanted land reform.  
- In the north: **Venustiano Carranza**, **Alvaro Obregon**, and **Pancho Villa**

---

## 5. United States actions in Mexico

United States president **Woodrow Wilson** supported **Carranza**.

- Wilson supplied Carranza’s forces with weapons and ammunition.  
- Wilson also ordered United States marines to invade Mexico.  
- He said this was to prevent damage to United States-owned property.

In **April 1914**, the United States navy took control of the Mexican port of **Veracruz**.

During the summer of **1914**, rebel groups fought each other.  
Each leader wanted to replace Huerta.  
Huerta fled into exile in **July**.

Carranza declared himself president.  
Villa and Zapata objected.

The United States supported Carranza, and Villa retaliated.  
In **March 1916**, Villa attacked **Columbus, New Mexico**.

Wilson responded by sending **five thousand** troops into Mexico to capture Villa.

- Villa escaped.  
- Within a year, the troops withdrew.

The invasion harmed relations with Carranza.  
Carranza saw it as an insult to Mexico’s right to govern itself.

By **1917**:

- Carranza was firmly in power.  
- Rebellion continued:  
  - Villa fought in the northern state of **Chihuahua**.  
  - Zapata fought in **Morelos** in the south.

Because of this situation, Carranza was not in a position to accept Germany’s offer, even if he had wanted to.

---

## 6. Reaction in the United States

When the Zimmermann offer became public, the United States was furious.

The United States was not yet fighting in the war.  
But Germany was already planning how to weaken it.

Some banks in the United States also supported entering the war.

- They feared loans to the European allied powers would not be repaid if Germany won.

Some businesses supported war as well.

- They hoped United States help would lead the allies to give them better access to world markets.

Public support for war against Germany grew quickly.

---

## 7. The United States enters the war (April 1917)

In **April 1917**, the United States entered the war on the side of the allied powers.

The United States was already angry about the sinking of:

- the **Lusitania**  
- the **Sussex**

## 7. the united states enters the war (april 1917)

The united states was already angry about the sinking of:

- the lusitania  
- the sussex

The long war forced every country to change life at home. Each “home front” had to adapt.

In Britain and France, many men volunteered or were drafted. Many of them were skilled workers. This left factories short of trained labor. New workers had to be found. Training them took time.

Germany faced a different problem. The Allied blockade cut off raw materials. Germany had to search for new sources.

Production problems became political problems. In 1915, British commanders said an attack failed because they did not have enough artillery shells. This became known as the “shell crisis.”

The shell crisis raised a key question. In a modern, government-directed economy, who was to blame? Was the government at fault for not producing enough shells? Were workers not working hard enough? The British government blamed the army. It said the military had not ordered enough shells. After this, shell output from British munitions factories increased during that year. Output also increased in other combatant countries.

The British government was under huge pressure. The Liberal Party was in power. Historically, it had been anti-war. World War I threw the party into confusion.

The shell crisis and the failures at Gallipoli made the government look weak. David Lloyd George, the minister of munitions and also a Liberal, worked against the prime minister. This deepened divisions inside the party. These divisions came to a head by the end of the war.

After the United States entered the war, it tried to control industry in a new way. It created the **War Industries Board (WIB)**. Financier Barnard Baruch ran the WIB. The WIB controlled prices and organized production to support the war.

But the United States had not embraced central planning or centralized economic control. Because of this, it did not control war production as strongly as Great Britain did. The WIB made some progress. However, it could not dictate to industry. It was shut down immediately after the war ended. Even so, it foreshadowed the stronger government controls used in World War II.

Many governments struggled to pay for the war. Usually, less than one-third of the cost came from taxes. Instead, governments borrowed money. They sold war bonds to the public. They printed more money. They also took on more debt.

Prices rose sharply. Inflation reached new highs. Debt, new money, and shortages made civilian life more expensive. Household budgets were squeezed.

Britain also needed more soldiers. The army began active recruitment campaigns. One popular method early in the war was the “pals” unit. Young men could sign up together. They were promised they would serve in the same unit, with their pals.

This encouraged enlistment. But it had a terrible cost. If a unit suffered heavy losses, one neighborhood or village could lose many young men at once. The practice ended after the high-casualty Somme campaign in 1916.

In Russia, the war showed how much industrialization was still needed. The railroads were not good enough. They could not move troops where they were needed and also deliver food to cities for factory workers.

Russian arms factories could not keep up. They could not produce enough guns and bullets for the army. This lack of equipment hurt troop morale. Soldiers felt the government was not supporting them. Many began to question the government’s decisions.

Many civilians supported the war effort.  
Others opposed the war. They criticized the reasons for fighting.

As the war continued, shortages grew worse.  
Morale on the home front fell.  
Disapproval became stronger.

## Food shortages and unrest

In Germany, soldiers came first in the food supply.  
They might not like the food. But there was usually enough for them.  
Many civilians struggled to find food.

This was especially hard for older people.  
It was also hard for people not working in war-related jobs.

The British blockade of Germany lasted from 1914 until the end of the war.  
It made shortages worse.

Germany began bread rationing in 1915.  
The winter of 1916–1917 was especially severe.  
Much of the potato crop was lost.  
Many tens of thousands of people had only turnips to eat.

Food shortages also led to food riots in Germany.  
These riots began in 1915.

Food shortages also happened in Austria-Hungary.  
Austria-Hungary had less developed infrastructure than Germany.  
So it had fewer ways to transport food.

Austria-Hungary also prioritized soldiers over civilians.  
As in many countries at war, disrupted food supplies hurt morale.  
Some civilians began to question how the government was fighting the war.

## Conscription and growing resistance

Civilian discontent rose as armies needed more young men.  
The war dragged on.  
The early enthusiasm of 1914 faded.

Some recruits did not believe their armies could win.  
Some did not think the risk was worth it.

Other young men were conscientious objectors.  
For religious or philosophical reasons, they did not believe in war.  
So they did not want to serve.

In empires, some men questioned fighting for imperial glory.

Canada faced a conscription crisis in 1917.  
It used a draft to meet Britain’s demand for troops.  
A protest in Quebec City was put down by the military.  
Soldiers fired on protesters and killed several people.

## Censorship and propaganda

Governments used censorship to manage discontent.  
They limited what people could learn about the war.

Newspapers gave vague descriptions of battles and losses.  
Government propaganda showed pro-war posters and messages.

Censorship began in all combatant nations in 1914.  
It expanded to the United States when it entered the war in 1917.

The U.S. government created the Committee on Public Information.  
It produced pro-war propaganda through speeches and posters.  
This campaign was remarkably effective.

Many posters showed German troops as bloodthirsty monsters.  
They warned that Germans would cross the Atlantic and attack the United States.  
The message was that they had to be stopped.

## U.S. laws against anti-war speech

In 1917, the U.S. government began suppressing criticism with the **Espionage Act**.  
It limited what could be mailed.  
It banned anti-war newspapers and pamphlets.

In 1918, Congress passed the **Sedition Act**.  
It banned “disloyal, profane, scurrilous, and abusive” language about:  
- the decision to enter the war  
- the draft  
- the flag  
- armed forces’ uniforms

The law focused on what could be seen as disloyal.  
It did not depend on whether a statement was true.

Anti-war speech was treated as disloyal.  
So it was treated as seditious.

People could not openly question the war without risk.  
They could face prison or heavy fines.

Today, the Sedition Act is seen as violating the First Amendment.  
The First Amendment protects free speech.

Even so, the Supreme Court upheld the act.  
About two thousand people were prosecuted under it.

A famous case involved Eugene V. Debs.  
He was the Socialist Party’s presidential candidate.  
He was sentenced to ten years.  
He served more than three years.

He was punished for anti-war comments.  
He questioned why working-class men had to die in a war.  
He argued they had no voice in declaring that war.

## Deportations and targeting “disloyal” groups

While Debs was in prison, others were also targeted.  
Russian immigrants were seen as disloyal.  
People who supported socialist causes were also seen as disloyal.

The U.S. government targeted some for deportation.

Emma Goldman was one of them.  
She was an anarchist.  
She came to the United States from Lithuania as a teenager.  
She became involved in radical politics.  
During the war, she spoke out against the draft.

In 1919, she was deported to Russia.  
More than two hundred others were deported with her.  
This was done under wartime U.S. legislation.

## Art and literature as criticism

Questioning the war was not only political speech.  
It also appeared in art and literature.

Poets like Wilfred Owen, Siegfried Sassoon, Rupert Brooke, and William Butler Yeats wrote about the war’s suffering.  
Their poems did not celebrate heroic charges.  
They showed the inhumanity of war.

Visual art also showed the war’s misery.  
German artist Käthe Kollwitz did this in her work.  
She lost her son in the fighting.  
She explored mourning and suffering in her art.

These personal depictions reached audiences clearly.  
They helped fuel criticism of the war.

## Bombing, displacement, and refugees

Aircraft changed civilian life in Europe.  
Civilians could be attacked even far from ground fighting.

Germany used zeppelins in 1915 to bomb London.  
Later, it used Gotha bombers to attack the city.

Hundreds of civilians were killed.  
Thousands were injured.

People who lost their homes became refugees inside their own country.  
The psychological impact was immense.

For the first time, civilians were at risk in places without ground battles.  
Bombing also felt unpredictable.  
A bomb might hit one street and miss another.  
This sense of chance made the danger feel even greater.

Refugees appeared across Europe.  
By the end of 1914, more than three million people in France and Belgium had left their homes.

Tensions between Ireland and Britain go back to the twelfth century. At that time, the English seized Ireland.

In the early twentieth century, the biggest political issue was **home rule** for Ireland. Home rule would give Ireland its own parliament. It would also let Ireland handle its own domestic issues. Ireland would not have to follow orders from London on these matters.

Support for home rule grew a lot. By the time of the war, it had been partly approved. However, Protestant Unionists in northern Ireland opposed it. They supported the union with Britain. They also feared a Catholic-led Irish government. They worried they would face discrimination if home rule became law.

Because Britain focused on the war effort, the home rule question was put on hold.

Many Irish nationalists were angry about the delay. Some wanted more than home rule. They wanted a fully independent Ireland.

Irish nationalism led some groups to contact Germany. Germany and Ireland shared a common enemy: Britain. The Irish Republican Brotherhood planned an uprising. They expected German weapons to support it. When the weapons did not arrive, the Brotherhood chose to rebel anyway.

The **Easter Rising** began on April 24, 1916. It lasted several days. Irish nationalists declared the creation of the Irish Republic. They also seized key buildings in Dublin.

Britain responded with military force. Fighting between the two sides caused thousands of casualties. Many civilians were among the dead and injured.

The Irish revolutionaries eventually surrendered. They could not withstand trained British troops. After the surrender, Britain punished them harshly. Many leaders of the rebellion were executed.

Britain’s response pushed many young Irish people toward more radical views.

After the war, the southern counties formed the Irish Free State. Today, this is the Republic of Ireland. The northern counties are still part of the United Kingdom.

Russia already had long-term problems. One major problem was a slow, stagnant bureaucracy. World War I made these problems worse.

The Romanov tsars had ruled since the 1600s. They saw themselves as absolute rulers. They believed no one should question their decisions.

chapter_key: Disarmament and the Commitment to Peace
text:
After World War I, many countries wanted peace.  
In the 1920s, the major powers often supported disarmament.  
They also tried to limit military growth.  
Many people hoped the next decades would be peaceful.  
Several agreements in the 1920s showed this hope and goodwill.

In 1921, the Washington Naval Conference began.  
Its goal was to address the naval arms race from before and during World War I.  
U.S. secretary of state Charles Evans Hughes made a proposal.  
He asked the three major naval powers to do two things.  
First, Britain, the United States, and Japan would each scrap (scuttle) some ships.  
Second, they would limit future shipbuilding.

The conference produced the Five-Power Treaty.  
This treaty limited the building of warships.  
It also limited the size of aircraft carriers.  
Aircraft carriers were a new type of naval ship at the time.

The treaty set ship ratios for the five powers.  
Britain and the United States could have the same number of warships.  
For every five ships Britain and the United States had, Japan could have three.  
France and Italy could have 1.75 each.

Britain and the United States were allowed more ships for a reason.  
They kept fleets in both the Atlantic and the Pacific.  
They used these fleets to protect their colonies.

By the late 1920s, optimism was strong.  
Many people thought the suffering of war might be over.  
In this spirit, the **Kellogg-Briand Pact** was created.

The pact came from talks between two leaders.  
They were U.S. secretary of state Frank Kellogg and French foreign minister Aristide Briand.  
The pact rejected war as a tool of national policy.

Fifteen nations signed the pact in 1928.  
Over the next years, forty-seven more nations signed it.  
But the pact had a major weakness.  
There was no way to enforce it.  
There were also no penalties for countries that broke it.  
Because of this, it did little to stop aggressive military policies in the next decade.

The League of Nations had similar problems.  
It was based on high ideals.  
It could issue statements, restrictions, or condemnations.  
But it could not force countries to change their actions.

Trade restrictions could have some effect.  
However, the League had no military force.  
It could not physically intervene in a member country’s actions.

As the 1930s began, the League faced repeated challenges.  
Aggressive acts happened around the world.  
The League was largely powerless to stop them.

Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931.  
Italy invaded Libya in 1931.  
Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935.

The League protested these actions.  
It protested especially the invasion of Ethiopia.  
But it could do little beyond economic sanctions against Italy.  
Even those sanctions were not supported by all countries.

It became clear that the League had no real power.  
No country needed to fear it.

Many people in the Soviet Union still felt hopeful under Stalin.

This art praised peasants and factory workers.

They believed the government would reward their hard work.  
They thought it would meet their needs better than the tsarist government had.

Lenin saw religion as dangerous.  
He saw it as a rival to socialism.  
From the early years of the Soviet Union, Communist leaders targeted religion.

Many people struggled to give up their faith and traditions.  
This was true even when government policies tried to discourage religion.

Millions of women took factory or farm jobs in the 1920s and 1930s.  
But their situation was difficult.

Women faced discrimination and emotional strain.  
They were rarely given positions of power at work.  
They were also rarely given power in Soviet politics.  
Yet they were expected to produce as much as men.

Women were still expected to be homemakers and mothers.  
That role did not disappear.  
So women had to do both paid work and home work.  
This showed the unequal burden between women and men.

The Soviet Union took revenge on Germany.

The western Allies took a different approach.

It also tried crimes against peace and crimes against humanity.

Twenty-two individuals were indicted.

The U.S. effort to stop the spread of communism led to a major aid program for Europe.  
This program was called the European Recovery Program.  
It became known as the **Marshall Plan**.  
It was named for Secretary of State George C. Marshall.

In 1947, Marshall asked for economic help to rebuild Europe after World War II.  
Many Europeans were poor and living in ruined cities.  
U.S. leaders feared that communism would look attractive in these conditions.

In 1948, Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act.  
This law provided money for Europe’s recovery.  
In total, the program sent about **$12 billion** to Europe.  
That is about **$147 billion** in today’s money.

The money helped Western Europe rebuild roads, bridges, and other infrastructure.  
It also helped restore factories and industrial production.  
Many supplies had to be bought from the United States.  
Because of this, the Marshall Plan also supported the U.S. economy.  
It helped reduce the risk of a postwar economic depression.

The United States offered this aid to all European countries.  
This included Germany and the Soviet Union.  
Joseph Stalin rejected the offer.  
He also ordered communist governments in Eastern Europe not to accept it.

Instead, the USSR created the **Molotov Plan**.  
This plan provided aid and trade agreements to communist countries in Eastern Europe.  
These included **Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, and Romania**.  
It also included the Soviet zone in Germany.  
That zone later became the **German Democratic Republic**, also called **East Germany**.

In 1949, the United States created the **Point Four Program**.  
This program offered technical assistance to industrializing countries.  
It focused on nations in **Latin America, Africa, and Asia**.  
Its goal was to improve living standards.

In the summer of 1963, South Vietnamese generals were disgusted by the corruption of Ngo Dinh Diem’s regime. They also saw that Diem was unpopular. They believed his unpopularity was hurting their fight against North Vietnam and the Viet Cong. The generals assassinated Diem and his brother, Nhu.

Most South Vietnamese celebrated the killings. But the killings did not create a democratic government. Instead, the country was ruled by a series of leaders. None of them were effective. None of them earned the loyalty of the people. The United States kept these leaders in power. The United States was willing to support any politician who promised a hard line against communism and who would continue the war against North Vietnam.

The U.S. role in the Vietnam War grew in 1964. In early August, U.S. ships in the Gulf of Tonkin, off the coast of North Vietnam, reported an attack. A crew member on duty believed he saw signs of a North Vietnamese torpedo strike on sonar. There was no other evidence to support this claim. The incident most likely did not happen. Peace came to Vietnam in 1975.  
But in nearby Cambodia, a nightmare was beginning.

For much of the Vietnam War, Cambodia stayed neutral.  
In 1970, Cambodia’s ruler, Prince Sihanouk, was removed from power.  
One of his generals, Lon Nol, deposed him.  
Lon Nol supported the United States.

After this, Sihanouk made an alliance with a Cambodian communist group.  
This group was called the Khmer Rouge.  
In 1975, after years of fighting, the Khmer Rouge overthrew Lon Nol’s government.

The Khmer Rouge was led by Pol Pot.  
Pol Pot admired Mao Zedong.  
Under Pol Pot, Cambodia began a plan to become a “perfect” communist state.

The Khmer Rouge took private property.  
They forced people in cities to move to the countryside.  
They made the population work in labor camps and on collective farms.  
Many people died from disease and starvation.  
People who could not work were killed.

The Khmer Rouge also carried out a planned campaign of extermination.  
They targeted professionals and intellectuals.  
“Intellectual” could mean something as simple as wearing glasses.  
They also targeted Christians, Muslims, and Buddhist monks.  
They targeted people with Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese ancestry.

The killing ended when Vietnam invaded Cambodia in 1978.  
By then, about three million people had died.  
This was about one-quarter of Cambodia’s population.

Southeast Asia stayed trapped in violence and turmoil.  
But in the West, there were new hopes for peace.  
The Cold War began to show signs of easing.

In 1972, the United States and the USSR met at the Moscow Summit.  
They signed the Strategic Arms Limitations Treaty (SALT).  
This was an agreement to limit antiballistic missiles.  
These missiles were meant to destroy incoming warheads.  
The goal was to reduce reliance on the strategy of “mutually assured destruction.”

This began a period called **détente**.  
Détente meant a relaxation of tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union.  
It included trade agreements and more arms-reduction talks.

In 1975, the United States and the Soviet Union signed the Helsinki Accords.  
Canada also signed.  
So did every country in Europe except Albania.

In the Accords, the United States and its allies agreed to respect the borders of Eastern Bloc countries.  
They also agreed not to interfere in those countries’ internal affairs.  
In return, the Soviet Union promised to respect human rights.

chapter_key: Decolonization in Africa in the Shadow of the Cold War
text:
After World War II, many African peoples wanted to end Western control. They wanted the right to govern themselves.

In 1941, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the Atlantic Charter. It promised self-determination for all peoples. Many Africans wanted that promise to become real.

In October 1945, the Fifth Pan-African Congress met in Manchester, England. Delegates came from African colonies in Europe’s empires. Others came from the Caribbean, the United States, India, Sri Lanka, and Central America. They called for an end to colonialism.

## European powers resist change
Many European colonial powers did not agree. World War II had badly damaged their economies. Some believed they needed Africa’s natural resources and markets to rebuild.

Britain’s colony of Gold Coast (Ghana) received a new constitution in 1946. It showed Britain’s desire to keep control. Africans could elect more members of a Legislative Council. But the council could only advise. The appointed governor held the real power.

## Ghana wins independence
In August 1947, Ghanaians formed the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC). It demanded self-government. Kwame Nkrumah was one of its founding members.

In January 1948, Nkrumah and another UGCC member spoke to Ghanaian ex-service members. Many people were angry about unemployment and inflation. They planned to petition the governor.

A few days later, riots broke out. The government blamed the UGCC. It arrested several members, including Nkrumah.

In 1949, Nkrumah formed a new party. It was the Convention People’s Party. In January 1950, he called for a general strike. He wanted Britain to allow a new constitution to be drafted.

Nkrumah was jailed again. He was still in prison when he won election in 1951. This was the first election in Africa with universal suffrage. Nkrumah became Ghana’s prime minister. On March 6, 1957, Ghana became independent.

## Kenya and the Mau Mau uprising
After Ghana, other British colonies also gained independence.

In 1944, Kenyans founded the Kenya African Union (KAU). It called for liberation from British rule. In 1947, Jomo Kenyatta became its leader.

Britain did not want to grant Kenya independence. Many White settlers owned profitable coffee plantations. They controlled more land than Black Africans did.

In 1952, the Kenya Land and Freedom Army began fighting. It was popularly called the Mau Mau.

The Mau Mau was a nationalist movement among the Kikuyu people. It supported violence to reach its goal. To spread fear, it attacked civilians, both White and Black. People were burned to death or killed with machetes. Africans loyal to the British government were also targeted.

Britain responded harshly. It banned all Kenyan political parties, including the KAU, even though the KAU did not advocate violence. Britain also fought the Mau Mau. Thousands were sent to internment camps. Whole villages were forcibly resettled, supposedly for protection from the Mau Mau. British forces also killed innocent civilians.

By 1956, the uprising was mostly ended. In 1960, Britain began talks about Kenyan independence. Kenya became independent in 1963. Kenyatta became prime minister.

## French colonies and violent struggles
Nationalism also grew in colonies ruled by other European powers.

Some empires tried moderate reforms first. In 1946, France proposed major reforms in its African colonies. It ended forced labor. It ended racially discriminatory practices. It allowed some self-rule. But it did not offer independence.

Many French colonial subjects wanted full independence. They fought for it.

From 1947 to 1949, the Malagasy Revolt took place in Madagascar. It cost thousands of lives.

Violence also ended colonialism in Cameroon in 1957.

In Algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962. France granted independence in 1962. More than one million people of European descent left Algeria.

## The Belgian Congo and Cold War conflict
In the Belgian Congo (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Cold War tensions increased violence.

In 1960, Belgium promised independence in thirty years. Nationalist groups rejected this. Groups included the Congolese National Movement and the Alliance of Bakongo. They demanded independence immediately.

Black Congolese protested. Protests often turned into riots. Many refused to pay taxes.

Many White residents formed citizens’ militias. They attacked Black residents.

Belgium saw how strong the nationalist movement was. It agreed to grant independence on June 30, 1960.

### Mutiny and outside вмешательство
Independence did not end violence.

A few days after independence, Émile Janssens spoke to Black troops. He was the White commander of the *Force Publique*, the security force. He made clear that White officers would stay in charge. Soldiers mutinied.

Patrice Lamumba was leader of the Congolese National Movement. He had been elected prime minister. He replaced Janssens with a Black commander. He renamed the force the National Congolese Army. He promoted Black soldiers.

The mutiny continued. White people were attacked across the country. Belgian forces invaded to protect them.

During the chaos, Katanga province in the south seceded. It was rich in minerals. Katanga declared independence.

Lamumba asked the United Nations for help. The UN had sent peacekeeping forces to restore order. Lamumba wanted the UN to end Katanga’s secession. The UN refused. It said secession was an internal political matter.

Lamumba then asked the United States for help. The United States refused.

Lamumba then turned to the Soviet Union. The Soviets sent weapons and military advisers. In Western eyes, this made Lamumba look like a communist.

Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu (Mobutu Sese Seko) led the security force. He used the chaos to act. He put Lamumba under house arrest. He placed Joseph Kasa-Vubu, leader of the Alliance of Bakongo, in charge of the government.
