## after world war two: new demands for freedom


after world war two, many african peoples wanted to end western control.  

they wanted the right to govern themselves.  



---

## the atlantic charter and pan-african congress


in 1941, the united kingdom and the united states signed the atlantic charter.  

it promised **self-rule for all peoples**.  

many africans wanted that promise to become real.  


in october 1945, the fifth pan-african congress met in manchester, england.  

delegates came from african colonies in europe’s empires.  

others came from the caribbean, the united states, india, sri lanka, and central america.  

they called for **an end to colonial rule**.  



---

## european powers resist change


many european colonial powers did not agree.  

world war two had badly damaged their economies.  

some believed they needed africa’s natural resources and markets to rebuild.  


britain’s colony of gold coast (ghana) received a new constitution in 1946.  

it showed britain’s desire to **keep control**.  


- africans could elect more members of a legislative council.  
- but the council could only advise.  
- the appointed governor held the real power.  



---

## ghana wins independence


in august 1947, people in ghana formed the united gold coast convention.  

it demanded self-government.  

kwame nkrumah was one of its founding members.  


in january 1948, nkrumah and another member spoke to former soldiers.  

many people were angry about unemployment and rising prices.  

they planned to present a petition to the governor.  


a few days later, riots broke out.  

the government blamed the united gold coast convention.  

it arrested several members, including nkrumah.  


in 1949, nkrumah formed a new party called the **convention people’s party**.  


in january 1950, he called for a **general strike**.  

he wanted britain to allow a new constitution to be written.  


nkrumah was jailed again.  

he was still in prison when he won election in 1951.  

this was the first election in africa with voting rights for **all adults**.  

nkrumah became ghana’s prime minister.  


on march 6, 1957, **ghana became independent**.  



---

## kenya and the mau mau uprising


after ghana, other british colonies also gained independence.  


in 1944, kenyans founded the kenya african union.  

it called for freedom from british rule.  

in 1947, jomo kenyatta became its leader.  


britain did not want to grant kenya independence.  

many white settlers owned profitable coffee farms.  

they controlled more land than black africans did.  


in 1952, the kenya land and freedom army began fighting.  

many people called it the **mau mau**.  


the mau mau was a nationalist movement among the kikuyu people.  

it supported violence to reach its goal.  


- it attacked civilians, both white and black.  
- people were burned to death or killed with machetes.  
- africans loyal to the british government were also targeted.  


britain responded harshly.  


- it banned all kenyan political parties, including the kenya african union, even though the union did not support violence.  
- britain also fought the mau mau.  
- thousands were sent to detention camps.  
- whole villages were forced to move, said to be for protection from the mau mau.  
- british forces also killed innocent civilians.  


by 1956, the uprising was mostly ended.  

in 1960, britain began talks about kenyan independence.  

kenya became independent in 1963.  

kenyatta became prime minister.  



---

## french colonies and violent struggles


nationalism also grew in colonies ruled by other european powers.  


some empires tried moderate reforms first.  

in 1946, france proposed major reforms in its african colonies.  


- it ended forced labor.  
- it ended some racist laws and practices.  
- it allowed some self-rule.  
- but it did **not** offer independence.  


many people in french colonies wanted **full independence**.  

they fought for it.  


from 1947 to 1949, the malagasy revolt took place in madagascar.  

it cost thousands of lives.  


violence also helped end colonial rule in cameroon in 1957.  


in algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962.  

france granted independence in 1962.  

more than one million people of european descent left algeria.  



---

## the belgian congo and cold war conflict


in the belgian congo (now the democratic republic of the congo), cold war tensions increased violence.  


in 1960, belgium promised independence in thirty years.  

nationalist groups rejected this.  

groups included the congolese national movement and the alliance of bakongo.  

they demanded independence **right away**.  


black congolese protested.  

protests often turned into riots.  

many refused to pay taxes.  


many white residents formed armed citizen groups.  

they attacked black residents.  


belgium saw how strong the nationalist movement was.  

it agreed to grant independence on **june 30, 1960**.  



### mutiny and outside involvement


independence did not end violence.  


a few days after independence, émile janssens spoke to black troops.  

he was the white commander of the force publique, the security force.  

he made clear that white officers would stay in charge.  

soldiers mutinied.  


patrice lamumba led the congolese national movement.  

he had been elected prime minister.  


- he replaced janssens with a black commander.  
- he renamed the force the national congolese army.  
- he promoted black soldiers.  


the mutiny continued.  

white people were attacked across the country.  

belgian forces invaded to protect them.  


during the chaos, katanga province in the south broke away.  

it was rich in minerals.  

katanga declared independence.  


lamumba asked the united nations for help.  

the united nations sent peacekeeping forces to restore order.  

lamumba wanted them to end katanga’s breakaway.  

the united nations refused.  

it said the breakaway was an internal political matter.  


lamumba then asked the united states for help.  

the united states refused.  


lamumba then turned to the soviet union.  

the soviets sent weapons and military advisers.  

in western eyes, this made lamumba look like a communist.  


colonel joseph-désiré mobutu (mobutu sese seko) led the security force.  

he used the chaos to act.  


- he put lamumba under house arrest.  
- he placed joseph kasa-vubu, leader of the alliance of bakongo, in charge of the government.  


lamumba was later killed by katangese troops.  

the central intelligence agency knew about it and supported it.  

the agency gave money and weapons to mobutu and kasa-vubu.  



---

## britain moves faster: the wind of change


british leaders watched nationalism grow.  

they saw it in kenya and elsewhere.  

they feared more violence like in congo.  


britain moved quickly to free colonies in africa, the caribbean, and asia.  


in 1960, prime minister harold macmillan visited africa.  

he gave a speech called **“the wind of change.”**  

he said a wind of change was sweeping africa.  

he said freedom was coming, even if white britons did not want it.  



---

## portugal refuses to let go


portugal did not follow britain, france, or belgium.  

portugal refused to give up its colonies.  


the second portuguese republic began in 1933.  

it was strongly nationalistic and close to fascism.  

it saw the colonies as part of portugal.  

it claimed portugal brought order and civilization to africa.  


independence movements formed in:  

- angola  
- portuguese guinea (now guinea-bissau)  
- mozambique  


some groups wanted western-style democracy.  

others wanted a communist system.  


in angola, portuguese troops fought several groups:  


- the national liberation front, mostly rural and made up of bakongo people  
- the people’s movement for the liberation of angola, a marxist group, mostly urban  
- the national union for the total independence of angola, mostly rural and mainly ovimbundu people  


in mozambique, the marxist mozambique liberation front fought for independence.  


in guinea-bissau, the african party for the independence of guinea and cape verde led the struggle.  

it was also marxist.  



### cold war involvement and independence


the cold war shaped these wars.  


- the soviet union, china, romania, cuba, and yugoslavia gave aid to independence groups.  
- the united states did not.  
- portugal was an ally in the north atlantic treaty organization.  


in 1974, leftist military officers overthrew portugal’s government.  

they created a democratic government.  

the new government ended the colonial wars.  

it granted independence to:  


- angola  
- guinea-bissau  
- mozambique  
- cape verde  
- são tomé and príncipe  


independence did not end violence.  

in 1975, civil war began in angola over control of the country.  

the united states supported the national union for the total independence of angola and the national liberation front against the people’s movement for the liberation of angola.  



---

## rhodesia becomes zimbabwe


violence also erupted in rhodesia (now zimbabwe).  


britain planned majority rule in its former colonies.  

white residents in rhodesia rejected this.  

they did not want a government controlled by black rhodesians.  


in 1965, white rhodesians declared independence from the united kingdom.  

ian smith became prime minister.  

britain opposed this move.  


civil war followed.  

the white government fought two black nationalist groups:  


- the zimbabwe african people’s union, led by joshua nkomo  
- the zimbabwe african national union, led by robert mugabe  


the soviet union supported the zimbabwe african people’s union.  

china supported the zimbabwe african national union.  


eventually, all three parties reached an agreement.  

britain officially recognized zimbabwe’s independence in 1980.  

mugabe became prime minister.  


after that, thousands of nkomo’s followers were tortured, imprisoned, or killed.  

this continued until nkomo and mugabe merged their parties in 1987.  



---

## south africa and apartheid


in south africa, black africans fought for freedom against white africans, not a european empire.  


in 1909, several territories were combined:  


- the british cape colony  
- natal  
- the boer republics of transvaal and the orange free state  


together they formed a self-governing dominion within the british empire.  


only the white minority could rule.  

power struggles were mainly between whites of british descent and afrikaner (dutch) descent.  


laws denied black africans the right to vote.  

laws also blocked them from claiming most land.  

black africans were barred from living in some areas.  

many were forced into separate homelands.  


in 1948, racial separation and discrimination became a formal system.  

it was called **apartheid**.  


in 1950, the government passed the suppression of communism act.  


- it banned the south african communist party.  
- it also banned actions meant to end racial discrimination.  


in 1960, britain allowed a vote on whether south africa should remain a dominion.  

most people could not vote.  

in 1961, south africa became a republic.  

but the freedom struggle continued.  



### resistance and the end of apartheid


groups like the african national congress and the pan-africanist congress opposed apartheid from the start.  

at first, they used peaceful protest.  


in 1960, peaceful protesters were killed in sharpeville.  

after that, the government banned both groups.  


many activists then used sabotage and attacks on police and military targets.  

they also used nonviolent tactics, such as strikes.  


in 1976, protests broke out in black townships.  

a new law required black students to learn afrikaans, the language of dutch colonizers.  

in soweto, police fired on schoolchildren.  

more than one hundred were killed.  


over decades, thousands of activists were arrested and imprisoned.  

nelson mandela, a leader in the african national congress, was among them.  

many activists were executed.  


by the 1980s, pressure increased.  


- opposition inside south africa continued.  
- other countries imposed economic sanctions.  
- there were boycotts of south african businesses.  
- international condemnation grew.  


in 1991, south africa officially ended apartheid.  

in 1994, the first elections were held with voting rights for **all races**.  

the african national congress won.  

the national assembly elected **nelson mandela** president.

## The Indian Mutiny of 1857 (Sepoy Rebellion)

The Indian Mutiny of 1857 is also called the Sepoy Rebellion.  
It was an attempt to overthrow British rule.

At first, the British East India Company often used indirect rule.  
Over time, the Company changed its approach.  
Its success in India convinced British leaders they could govern India directly.

Many Indian elites saw their power shrinking.  
This made them more willing to oppose British rule.

European Christian missionaries also arrived in large numbers.  
They tried to convert Indians to Christianity.  
This offended many Indians who wanted to protect their own traditions.

## The doctrine of lapse

Missionaries were only one cause of resentment.

Lord Dalhousie was governor-general of India from 1848 to 1856.  
He created a way for Britain to take direct control of more Indian states.

In Hindu custom, a ruler without a natural heir could adopt an heir.  
The adopted heir would inherit the kingdom when the ruler died.

Dalhousie introduced the doctrine of lapse.  
This policy gave Britain the right to approve adoptions.  
It also allowed Britain to annex states that had no heirs.

Starting in 1848, Britain rejected some adoptions and annexed states.  
This mainly affected states with Hindu rulers.  
However, it alarmed the entire Indian aristocracy.

## British cultural changes

Britain believed its culture was superior.  
This led British leaders to change Hindu customs in ways that angered many Indians.

The British tried to end *sati* (*suttee*).  
In *sati*, some Hindu widows were expected to burn themselves alive on their husbands’ funeral pyres.  
The British also passed a law allowing widows to remarry.

The British introduced Western schooling.  
English became the language of instruction.  
This replaced Persian, which the Mughals favored.  
Persian was also a major language of literature and scholarship in many Islamic empires.

Young men educated in these schools were favored for jobs in business and government.  
British schools were more common in Hindu-majority areas.  
Because of this, many Muslims feared Hindus would replace them in positions of authority.  
Muslims had held many of these positions for centuries.

## The Enfield Rifle and the outbreak of revolt

Anger against the British had been building for a long time.  
It turned into violence after the British introduced the Enfield Rifle.

The Enfield Rifle used lubricated cartridges.  
Soldiers had to bite the cartridges open before loading.

The lubricant had been beef or pork fat.  
Pork is taboo for Muslims.  
Hindus consider cows sacred.

The British tried to fix the problem by using a different lubricant.  
Indian troops still did not trust them.  
Some sepoys believed the British were doing it on purpose.  
They thought the British wanted to emasculate the sepoys by forcing them to use offensive materials.

In March 1857, a sepoy named Mangal Pandey attacked two British officers.  
Pandey was a devout Hindu from the high-ranking Brahmin caste.  
The British executed him.  
Then India erupted into a mass revolt.

## British victory and the British Raj

During the mutiny, the rebelling Indians outnumbered the British.  
However, the British were unified.  
The Indians could not cooperate across religious, ethnic, and geographic divisions.

Both sides committed war crimes.  
There were many fierce battles.

The British declared victory on July 8, 1859.  
They celebrated with mass executions of rebel leaders.  
Some British officers criticized these executions.

The mutiny convinced the British government that the British East India Company could not govern India effectively.  
In 1858, the government abolished the company.  
It took direct control of British India.

Britain ruled India directly until India became independent in 1947.

The period from 1858 to 1947 is called the **British Raj**.  
*Raj* means “rule” in Sanskrit.  
It is also called the British Paramountcy.  
This meant rule by the British government through the Viceroy of India.

## Opium and conflict in China

Economic relationships also caused conflict in China.

Britain wanted to end China’s positive balance of trade.  
To do this, Britain imported opium into China.  
The opium came from British territories in India.

The Chinese had used chewed opium for thousands of years.  
They used it as medicine and as a mild recreational drug.

In the early nineteenth century, many users began smoking dried opium.  
This was inspired by tobacco smoking.  
Tobacco had been imported from the Americas.

Smoking opium produced a much stronger high than chewing it.  
Opium addiction became a serious problem in China.

The Chinese government outlawed recreational opium in 1729.  
British traders refused to stop selling it.  
The price of opium rose sharply.

Merchants from other countries also sold opium in China.  
These included France and the United States.  
However, the British dominated the trade from their bases in India.

## The First Opium War

In 1839, the Chinese government seized opium stored in British warehouses in Canton.

Britain responded by sending military forces to China.  
Britain said it wanted to punish the Chinese government and protect British merchants.  
This conflict became known as the First Opium War.

Britain had better military technology and organization.  
It defeated the outdated Chinese military in most battles.

Britain could not conquer the entire country.  
China was too large.  
Instead, Britain carried out repeated raids.  
China could not defend itself effectively against these raids.

In 1842, Britain and China signed the Treaty of Nanjing.  
China had to surrender Hong Kong to Great Britain.  
China also had to open five ports to European traders.  
Britain received favorable trading status.  
China also had to pay a huge fine.

In the next year, a second treaty was signed.  
It allowed British citizens in China to be tried in British courts.  
This made them immune from prosecution by Chinese authorities.

## The Second Opium War

After a short period of relative peace, war began again in 1856.

Chinese soldiers seized a British ship in Chinese waters.  
The ship was crewed by Chinese sailors.  
The sailors were suspected of piracy.

Britain demanded the ship and crew be returned immediately.  
Britain also demanded an apology.

The Qing government refused.  
The British navy then bombarded the Chinese coast.

France supported Britain.  
France hoped to gain more access to Chinese markets.

The United States and Russia did not officially join the alliance.  
However, they gave limited support to British and French operations.

Like the First Opium War, the Second Opium War involved European raids.  
These raids damaged and humiliated China.  
They did not threaten China’s existence.

## The Convention of Beijing and “unequal treaties”

The war ended in 1860 with the Convention of Beijing.

This agreement ceded certain Chinese territories to Russia.  
It expanded the borders of British-controlled Hong Kong.  
It prevented religious discrimination against Christians.  
It removed almost all restrictions on foreign access to China.

The treaty also led to many more treaties between the West and China.  
Later, the Chinese called these “unequal treaties.”  
They used this term because the treaties were imposed, not negotiated.

Hong Kong was returned to China in 1997.

## 1. The indian mutiny of 1857 (sepoy rebellion)

The indian mutiny of 1857 is also called the sepoy rebellion.  
It was an attempt to overthrow british rule.

At first, the british east india company often used indirect rule.  
Over time, the company changed its approach.  
Its success in india convinced british leaders they could govern india directly.

Many indian elites saw their power shrinking.  
This made them more willing to oppose british rule.

European christian missionaries also arrived in large numbers.  
They tried to convert indians to christianity.  
This offended many indians who wanted to protect their own traditions.

---

## 2. The doctrine of lapse

Missionaries were only one cause of anger.

Lord dalhousie was governor-general of india from 1848 to 1856.  
He created a way for britain to take direct control of more indian states.

In hindu custom, a ruler without a natural heir could adopt an heir.  
The adopted heir would inherit the kingdom when the ruler died.

Dalhousie introduced the doctrine of lapse.

- This policy gave britain the right to approve adoptions.  
- It also allowed britain to take over states that had no heirs.

Starting in 1848, britain rejected some adoptions and took over states.  
This mainly affected states with hindu rulers.  
However, it worried the whole indian aristocracy.

---

## 3. British cultural changes

Britain believed its culture was better.  
Because of this, british leaders changed hindu customs.  
These changes angered many indians.

The british tried to end sati (also spelled suttee).  
In sati, some hindu widows were expected to burn themselves on their husbands’ funeral fires.  
The british also passed a law allowing widows to remarry.

The british introduced western schooling.

- English became the language of instruction.  
- This replaced persian, which the mughals favored.  
- Persian was also an important language of literature and learning in many islamic empires.

Young men educated in these schools were favored for jobs in business and government.  
British schools were more common in hindu-majority areas.  
Because of this, many muslims feared hindus would replace them in positions of authority.  
Muslims had held many of these positions for centuries.

---

## 4. The enfield rifle and the outbreak of revolt

Anger against the british had been building for a long time.  
It turned into violence after the british introduced the enfield rifle.

The enfield rifle used lubricated cartridges.  
Soldiers had to bite the cartridges open before loading.

The lubricant had been beef or pork fat.

- Pork is forbidden for muslims.  
- Hindus consider cows sacred.

The british tried to fix the problem by using a different lubricant.  
Indian troops still did not trust them.

Some sepoys believed the british were doing it on purpose.  
They thought the british wanted to insult and weaken the sepoys by forcing them to use offensive materials.

In march 1857, a sepoy named mangal pandey attacked two british officers.  
Pandey was a devout hindu from the high-ranking brahmin caste.  
The british executed him.  
Then india erupted into a mass revolt.

---

## 5. British victory and the british raj

During the mutiny, the rebelling indians outnumbered the british.  
However, the british were unified.  
The indians could not cooperate across religious, ethnic, and geographic divisions.

Both sides committed war crimes.  
There were many fierce battles.

The british declared victory on july 8, 1859.  
They celebrated with mass executions of rebel leaders.  
Some british officers criticized these executions.

The mutiny convinced the british government that the british east india company could not govern india effectively.

- In 1858, the government abolished the company.  
- It took direct control of british india.

Britain ruled india directly until india became independent in 1947.

The period from 1858 to 1947 is called the british raj.

- Raj means “rule” in sanskrit.  
- It is also called the british paramountcy.  
- This meant rule by the british government through the viceroy of india.

## 6. Opium and conflict in china

Economic relationships also caused conflict in china.

Britain wanted to end china’s positive balance of trade.  
To do this, britain imported opium into china.  
The opium came from british territories in india.

The chinese had used chewed opium for thousands of years.  
They used it as medicine and as a mild recreational drug.

In the early nineteenth century, many users began smoking dried opium.  
This was inspired by tobacco smoking.  
Tobacco had been imported from the americas.

Smoking opium produced a much stronger effect than chewing it.  
Opium addiction became a serious problem in china.

The chinese government outlawed recreational opium in 1729.  
British traders refused to stop selling it.  
The price of opium rose sharply.

Merchants from other countries also sold opium in china.  
These included france and the united states.  
However, the british dominated the trade from their bases in india.

## 7. The first opium war

In 1839, the chinese government seized opium stored in british warehouses in canton.

Britain responded by sending military forces to china.  
Britain said it wanted to punish the chinese government and protect british merchants.  
This conflict became known as the first opium war.

Britain had better military technology and organization.  
It defeated the outdated chinese military in most battles.

Britain could not conquer the entire country.  
China was too large.

Instead, britain carried out repeated raids.  
China could not defend itself effectively against these raids.

In 1842, britain and china signed the treaty of nanjing.

- China had to give hong kong to great britain.  
- China also had to open five ports to european traders.  
- Britain received favorable trading status.  
- China also had to pay a huge fine.

It allowed british citizens in china to be tried in british courts.  
This made them protected from prosecution by chinese authorities.

The ship was crewed by chinese sailors.

Britain also demanded an apology.

The british navy then bombarded the chinese coast.

France supported britain.  
France hoped to gain more access to chinese markets.

The united states and russia did not officially join the alliance.  
However, they gave limited support to british and french operations.

Like the first opium war, the second opium war involved european raids.  
These raids damaged and humiliated china.  
They did not threaten china’s existence.

## The Holy Alliance and the Monroe Doctrine

The United States feared European intervention in the Americas. It worried about national security and trade.

In 1815, after Napoléon’s defeat at Waterloo, Austria, Prussia, and Russia formed the Holy Alliance. The alliance aimed to protect European empires by discouraging revolution. At conferences in 1820 and 1821, the Holy Alliance claimed the right to intervene in rebellions. These were rebellions that threatened European monarchs. In 1820–1821, Austrian troops crushed a rebellion in Naples.

The Holy Alliance did not intervene in 1820 to help Fernando VII. That year, Spanish liberals forced him to restore the Constitution of 1812. But in 1822, the Holy Alliance agreed to support a French invasion of Spain. France’s Louis XVIII would invade to end Spain’s revolutionary movement. The goal was also to restore the imprisoned Fernando to the throne.

The Holy Alliance also wanted to restore Fernando VII’s control over Spain’s American colonies. The United States opposed this. Britain also opposed it, because Britain traded heavily with Latin America.

Britain’s foreign minister suggested a joint warning by Britain and the United States. The warning would tell France and the Holy Alliance not to interfere in the former Spanish colonies. With reluctant support from President James Monroe, Adams announced the **Monroe Doctrine** in 1823. This U.S. foreign policy warned European nations not to interfere with independent countries in the Western Hemisphere.

In 1826, Bolívar called the Congress of Panama. He wanted to strengthen ties among the new nations of former Spanish America. He also wanted programs of mutual cooperation. He hoped to create a permanent alliance.

The United States, Haiti, and Brazil were notably absent. But the biggest problem was internal weakness in the new nations.

The legacy of the revolutions was mixed. The new nations were free from Spain. But colonial social hierarchies remained. These tensions grew into social conflict. Groups included enslaved Africans, Indigenous peoples, mestizos, pardos, and White people.

Provinces fought each other. After defeating royalist forces, popular armies faced civil wars. They fought over what the new postcolonial order would be.

Creole leaders like Bolívar and San Martín were not the only heirs of independence. Local military chieftains became the main postcolonial leaders. They often allied with wealthy creole landowners. They kept their power in place.

Latin American independence movements wanted to end the rule of their mercantilist “parent” countries. They also wanted to end an economic system that slowed the growth of the colonies.

Many successful movements were led by well-educated elites. These leaders often faced resistance from most of the race-mixed population. Many people in this majority group supported the homeland instead.

Because they lacked broad popular support, the White creole minority had to move carefully. This group was exploitative. It also feared the oppressed mixed-race majorities. So the creole leaders often had to negotiate their gains step by step.

Liberators such as Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín, Pedro I, and Agustín de Iturbide got no major help from outside powers. They also often lacked a single, unified plan or strategy. They faced huge distances and difficult natural barriers. They also faced economic and cultural isolation between the regions they tried to unite.

Brazil’s independence showed more continuity with its colonial past than any other Latin American country. Brazil ended Portuguese rule after 1822. But it did not become a republic. It became an independent empire.

Brazil’s first emperor, Pedro I, was a prince from the Portuguese royal family. He was also an heir to the Portuguese throne. Portuguese-born men still controlled trade. They also held powerful positions in the bureaucracy, the army, and the church.

Politics in imperial Brazil was shaped by a conservative-liberal split. This division reflected conflicts between different economic groups. Independence did not bring major changes to colonial social and economic structures. The new constitutional monarchy mainly made the existing system official. It regularized the status quo.

Latin American independence created strong interest outside the region. This interest encouraged foreign travel and travel writing. Many people in the United States and Europe learned about South America through these accounts.

In the nineteenth century, European women usually did not travel for pleasure. Tourism is mainly a twentieth-century invention. Maria Dundas Graham Calcott came to South America in the 1820s with her husband, a navy officer. She served as governess to Pedro I’s daughter. This daughter was Princess Maria da Glória, the future queen of Portugal.

Graham kept diaries from 1821 to 1823. These diaries give a rare view of the Brazilian court during the independence process. They also show her broad interest in everyday life. She wrote about Brazil, including Salvador and Rio de Janeiro. She also wrote about Chile, including Santiago.

In Chile, Graham studied science and botany. She did this with her family’s friend Thomas Cochrane. Cochrane was a former British navy officer.

Graham wrote to inform and entertain people of her own time. Today, her writing helps historians in other ways. It offers insight into gender relations in the newly independent South American nations. It also shows the elite social world Graham moved in during the early nineteenth century.

She focused on topics she saw as “suitable.” These included fashion and motherhood. These topics connected to the lives of Brazilian women. Public life was mostly controlled by men. Her diaries show that foreign women observers like her were still outsiders.

Graham was an urban elite woman. She was also Protestant. Her writing presented English customs and behavior as a “civilized” model for the world. This was a clear bias. Yet her focus on private life still reveals a great deal. It shows details about Brazilian women’s lives. It also helps explain public events in South American society. At the same time, it shows Graham’s own ideas about femininity.

Her travel narrative is a window into her perspective. It shows how she believed nineteenth-century Brazilian women shaped their lives and their surroundings.

By the end of the nineteenth century, chattel slavery remained in only a few places.  
Chattel slavery is a system where one person is owned by another.  
An enslaved person can be bought or sold.

Some nations ended slavery before the Second Industrial Revolution began.

Japan officially abolished slavery in the sixteenth century.  
Britain abolished the slave trade and ended slavery completely in 1834.  
France banned slavery in 1848. This freed nearly all enslaved people in the Caribbean.  
In India, the Penal Code of 1861 punished people who tried to enslave others.

The Netherlands and the United States were among the last industrialized nations to end slavery.  
The Dutch freed enslaved people in Suriname, a South American colony, in 1863.  
The United States abolished slavery in 1865. It did this through the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution.

Most Latin American nations ended slavery after their wars of independence.  
These wars happened in the early nineteenth century.

Brazil was different.  
Brazil had a mainly agricultural economy.  
It resisted reformers who demanded emancipation.

In 1850, Brazil finally gave in to pressure from Great Britain.  
Britain was Brazil’s chief trading partner.  
Britain had taken on what it saw as a moral duty to end slavery worldwide.  
This happened soon after Britain freed its own enslaved people.

Brazil ended its slave trade.  
In 1871, Brazil passed a law that freed all children born to enslaved women from that point forward.  
In 1885, Brazil declared that enslaved people would be free when they turned sixty.  
In 1888, Brazil completely abolished slavery.

British pressure was not the only reason for Brazil’s decision.

During Brazil’s war with Paraguay (1864–1870), enslaved men fought on the battlefield.  
Many White soldiers admired the Afro-Brazilian fighters.  
They became less willing to recapture people who escaped.

Many White Brazilians also believed Brazil could not become modern and industrialized with a large population of African ancestry.  
For them, ending slavery was a first step toward making Brazil more White.

Serfdom also mostly disappeared in the second half of the nineteenth century.

Serfs were unfree peasants.  
They were legally bound to work the land where they lived.  
That land was owned by someone else.

Russia had nearly all of Europe’s remaining serfs.  
About eleven million were owned by private citizens.  
Another twelve to thirteen million were owned by the state.

Tsar Alexander II abolished serfdom in Russia in 1861.  
This did not always improve serfs’ lives.

Even after emancipation, serfs had to serve their former masters for two more years.  
After that, they could stay on the land they had worked.  
But they had to buy it, often for high prices.

Domestic serfs were household servants.  
They received no land.

In some parts of the Russian Empire, serfdom continued for a few more decades.

The idea of **natural rights** was a major topic in the eighteenth century.  
Natural rights are rights that all human beings have.  
Examples include the right to life and the right to liberty.

Many thinkers believed these rights are **fundamental and inalienable**.  
That means human laws cannot take them away.  
The idea did not begin in the Enlightenment.  
It came from older traditions of justice and natural law.

For example, in ancient Persian Zoroastrianism there was the idea of *asha*.  
*Asha* means “God’s will.”  
It referred to an unchangeable law from the divine.  
This law was believed to govern the universe.

Many ancient religious and philosophical traditions had ideas about natural law.  
Enlightenment thinkers in Europe changed these ideas into a political system.  
This was new for the time.  
In the eighteenth century, people valued reason more strongly.  
They also wanted to improve human life.  
So philosophers imagined governments based on natural rights.  
They rejected the divine right of kings and traditional Christian social hierarchies.

One early Enlightenment thinker on natural rights was John Locke.  
Locke was an English philosopher.  
He argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property.  
He wrote about this in *Two Treatises of Government*.  
He said people are born free.  
He also said government should exist only with the people’s consent.  
This idea is called **popular sovereignty**.

Locke and other European thinkers said all humans are inherently equal.  
But their idea of equality was paradoxical.  
In practice, many supported colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade.  
These systems denied natural rights to most people.  
They denied them to everyone except White men.

French Enlightenment thinkers also debated natural rights.  
François-Marie d’Arouet was known as Voltaire.  
He strongly supported basic rights and freedoms.  
He criticized the Catholic Church, the aristocracy, and the French monarchy.  
He defended religious toleration.  
He defended freedom of speech.  
He also defended the value of reason.  
He did this in works like *Treatise on Tolerance* and *Republican Ideas*.  
In his 1759 satire *Candide*, he mocked both religion and government.

Montesquieu was another important French thinker.  
He wrote about laws and rights.  
He focused on political liberty.  
He argued for separating government power.  
He wanted separate legislative, executive, and judicial branches.  
This separation would keep government in check.  
He explained this in his 1748 book *The Spirit of the Laws*.

Questions about state power and individual choice also shaped Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s work.  
Rousseau wrote *The Social Contract*.  
The idea of the **social contract** is much older than Rousseau.  
It goes back to Plato and Socrates in the fourth and fifth centuries BCE.  
It also appears in the second-century BCE Buddhist text *The Mahāvastu*.  
Social contract theory says individuals give up some natural rights to the state.  
In return, the state must protect those rights.

Rousseau said human communities create interdependence.  
Because of this, societies must balance freedom and state authority.  
People should be free to choose their actions.  
But government must sometimes limit actions.  
It does this to protect everyone’s rights.

Rousseau also wrote about the **general will**.  
He said a state is legitimate only when it follows the will of the people as a whole.  
It should not follow the wishes of a small elite minority.

Not all Enlightenment thinkers accepted natural rights.  
Some doubted that natural rights existed at all.  
Two examples are Jeremy Bentham and Edmund Burke.

Bentham was an English lawyer.  
He supported utilitarianism.  
Utilitarianism aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.  
Bentham argued that rights come only from the state.  
He said rights do not exist outside civil society.  
He also warned that challenging a government’s legitimacy could cause chaos.  
This could happen even if the government ignored the general will.  
It could also happen even if it ignored natural law.

Edmund Burke was an Irish philosopher.  
Like Bentham, he rejected popular sovereignty.  
Burke did not deny natural law.  
But he said natural rights stop mattering once civil society exists.  
He believed political power should be used only by people with virtue and good judgment.  
He thought such leaders would act in the people’s best interests.  
He also believed people would give up selfish desires for the good of the state.

The Enlightenment produced many different views on natural rights.  
It also encouraged people to think more critically about the state.  
It raised questions about when revolution is legitimate.  
Some thinkers, like Burke and Bentham, defended state power over individual rights.  
Others, like Locke and Voltaire, defended natural rights and political liberty.  
As debate continued, it expanded into social contract theory.  
These discussions focused on the ethics and legitimacy of law and political order.

They imagined governments built on natural rights.  
They rejected:  
- **the divine right of kings**  
- **old Christian social hierarchies**

One early thinker was **John Locke**, an English philosopher.

Locke argued that people have natural rights to:  
- **life**  
- **liberty**  
- **property**

He wrote about this in **Two Treatises of Government**.

Locke also said people are **born free**.  
He said government needs the **people’s consent**.

This idea is called **popular sovereignty**.


---

## 4. A Problem in Practice: Equality and Exclusion

Locke and others said all humans are equal.

But this idea had a clear contradiction.

In practice, many supported colonialism.  
Many also supported the Atlantic slave trade.

These systems denied rights to many people.  
Often, rights were treated as if they were for **white men only**.


---

## 5. French Debates: Voltaire

French thinkers also debated natural rights.

François-Marie d’Arouet was known as **Voltaire**.

He supported basic rights and freedoms.  
He criticized:  
- **the Catholic Church**  
- **the aristocracy**  
- **the French monarchy**

He defended:  
- **religious toleration**  
- **freedom of speech**  
- **the value of reason**

He wrote about these ideas in **Treatise on Tolerance**.  
He also wrote about **republican ideas**.

In **1759**, he wrote **Candide**.  
In it, he mocked both religion and government.


---

## 6. French Debates: Montesquieu

**Montesquieu** was another key French thinker.

He wrote about laws, rights, and political liberty.

He argued that power should be split into:  
- **a legislative branch**  
- **an executive branch**  
- **a judicial branch**

He believed this could limit abuse of power.

He explained this in his **1748** book **The Spirit of the Laws**.


---

## 7. Rousseau: The Social Contract and the General Will

Questions about state power shaped Rousseau’s work.  
So did questions about personal choice.

Rousseau wrote **The Social Contract**.

The idea of a social contract is older than Rousseau.  
It appears in:  
- ideas linked to Plato and Socrates (**fourth and fifth centuries BCE**)  
- the Buddhist text **The Mahāvastu** (**second century BCE**)

Social contract theory says people give up some freedom.  
In return, the state must protect their rights.

Rousseau said communities create interdependence.  
Because of this, society must balance:  
- **personal freedom**  
- **state authority**

People should be free to choose their actions.  
But government may limit actions to protect everyone.

Rousseau also wrote about the **general will**.

He said a state is legitimate only when it follows the people.  
It must not serve a small elite minority.


---

## 8. Critics of Natural Rights: Bentham and Burke

Not all thinkers accepted natural rights.

Some doubted that natural rights exist at all.  
Two examples are **Jeremy Bentham** and **Edmund Burke**.


### Jeremy Bentham

Bentham was an English lawyer.

He supported **utilitarianism**.  
This aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.

Bentham argued that rights come only from the state.  
He said rights do not exist outside civil society.

He also warned about challenging a government’s legitimacy.  
He thought it could lead to chaos.

He said this risk exists even with unjust government.  
It could happen even if leaders ignore natural law.


### Edmund Burke

Edmund Burke was an Irish philosopher.

Like Bentham, he rejected popular sovereignty.

Burke did not deny natural law.  
But he said natural rights matter less in civil society.

He believed power should be used by people with virtue.  
He also wanted leaders with good judgment.

He thought these leaders would act for the public good.  
He also believed people should limit selfish desires.

He thought this was needed for the good of the state.


---

## 9. Summary: Why These Debates Mattered

The Enlightenment produced many views on natural rights.

It pushed people to think more critically about government.  
It also pushed them to think about law.

These debates raised key questions, such as:  
- **when is revolution legitimate**  
- **how much power should the state have**  
- **what rights should individuals keep**

Some thinkers defended state power over individual rights.  
Examples include **Burke** and **Bentham**.

Others defended natural rights and political liberty.  
Examples include **Locke** and **Voltaire**.

Over time, the debate grew into social contract theory.  
It focused on the ethics and legitimacy of political order.

When the war ended, the suffrage movement had already been active for decades. This was true in the United States and in Britain.

People who protested for women’s right to vote were called **suffragists**. Some suffragists took radical action to draw attention. In 1913, Emily Davison threw herself in front of the King of England’s horse at a derby. She was killed.

Suffragist leaders in both countries were often arrested. Many went on hunger strikes in jail. Officials responded with forced feedings. Suffragists used this suffering to bring more attention to their cause.

Women supported the war in many ways. They worked in war industries. They also served in the medical corps. Because of this, politicians became more open to women voting.

In the United States, women won the right to vote in 1920. Many leaders described it as a reward for women’s war service.

Britain used a step-by-step approach. In 1918, women over thirty could vote if they met a property requirement. In 1928, the vote was extended to women age twenty-one and older.

In Britain, property requirements for men were abolished in 1918. All men age twenty-one and older could vote. For men in the military, the voting age was lowered to nineteen.

Other countries followed this trend. German women won the right to vote in 1918. The new country of Poland gave women the vote right away.

Some countries still limited women’s voting rights. They used rules like property requirements. Some required a woman to be a war widow in order to vote.

France and Italy moved more slowly. Women could not vote in either country until 1945.

In Japan, women’s activist groups argued for a political role during the 1920s and 1930s. Japanese law changed to allow women to attend political rallies. However, women did not gain the right to vote until after World War II.

In China, rising feminism was linked to the May Fourth Movement. This helped women gain individual property rights under the law.

Individual women also became well known for their activism. Huda Sha’arawi founded the Egyptian Feminist Union in 1923. She stopped wearing her veil and headscarf. She had already worked to expand education for girls. She was also active in the Egyptian independence movement. In the 1930s, she became vice president of the International Women’s Union.

Zaynab al-Ghazali founded the Muslim Women’s Society in Europe in 1936. She argued that women could take part in politics outside the home. She also argued they could do this while still following Islam.

In the United States, several minority groups hoped military service would bring greater acceptance and rights. More than eleven thousand Native Americans served in the military during the war. Many hoped this volunteer service would lead to U.S. citizenship. Native Americans were granted citizenship in 1924.

African Americans also hoped for change. They had long faced discriminatory laws and racial segregation. Many believed World War I gave them a chance to prove they were loyal citizens.

The United States military was segregated. All-Black units who served overseas saw how people treated them in other places. In France, many were struck by the freedom of movement and acceptance they experienced. They were allowed in combat. In contrast, U.S. units often kept them in support roles. Many felt real optimism that life in the United States would improve after the war.

After 1918, many found that little had changed. Discriminatory laws remained. Even veterans were often treated poorly.

One new possibility was mobility. In 1917, good-paying industrial jobs began to draw African American workers and families north. These jobs were tied to war production. After the war, the movement continued as factories produced consumer goods. By 1920, more than a million African Americans had left the South. This was part of the Great Migration. The Great Migration continued for decades.

Racism also existed in the North. In the summer of 1919, race riots broke out in many cities. In the 1920s, the Ku Klux Klan spread across the nation. The Klan was a White supremacist group formed after the Civil War.

Even so, many African Americans felt northern racism was less severe than what they faced in the South. The North and Midwest also offered more job and education opportunities. These opportunities continued to draw people to northern cities.

New jobs and involvement in civil rights groups, such as the NAACP, helped shape the **New Negro movement** in the 1920s. This movement “promoted a renewed sense of racial pride, cultural self-expression, economic independence, and progressive politics.”

One early goal of the movement was a federal anti-lynching law. Lynching was a vigilante crime. Its victims were overwhelmingly African American. Activists knew that White men who murdered African Americans were unlikely to be punished in southern state courts. They hoped that making lynching a federal crime would lead to more justice.

Congress voted on an anti-lynching bill in 1922, but it was rejected. Another attempt in 1935 was also rejected. White southern politicians resisted federal involvement, even for humanitarian causes.

Racial pride also shaped the Harlem Renaissance. This was a major surge of African American literature, art, and music. It was named after Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City. Many African Americans who moved north settled there.

The Harlem Renaissance flourished in the 1920s. It brought the work of many African American writers into the mainstream. These included poet Langston Hughes. They also included Zora Neale Hurston, who wrote novels, short stories, and plays about the racial struggles of twentieth-century African Americans.

Music from Harlem and other African American communities featured blues and jazz. Both styles became international. They also became the soundtrack for the fast changes of the decade after World War I.

The Harlem Renaissance also influenced writers outside the United States. The work of Jamaican-born Claude McKay helped inspire the Négritude movement. Négritude was a literary movement in French-speaking parts of Africa and the Americas.

Léopold Sédar Senghor helped found the movement. He was a Senegalese poet and university professor. The term “Négritude” was coined by Aimé Césaire. Césaire was a poet and playwright from Martinique, a Caribbean island that was then a French colony.

Négritude called on Black people to reject European culture and values. It urged them to embrace African culture and values instead.

Jewish people had been part of German society and culture since the Enlightenment. Many were deeply assimilated.  
But anti-Semitism had existed in Europe for centuries. It was always present in the background.

After Germany lost World War I, anti-Jewish propaganda increased. Jewish people were blamed for Germany’s problems.  
This continued in the 1920s and 1930s, encouraged by the Nazis.

Joseph Goebbels led Nazi propaganda. His job was to convince Germans that Jewish people were a deadly threat.  
Nazi messages appeared constantly in newspapers, radio, posters, and other media.

The propaganda pushed three main ideas.  
1) Jewish people were a “problem.”  
2) Jewish people were like vermin. This was meant to dehumanize them.  
3) Removing them would create a better Germany and a better world.

## The start of mass murder in Poland

In 1939, the Wehrmacht invaded Poland. Poland had the largest Jewish population in the world.  
This gave the Nazis the chance to begin genocide on a huge scale. This genocide is called the **Holocaust**.

Special killing units followed the German army. They were called the *Einsatzgruppen* (“operational groups”).  
They killed “enemies” and “undesirables,” especially Jewish people.

The Nazis forced many Jewish people into ghettoes. This made them easier to control.  
People in ghettoes were also forced to do labor.

The largest ghetto was in Warsaw. By 1941, it held 441,000 people.

In 1941, the Nazis created six major concentration camps.  
Railroad lines were built to transport prisoners to these camps.

There had been anti-Jewish pogroms (massacres) in Poland before the war.  
During the war, some Polish citizens joined German extermination activities.

## Camps and the “Final Solution”

The concentration camps were both labor camps and death camps.

In 1941, Adolf Eichmann, a leader in the German SS, spoke about winter conditions. He said:  
“the Jews can no longer be fed. It is to be seriously considered whether the most humane solution might not be to finish off those Jews not capable of labour by some sort of fast-working preparation.”

In January 1942, Nazi leaders met at the Wannsee Conference.  
They discussed the **Final Solution** to the “Jewish question.”

They decided that German state policy would eliminate European Jewish people.  
This would happen through forced labor until death, starvation, and other forms of extermination.  
People were killed where they lived, or they were sent to death camps.

## Auschwitz

Auschwitz, in western Poland, was the largest death camp.

It was first built in 1940. At first, it held Polish political prisoners.  
It became a death camp in 1941. That year, Polish and Soviet prisoners were executed there.

Also in 1941, a new camp was built nearby. It was called Auschwitz II, or Birkenau.  
Its main purpose was to kill Jewish people brought by freight train from across Europe.

Auschwitz also included other camps. Some were labor camps.  
In these camps, prisoners worked for the chemical company I.G. Farben.

About 1.3 million people were sent to Auschwitz-Birkenau.  
In January 1945, Heinrich Himmler, the SS leader, ordered the camp closed and evacuated.  
This happened as the Soviet army advanced quickly.

Of the 1.3 million sent there, about 1.1 million died.  
Nearly one million of those killed were Jewish.

Most victims were murdered with poisonous gas. Many were killed soon after arrival.  
Others were shot or beaten to death.  
Many also died from disease, starvation, or exhaustion from hard labor.

## Other death camps and the scale of the Holocaust

In 1942, the Nazis built gas chambers at Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka.  
Prisoners judged “unfit for work” were often sent almost immediately to the “showers.”  
These “showers” were actually gas chambers.

These policies required help from tens of thousands of people across Europe.  
The result was the murder of more than six million Jewish people.  
At least three million people from other minority groups were also murdered.  
These included gay people, Roma people, communists, socialists, and Jehovah’s Witnesses.

Historians disagree about how many people died in the camps.  
The true number may never be known.

## Resistance and rescue

There were many acts of resistance.

One major example was the Warsaw ghetto uprising in 1943.  
German forces crushed it. Thirteen thousand Jewish people were killed.

There were also uprisings in three concentration camps.  
One was at Sobibor. It may have saved lives by forcing the camp to close.

Some people worked to rescue Jewish people.

Beginning in 1942, Irena Sendler joined the Polish Underground Resistance.  
During the Great Action in the Warsaw ghetto, she helped smuggle out Jewish children.  
She is credited with saving about 2,500 children before she was discovered.

Oskar Schindler was a member of the Nazi Party. He ran a factory in Poland.  
He protected his Jewish workers from the Nazis. He saved thousands of lives.

Loukas Karrer was the mayor of the Greek island of Zakynthos.  
He saved all 275 Jewish residents. He refused to hand them over and helped hide them.

In Bulgaria, Dimitar Peshev was deputy speaker of the National Assembly.  
He had supported anti-Semitic laws.  
But he refused a German request to deport 48,000 Jews.  
He helped persuade the government to cancel the deportation order.

Even with resistance and rescue efforts, the Nazis still sent millions to their deaths.

## 1. Jewish life in Germany before the Nazis

Jewish people had been part of German society and culture since the Enlightenment.

## 2. Nazi propaganda and anti-semitism

After Germany lost World War I, anti-Jewish propaganda increased.

Many people blamed Jewish people for Germany’s problems.

This continued through the 1920s and 1930s.  
The Nazis encouraged it.

### How Nazi propaganda worked

Joseph Goebbels led Nazi propaganda.

His goal was to convince Germans that Jewish people were a deadly threat.

Nazi messages appeared again and again in:
- newspapers  
- radio  
- posters  
- other media  

### The three main messages

Nazi propaganda pushed these ideas:
1. Jewish people were a “problem.”  
2. Jewish people were like vermin. (This compared people to pests to make them seem less human.)  
3. Germany and the world would be “better” if Jewish people were removed.  

---

## 3. The start of mass murder in Poland

In 1939, the German army invaded Poland.

Poland had the largest Jewish population in the world.

This gave the Nazis the chance to begin genocide on a huge scale.  
This genocide is called the Holocaust.

### Killing units followed the army

Special killing units followed the German army.

People called them the Einsatzgruppen (this means “operational groups”).

They killed people the Nazis called:
- enemies  
- undesirables  

They targeted Jewish people in particular.

### Ghettos

The Nazis forced many Jewish people into ghettos.

They did this to control people more easily.

They also forced people in ghettos to work.

**Warsaw ghetto**
- The largest ghetto was in Warsaw.  
- By 1941, it held about 441,000 people.  

### Camps and transport

In 1941, the Nazis created six major concentration camps.

They built railroad lines to move prisoners to these camps.

### Violence in Poland

Anti-Jewish pogroms (massacres) had happened in Poland before the war.

During the war, some Polish citizens joined German killing actions.

---

## 4. Camps and the “final solution”

The Nazis used concentration camps for two main purposes:
- forced labor  
- mass killing  

### A statement from 1941

In 1941, Adolf Eichmann, a leader in the German SS, spoke about winter conditions. He said:

“the jews can no longer be fed. it is to be seriously considered whether the most humane solution might not be to finish off those jews not capable of labour by some sort of fast-working preparation.”

### The Wannsee Conference (January 1942)

In January 1942, Nazi leaders met at the Wannsee Conference.

- forced labor until death  
- starvation  
- mass killing in many forms

## 5. Auschwitz

Auschwitz, in western Poland, was the largest death camp.

### How Auschwitz changed over time

- 1940: The Nazis built it first to hold Polish political prisoners.  
- 1941: It became a death camp.  
- 1941: The Nazis executed Polish and Soviet prisoners there.  

### Birkenau (Auschwitz II)

Also in 1941, the Nazis built a new camp nearby: Auschwitz II, also called Birkenau.

Auschwitz included other camps, including labor camps.

Of the 1.3 million people sent there, about 1.1 million died.

- shootings  
- beatings  
- disease  
- starvation  
- exhaustion from hard labor

In 1942, the Nazis built gas chambers at:
- Belzec  
- Sobibor  
- Treblinka

These policies needed help from tens of thousands of people across Europe.

- Roma people  
- gay people  
- communists  
- socialists

Historians disagree about the exact number of people who died in the camps.

The true number may never be known.

There were also uprisings in three concentration camps.

One was at Sobibor.  
It may have saved lives by forcing the camp to close.

Some people worked to rescue Jewish people.

- He was a member of the Nazi Party.  
- He ran a factory in Poland.

- He was the mayor of the Greek island of Zakynthos.  
- He saved all 275 Jewish residents.

- He was deputy speaker of the National Assembly in Bulgaria.  
- He had supported anti-semitic laws.  
- Later, he refused a German request to deport 48,000 Jews.  
- He helped persuade the government to cancel the deportation order.

World War II, like World War I, led to major scientific and technological change.  
These changes quickly became matters of life and death.

Total war changed the relationship between governments and scientists.  
States needed new tools to fight and to protect national security.  
Governments invested in both lethal and nonlethal technology.  
In fall 1939, British scientists quickly shifted from pure research to war work.

New knowledge about radio waves helped create radar.  
Radar gave early warning of enemy attacks.  
Other advances improved electronics for the military.  
These included microwaves and early digital computing devices.  
After the war, these advances helped electronics spread into everyday life.

Allied codebreaking helped create the first basic computers.  
British mathematician Alan Turing led a team for the British Secret Service.  
They tried to break the Nazi Enigma code.  
They built an electromagnetic device.  
It tested hundreds of thousands of key and letter combinations in intercepted messages.  
They eventually broke the code.

Another computing breakthrough was **ENIAC**.  
ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer.  
It was first built to calculate artillery trajectories for the U.S. Army.  
It worked at electronic speed, not mechanical speed.  
By 1955, ENIAC had done more calculations than humans had ever completed up to that time.

The war also brought life-saving medical advances.  
One major development improved the use and mass production of penicillin.  
Another advance came from Charles Drew, an African American physician.  
He developed a process to render blood plasma.  
Plasma was easier to store for longer periods.  
It also provided an effective replacement for whole-blood transfusions.

Racial bias affected this work in 1941.  
The American Red Cross agreed with a War Department decision.  
They labeled blood and plasma as either “White” or “Negro.”  
Dr. Drew resigned from the National Blood Bank.  
He did so because the policy was racist and unscientific.

One of the most dramatic efforts was the push to build the atomic bomb.  
In December 1938, German physicists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split atoms by accident.  
They discovered nuclear fission.  
A few months later, Germany created a secret weapons program.  
It was called the Uranium Club.  
Its goal was to build an atomic bomb.

Albert Einstein saw the danger of this research.  
Einstein was a German-born physicist who had recently moved to the United States.  
He sent a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt.  
The letter was written by physicist Leo Szilard.  
It warned Roosevelt about the German work.  
It urged the United States to increase its own research.

By the late 1930s, British and other scientists believed an atomic bomb was possible.  
Teams of physicists began experiments with nuclear chain reactions.  
Chain reactions are what drive an atomic explosion.  
Some of these scientists were refugees from Nazi Germany.

In August 1942, the U.S. government expanded the effort.  
It created the top-secret **Manhattan Project**.  
Work took place at many sites across the United States.  
Key locations included Los Alamos, New Mexico.  
They also included Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and Hanford, Washington.  
About 600,000 workers joined a fast race to build the first atomic bomb.

Germany and Japan also tried to build atomic bombs.  
Germany faced technical and other problems.  
Many top German scientists had fled Germany.  
Some of them helped the Manhattan Project.  
Hitler also chose to support V2 bombers for the air war with England.  
He did this instead of focusing on an atomic bomb.

In 1941, Japan started its own effort.  
Japan asked physicist Yoshio Nishina to work on an atomic bomb.  
The project was called Ni-Go.  
Japan lacked information from Germany.  
U.S. air raids also damaged progress.  
The project did not advance much.

In July 1945, the Manhattan Project succeeded.  
The first successful test explosion was the **Trinity Test**.  
It took place at Alamogordo, New Mexico.  
William L. Laurence was the project’s official historian.  
He described the test in dramatic words:  
“On that moment hung eternity. Time stood still. Space contracted to a pinpoint. It was as though the earth had opened and the skies split. One felt as though they had been privileged to witness the Birth of the World—to be present at the moment of Creation when the Lord Said: Let there be light.”

President Roosevelt died suddenly in April 1945.  
Vice President Harry S. Truman became president.  
Truman had to decide whether to use the new weapon.

The United States wanted a world of democratic countries.  
It wanted nations to live in peace.  
It also wanted economic growth through capitalism.

The Soviet Union wanted a world led by communism.  
It believed communism would bring peace and prosperity.  
The Soviet Union also wanted to prevent another invasion from the west.

This fear helped explain Stalin’s demand for **satellite states** in Eastern Europe.  
Satellite states were countries controlled by the Soviet Union.

In 1944, leaders met at the Moscow Conference.  
U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt did not attend.  
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill agreed to let Stalin support Soviet-allied communist parties in Romania and Bulgaria.  
Romania and Bulgaria had been German allies during the war.  
In return, Stalin promised to leave control of the Balkans to Britain.

In summer 1945, the Allies met at Potsdam.  
They planned how to divide Germany and its capital, Berlin.  
By then, Churchill no longer wanted Stalin to have so much power in Eastern Europe.  
He warned the new U.S. president, Harry Truman.  
Truman did not know what had been agreed to at the Moscow Conference.  
Even so, Stalin strengthened his control in Eastern Europe.  
He did this by putting a pro-Soviet government in power in Poland.

In March 1946, Churchill gave a speech in Fulton, Missouri.  
He said that “an iron curtain” had cut Europe in two.  
He warned that half of Europe was trapped under Soviet control.

This split became a key feature of the **Cold War**.  
The Cold War divided the world into U.S.-allied and Soviet-allied sides.  
It was a struggle for ideological, social, economic, technological, and military power.  
It lasted until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

It was called “cold” because U.S. and Soviet forces did not fight each other directly.  
A “hot” war is when countries fight each other with weapons.

The division in Europe grew worse in 1948.

Containment meant limiting Soviet influence to Eastern Europe.

Kennan was a U.S. diplomat in Moscow.  
He wrote a message to the State Department called the Long Telegram.  
He said the Soviet government was paranoid.  
He said it was committed to a struggle against capitalism.  
He believed Soviet leaders could not be persuaded by reason.  
He believed they understood only force.  
So, he argued, efforts to spread communism had to be met with strong resistance.

It kept close ties with communist parties around the world.

The Soviet Union saw itself as the main opponent of European and U.S. imperialism.  
Because of this, it supported independence movements in Asian and African colonies.

chapter_key: Life in the Trenches, the Mountains, and the Desert
text:
The trenches on the Western Front began after a stalemate.  
This stalemate trapped the Allies and the Central Powers in the fall of 1914.  
The trenches soon became a symbol of the war.

Life there was brutal.  
Artillery fire was constant.  
Mud was everywhere.  
Soldiers dug trenches to protect themselves from shelling.  
Then they became stuck living in those trenches.

From the start, German troops dug deeper trenches.  
They also built more complex trench systems.  
It was as if they expected to stay a long time.  
Early Allied trenches were simpler.  
Over the years, Allied trenches became more developed.

At its height, the trench system stretched nearly 500 miles.  
The front line held the soldiers closest to the enemy.  
They usually stayed there for several days.  
Then they moved back to second-line support trenches.  
After that came third-line reserve trenches.

Farther back were long-range artillery positions.  
Behind the trenches were field hospitals.  
There were also villages across the French and Belgian countryside.

Most soldiers found trench life boring and exhausting.  
There was little to do.  
But death could come at any moment.  
It was often just above the parapet.

Rain fell regularly.  
The trenches filled with mud.  
Soldiers laid wooden planks to walk on.  
Even so, many still became very cold.  
Some suffered hypothermia.

Constant wetness caused trench foot.  
The skin could not dry.  
It split, and sometimes it came off.  
This was intensely painful.  
It was also hard to prevent.

Trenches filled with debris and trash.  
Men lived very close together.  
Disease spread easily in these conditions.

Sometimes, the closeness of the two armies led to rare friendly contact.  
One famous example happened at Christmas in 1914.  
German and British soldiers faced each other from their trenches.  
Some began calling out across no-man’s land.

First one side sang Christmas carols.  
Then the other side sang back.  
After that, soldiers carefully climbed out of their trenches.  
They met in no-man’s land.  
They exchanged cigarettes, candy, and souvenirs.  
Many soldiers reported similar events.

This Christmas truce showed that humanity still existed in the war.  
However, it angered leaders at headquarters.  
They did not allow this kind of friendliness again.

In other regions, armies moved more than they did in the West.  
But mobile fighting had its own problems.

In the Italian Alps, Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces fought in the mountains.  
Soldiers fought at high altitude.  
They had few chances to resupply.  
They sometimes lived in caves.  
They also had to climb steep mountain heights.

Snow fell often.  
Temperatures were below freezing.  
Frostbite was a serious threat.  
Avalanches were also a danger.  
The harsh conditions caused more than half of the casualties in this mountain fighting.  
The narrow Alpine passes also made retreat difficult.

Fighting in the Caucasus began in 1914.  
Russians fought the Ottomans there.  
This front was isolated.  
The Ottomans lacked rail lines to supply operations far from the front.

Snow was many feet deep.  
Temperatures dropped below zero.  
Ottoman troops could not continue because they lacked supplies.  
They suffered tens of thousands of casualties.

In dry regions around the Mediterranean and the Middle East, water was critical.  
Armies had to secure enough water in the desert.  
It was also hard to find enough feed for horses.  
Because of this, especially in the Middle East, troops relied more on camels.  
Camels carried supplies.  
They also sometimes carried people.

Soil erosion is not a widespread problem in West Africa under indigenous farming systems.  
However, it is a long-term problem in some local areas.  
In many places, it could become a serious risk as farming practices change.

Soil erosion is closely linked to water control and desertification.  
For this reason, it is useful to discuss these issues together.  
This chapter also includes a special section on drought in the Sahel region.

## Rainfall and water supply

In much of tropical Africa, yearly rainfall provides less water than most crops would use if they had enough moisture.  
Rainfall is also unreliable.  
It varies by season and from year to year.  
Rainfall is often very intense.

Because of this, conservation must focus on two needs.  
First, farmers must use available moisture efficiently.  
Second, they must reduce damage from intense rain, such as flash floods.

## Plant cover and mulching

Keeping plant cover, using mulch, or using both can help.  
But keeping plants that are not useful only for conservation can waste moisture.  
That moisture could otherwise go to the crop.  
This approach works only where water supply is more or less adequate for the crops being grown.

Mulching with dead plant material is usually not practical.  
Materials like straw, stems, and leaves have other urgent uses.  
People need them for other purposes, so they are not available for mulching.

Artificial mulches can work.  
One example is bitumen-in-water.  
However, these methods are usually not economically or technically possible in the current socio-economic situation.  
This is especially true in the areas where they are most needed.

## Contour ridging and tie-ridging

Contour ridging and tie-ridging can conserve water.  
They also reduce the speed of runoff.  
Using both methods together has proven effective.

These methods offer simple and satisfactory ways to control water use and prevent soil erosion.  
However, soil differences still matter.  
Farmers must take soil type into account.

The importance of these measures is very great.  
They often require major rehabilitation schemes.  
These schemes can include engineering works and afforestation.  
They can also require major changes to traditional farming practices.  
In some cases, they even require changes to settlement patterns and land apportionment.

These changes cost money and require expert skills.  
That money and expertise could otherwise be used to improve agriculture.  
Instead, it may be used to stop the effects of past poor practices.

## Rainfall variability and drought in West Africa and the Sahel

Rainfall variability and prolonged drought have been major environmental problems in Africa.  
In the west, the Sahel has long been known for extreme drought.  
But many West African countries have also faced serious environmental challenges.

For the past thirty years, rainfall has been inconsistent and highly variable.  
This has harmed agriculture.  
Rainfall keeps soil moist and helps soil aeration.  
This supports large-scale agricultural production.

In rice production, rainfall variability has caused changes in output.  
This has happened in countries such as Sierra Leone and Gambia.

The most damaging climate condition for agriculture in West Africa has been drought.  
This drought has continued since the 1960s.  
The 1970s and early 1980s saw the worst conditions.

Drought changed which food crops people could grow.  
It also sharply reduced production of other crops.  
Examples include sorghum, millet, and rice.

### The case of Gambia

In Gambia, farmers said drought affected rainfall negatively.  
In this country and other Sahelian states, rainfall is the main source of irrigation water.

Agricultural production increased in the 1950s and 1960s because rains were favourable.  
But in the late 1960s and early 1970s, rainfall declined.

In southern Gambia, farmers said June rains in the 1970s were lower than in the 1950s.  
They also said the rains in the 1970s lasted only one month.

Rice has been the crop most affected by drought.  
Rice is a major staple in Sierra Leone, Gambia, and many Sahelian states.

In Gambia, about 20–30% of land is converted to upland rice cultivation.  
Rice production has mainly been dominated by women.  
It is a major source of income.

Since the drought began, rice production has fallen to about half of what it used to be.  
This has caused many people to rely on imported rice.

A key problem is reduced rainfall.  
Reduced rainfall also reduces runoff to the main rice-growing lands.  
Rivers have also dried because of the same issue.

### Other affected crops and land pressure

Drought has also affected millet, sorghum, and groundnuts.  
Farming patterns for these crops depend strongly on natural rainfall.

With drought, men have chosen lands that are richer and have more moisture.  
These lands can better support crop growth.  
This has increased land degradation in places such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and Gambia.

Farming closer to water bodies has also increased water pollution.

Since 1968, many years of poor and erratic rainfall have reduced yields.  
It has also reduced seed germination potential.  
Millet and sorghum seeds have been especially affected.

## Ghana and desertification

Ghana, like many tropical countries, is highly vulnerable to climate change and variability.  
About 35% of Ghana’s total land mass is desert.  
Since the 1980s, desertification has increased in the northern part of the country.

Desertification in Ghana is estimated at about 20,000 hectares per year.  
This threatens water resources.

In northern Ghana, farmers grow staple grains.  
These include maize, rice, millet, sorghum, soybean, cowpea, and groundnut.  
They also raise small ruminants such as sheep and goats.
